title: Educators warn AI debate has focused too much on cheating, not enough on student learning
excerpt: First Lady Melania Trump, in a Fox News op-ed, encourages the use of artificial intelligence in education to provide a world-class education for children. David Marchick, Dean of Kogod School of Busin...
body_text:
First Lady Melania Trump, in a Fox News op-ed, encourages the use of artificial intelligence in education to provide a world-class education for children. David Marchick, Dean of Kogod School of Business at American University, discusses integrating AI into their curriculum, stressing AI literacy as crucial for students' future careers. He notes employer demand for AI skills has risen 3.5 times in three years.

As the world scrambles to understand and use generative artificial intelligence in a variety of areas, the discourse about its implementation in higher education often centers around plagiarism and cheating. However, educators who spoke to Fox News Digital warned that the public is missing the point.

They argue that the real issue is determining what students have learned.

"I don't think cheating is the right concept to use here," Georgia Institute of Technology Regents’ Professor and Senior Associate Chair in the School of Interactive Computing Amy Bruckman told Fox News Digital. "I am not commenting on whether I think AI should be in the workplace. I'm simply saying, it seems like it will be, and therefore, banning students from using it at the university level seems like burying your head in the sand."

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

Higher education institutions are grappling with how to approach AI, as some instructors say the focus must be on teaching responsible use rather than catching cheaters. (Hispanolistic via Getty Images)

Bruckman argued that in order for universities to work with students learning in the age of AI, they must redesign what they are teaching in order to help students learn through using AI. However, Bruckman said that rather than taking advantage of technology to further their education, students are "avoiding learning" by using AI.

"Some of the current students are learning absolutely nothing in school," she said.

To understand what their students have actually learned, some professors have resorted to traditional methods of evaluation, such as handwritten exams that eliminate the possibility of relying on AI.

Bruckman told Fox News Digital that she is among the educators returning to analog evaluations by giving closed-book tests on paper to ensure that she is actually seeing what her students know. She said that this model separates students who used AI to complete their assignments without taking in the information from those who actually engaged with the content.

"I think we have to redesign our assessments to be resistant to AI," she said. "To say, 'I don't care whether you used AI or not, I'm going to give you a test that shows whether you learned the content that was part of the learning objectives.'"

CALIFORNIA PROFESSOR ARGUES NEED FOR 'OBJECTIVE MEASURES' AFTER STATE DROPS ACT/SAT REQUIREMENT

As AI becomes more commonplace, some professors have gone back to using handwritten exams to evaluate how much information their students are grasping. (Antonio Guillem via Getty Images)

The Georgia Tech professor is not alone in rethinking how student learning is evaluated. Several educators are not pushing for a ban on AI, but for changes so they can truly evaluate students' understanding of the material.

Generations College Chancellor Dr. Grace Alexis told Fox News Digital that many faculty members initially viewed AI through the lens of potential cheating and plagiarism before realizing that they needed to rethink how to use the revolutionary technology in the classroom. Alexis said that this happened at her own institution and that instructors had not only learned how to use AI, but how to train students to use it in a way that enhances their critical thinking skills.

Alexis argued that the challenge is not simply allowing students to use AI, but ensuring that they do not end up relying on it. She compared it to the way previous generations used encyclopedias, noting that AI could be used to inform students' work without doing it for them.

"It's important for our students to understand that it is OK to use AI in the classroom ... It's really up to the faculty members to not only embrace the technology, but help their students embrace it properly and train them how to do that," she said.

While both educators who spoke to Fox News Digital agree that AI should be incorporated rather than banned outright, they warned that students still need to develop the critical-thinking skills that higher education is meant to cultivate.

"The students in my class fall into two groups," she explained. "The bottom half are definitely losing their critical thinking skills. I would not hire them to feed my cat, and I do not have a cat."

She said the other half of her students are still engaging with the material and are working to learn, adding that "we're not losing everyone, but we're losing a good chunk."

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

Educators say too much of the discourse about AI has focused on plagiarism and cheating, rather than teaching students how to use the technology wisely. (PixelVista via Getty Images)

Despite her concerns about the risks of generative AI use, Bruckman said that she has no interest in becoming an "AI cop." She recognized that despite whatever skepticism higher education has about AI, their students will need to use it when they enter the workforce.

"I don't want to waste my whole semester accusing people of AI use when they're going to need AI in their jobs," she said. "Teaching them appropriate use and redesigning assignments so that they can learn while using whatever tools they have at their disposal, I think, is the only way to go."

Bruckman believes that higher education will eventually adapt to AI, but she remains concerned that students will be lost during the transition.

"We will meet this challenge," she said. "My concern is that we will lose a generation of students in the gap while we're figuring it out."

Rachel Wolf is a media and culture reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Baywatch' star Brandy Ledford shares fitness secrets at 57, says she's 'not ready to hang up my bikini yet'
excerpt: The actress reveals why strength training has become the foundation of her health, confidence and longevity. Ledford also weighs in on the upcoming "Baywatch" reboot and shares her advice for the new ...
body_text:
The actress reveals why strength training has become the foundation of her health, confidence and longevity. Ledford also weighs in on the upcoming "Baywatch" reboot and shares her advice for the new cast.

Brandy Ledford has no problem revealing the secrets behind her youthful glow.

The "Baywatch: Hawaii" alum said her beauty routine boils down to two Bs: "Botox and bleach."

The star, 57, who made hearts race as lifeguard Dawn Masterton, is hosting a luxury wellness retreat for women in September. She is also a creator on Passes, where she shares exclusive content and connects directly with fans.

JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'

"Baywatch: Hawaii" alum Brandy Ledford, now a content creator on Passes, previously spoke to Fox News Digital about her sobriety journey. (Caroline Malouf)

Ledford told Fox News Digital that she has zero qualms about still being recognized as a sex symbol by fans today.

"I love, I mean, I'm a grandmother," she gushed. "I mean, what? That's so great! I think it's so fun. I'm not ready to hang up my bikini yet."

As she has gotten older, Ledford said her fitness philosophy has evolved.

Brandy Ledford doesn't mind being called a sex symbol. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

"My fitness routine these days focuses on strength training more than ever," she said. "When you get to be my age, you need to lift weights for bone density and longevity. My doctor is really stressing weight training using heavier weights for me."

WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH: HAWAII’ ALUM BRANDY LEDFORD REVEALS HER FITNESS SECRETS

"For the last few years, I was pretty addicted to yoga sculpt, a high-intensity yoga workout with light weights. I'm really trying to use much heavier weights now to strengthen my bones and muscles."

"I also still love walking, and I still love yoga," Ledford said. "I love to go on hikes. But I'd say right now, I'm really, really, really focused on serious weight training."

Brandy Ledford still does yoga daily, along with weightlifting, to look and feel her best. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

Ledford's commitment to fitness is not new. Looking back, she said landing "Baywatch" required her to kick one unhealthy habit.

WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH’ STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS FAITH HELPED TRANSFORM HER SOBRIETY JOURNEY

"I'm a really good swimmer," she said. "I'm from the beach, so we grew up swimming in the ocean. But at the time, I was a smoker, and there were stamina tests. They would throw quarters to the bottom of the deep end of the pool, and you'd have to swim down. They wanted to see how long you could hold your breath. It was kind of hard for me at the time, so I quit smoking."

Brandy Ledford gave up smoking after she was cast in "Baywatch." (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

"I did end up getting a lot better at holding my breath underwater and became a lot better at swimming," she added.

Ledford also "hired a trainer immediately" to make sure she always looked swimsuit-ready for every scene.

Brandy Ledford is seen here as Dawn Masterton in "Baywatch: Hawaii." (ZUMA Press Inc./ALAMY)

"He trained me in the water and got me really comfortable working and exercising in the water," she said. "Then I worked out with weights. I also did a lot of workouts in the sand. The sand is an incredible workout. Even walking in the sand is a great workout. And when we got to Hawaii, we worked out at the gym there."

"I just trained a lot," she said. "I really wanted to be comfortable in my swimsuit and not be self-conscious. I think that shows. When you're self-conscious, it shows. So I wanted to feel comfortable, and the only way I knew how was to work out and take care of my body."

Brandy Ledford is a yoga teacher who splits her time between Los Angeles, Vancouver and Kauai. (Caroline Malouf)

"We all made it a priority to get our workouts in and swim in the ocean. Walking from our trailer to the set in the sand was a workout in itself. That was really important to me, and it became part of my lifestyle. I've actually maintained it to this day."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Today, Brandy Ledford is also a wellness advocate. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

Ledford noted she still works out daily to look and feel her best.

"I think health is our greatest wealth," Ledford said. "I really believe that what you feel on the inside is going to come out on the outside. I've been sober for 14 years, and that's been a big life changer. I have a really strong faith in God. Listen, I do all the things, but it starts from the inside. I love really good skincare. I think healthy hair is a big part of it. And I think a beautiful smile is important. I'm always drinking water."

Brandy Ledford and Carmen Electra attend the 33rd Annual Race To Erase MS Gala at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles, Calif., on June 5, 2026. (Getty Images for Race to Erase MS)

The actress said maintaining her appearance involves more than workouts and beauty treatments.

Brandy Ledford told Fox News Digital she continues to lean on her personal relationship with God after getting sober. (Matt Kallish)

"I value what I look like on the outside because I value so much of the work I do on the inside," Ledford said. "I always say I do so much work in my inner life. The second I get up, I'm in prayer and meditation. I want to look as good on the outside as I feel on the inside, so I make it a priority. But I'm just as comfortable with no makeup, sweats, a hoodie and my fluffy slippers."

Ledford said she's feeling so good these days that she's even tempted to pull out her "Baywatch" swimsuit and rock it again.

Brandy Ledford attends the 30th anniversary of "Baywatch" at the Viceroy Hotel in Santa Monica, California, on Sept. 24, 2019. (Presley Ann/Getty Images)

"It's in storage somewhere," she said. "I might pull it out and do a photo shoot in it. It was pretty iconic — yellow — because red is what's known as the 'Baywatch' one-piece. But in 'Baywatch: Hawaii,' we wore yellow because it came from the Australian lifeguards. They wear yellow. It's not an easy color to pull off, but we had so much body makeup on that it all looked good."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Brandy Ledford and Jason Brooks are seen here in Hawaii on June 1, 1999. (ZUMA Press, Inc.)

Ledford said she's excited to check out the new "Baywatch" reboot, which stars Brooks Nader, Shay Mitchell and Livvy Dunne, among others.

"The advice I'd give the ladies to look glamorous and effortless on the beach in all those scenes is to stay hydrated, wear sunscreen, work out and feel comfortable in your body. They're all so beautiful, fit and in great shape. Every one of those girls looks amazing."

Brandy Ledford made her film debut opposite Sylvester Stallone in the 1993 action hit "Demolition Man." (Matt Kallish)

"I think we tend to look back at our younger selves and say, 'I wish I'd known how cute I was. I wish I'd realized I looked good in that bikini.' So just know that you look amazing and let it shine from the inside."

Brandy Ledford attends the premiere of ABC News Studios docuseries "After Baywatch: Moment in the Sun" at The Bungalow on Aug. 26, 2024, in Santa Monica, California. (Variety via Getty Images)

Ledford said she isn't surprised "Baywatch" is still making a splash decades later.

Brandy Ledford attends the 6th Jam For Janie Grammy Awards Viewing Party presented by Live Nation at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles, on Feb. 2, 2025. (Getty Images for Janie's Fund)

"First of all, it's iconic," she said. "It's a fantasy. People got to escape. The men were hot, and the women were beautiful. But there was also drama and really good action. It was just the perfect show. I think we need that in our lives again these days."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Nearly 2,000 ocean rescues occur as dangerous surf slams popular beaches this summer
excerpt:
A 16-year-old lifeguard in Santa Cruz, Calif., Ryder Williams, springs into action to rescue a young boy from powerful surf and rip currents.

A 10-year-old boy was standing in ankle-deep water at a C...
body_text:
A 16-year-old lifeguard in Santa Cruz, Calif., Ryder Williams, springs into action to rescue a young boy from powerful surf and rip currents.

A 10-year-old boy was standing in ankle-deep water at a California beach recently when he lost his footing and was pulled into the ocean by powerful surf.

Ryder Williams, a 16-year-old California State Parks lifeguard, radioed for help and raced into the water at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz during the July 25 emergency, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

The lifeguard's dramatic and widely hailed rescue of the boy — including by President Donald J. Trump, who invited the "heroic young man" and his family to the White House to be recognized — came during a weekend of extremely hazardous conditions along the California coast.

TEXAS TEEN BITTEN BY BARRACUDA IN POPULAR VACATION SPOT AFTER BRACELET GLINTS IN WATER

Hundreds of miles south, Los Angeles County lifeguards performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues as extreme heat sent large crowds to the beaches, according to the Los Angeles County Lifeguard Division.

Water safety experts interviewed by Fox News Digital are urging beachgoers to take extra precautions as elevated surf and strong rip currents continue to affect portions of the Southern California coast, according to the National Weather Service.

Los Angeles County lifeguards performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues over a single weekend this summer. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

The Los Angeles County Lifeguard Division shared the rescue totals in an Instagram post, urging visitors to remain vigilant and speak with an on-duty lifeguard before entering the water.

"In total, @lacolifeguards performed just under 2,000 rescues as millions flocked to Los Angeles County beaches to beat the heat," the Instagram post read.

SHARK WEEK DANGERS HIT HOME AS MAN IS BADLY BITTEN WHILE SAVING PREGNANT FIANCÉE FROM HARM

"With a heat advisory continuing across the Southland and a Southern Hemisphere swell expected to keep surf elevated throughout the week, we encourage everyone to take proper precaution, and talk to a lifeguard about conditions before entering the water," officials said in the post.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Los Angeles County Fire Department, which oversees the Los Angeles County Lifeguard Division, for additional comment.

Experts are urging beachgoers to take extra precautions this summer as elevated surf and strong rip currents are increasing. (Apu Gomes/Getty Images)

Swells from Hurricane Fausto affected Southern California during the rescue weekend and were expected to produce life-threatening surf and rip currents, according to the National Hurricane Center.

A later swell from Tropical Cyclone Genevieve was expected to bring high surf to Los Angeles and Ventura County beaches through Saturday, the National Weather Service said.

ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST MAJOR LINE OVER SURPRISE DAILY GRATUITY HIKE

The agency warned of very strong rip and longshore currents.

The conditions should not be viewed as a one-time event, said Dr. Molly O’Shea, a Detroit-based pediatrician with Goldfish Swim School.

Lifeguard Ryder Williams, 16, is shown battling towering waves while refusing to let go of a child swept into dangerous California surf in Santa Cruz, California on July 25, 2026. The dramatic rescue of the child has captured national attention. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center said El Niño is expected to strengthen.

O’Shea said the El Niño pattern, combined with swells, could produce elevated surf throughout the summer.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"That combination can keep surf elevated on and off for weeks at a time," she told Fox News Digital.

O’Shea recommended that people swim near an open lifeguard tower and ask a lifeguard about the conditions before entering the water.

Also, "if you see someone struggling, don’t swim out after them without something that floats," she added.

"Throw it, don’t go — a lot of rip current deaths are bystanders who tried to help and got caught themselves."

The National Weather Service advises beachgoers to seek out a lifeguard or call 911 when someone is caught in a rip current. A flotation device should be thrown to the person when possible, and would-be rescuers should not enter the water without flotation equipment, according to the agency.

When caught in a rip current, swimmers should remain calm and avoid swimming directly against it, an expert said. (Don Leach/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

When caught in a rip current, swimmers should remain calm and avoid attempting to swim directly against it, O’Shea said.

"Panic makes people swim as hard as they can against it, and that’s exactly backwards — you’ll exhaust yourself before you get anywhere," she said.

"If you see someone struggling, don’t swim out after them without something that floats."

"The move is to relax, swim parallel to the beach until you’re out of the current, then let the waves angle you back in."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Similarly, the National Weather Service advises swimmers caught in a rip current to move parallel to the shoreline until they escape its pull, then swim at an angle toward shore. Those who can't escape should float or tread water and signal for help, according to the agency.

Thomas Gill, president of the United States Lifesaving Association, urged beachgoers not to turn their backs on the ocean.

A lifeguard is shown extending a rescue buoy to a struggling swimmer caught in a strong rip current in Newport Beach, California. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times)

Gill, based in Virginia, told Fox News Digital that swimmers should "not overestimate [their] ability to handle rough conditions."

"The larger surf leads to more opportunity for strong rip currents," he said.

Rescue events, he added, "are not as uncommon as they seem," particularly during periods of dangerous surf.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: Infantino’s FIFA crisis: What is reaction to World Cup investment U-turn?
excerpt:
FIFA President ‌Gianni Infantino has said that world football’s governing ⁠body had ⁠scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup and other events to private investors after widespread backlash.

T...
body_text:
FIFA President ‌Gianni Infantino has said that world football’s governing ⁠body had ⁠scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup and other events to private investors after widespread backlash.

The response to the plan, which was announced on Tuesday by Infantino, was overwhelming.

The wording of the outcry from around the globe was damning of the proposal, but stopped short of directly criticising Infantino.

The reaction to Infantino’s decision late on Friday to scrap the investment scheme, which would have sold minority stakes in World Cups and other FIFA events, ranges from overt votes of no confidence in the FIFA president to more subtle, but equally notable, condemnation of the week’s events.

“UEFA welcomes FIFA’s decision to withdraw its plan to sell a stake in ⁠its competitions – including the World Cup – into private hands,” European football’s governing body said.

“The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.”

“UEFA will begin ⁠work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing FIFA Forward programme.”

“This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal ‌has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.”

“The future of global football must always be shaped through ⁠proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game,” said Sheikh Salman, president of the Asian Football Confederation.

“The AFC stands ready to support any initiative that strengthens the unity of the football family, contributes to ‌the continued growth of the game globally and delivers meaningful benefits to all stakeholders.”

“We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view,” an FA spokesperson wrote on its website.

“We oppose FIFA’s plans – the FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

“With the withdrawal of the proposal, the matter is not settled for the KNVB,” the Dutch statement read.

“The ⁠way this process has unfolded has led to a fundamental breach of trust in the leadership of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has confidence in his leadership.”

“We welcome FIFA’s ⁠decision not to proceed with the proposal. It is in line with our expectations in light of the flawed process and the reactions the proposal ‌has provoked,” Astrom said.

“At the same time, we are still concerned about deficiencies in transparency and governance, and want to emphasize ‌the ‌importance of continued discussion and dialogue about how football should be governed and developed.”

“As a founding member of FIFA and a representative on the FIFA Council, the RBFA remains committed to a strong, independent and sustainable model for international football,” Van Damme said.

“Football has never stood still, nor should it,” Isaac said.

“Throughout its history, our game has evolved through innovation, investment and new ideas that have strengthened football, created greater opportunities for players, ⁠coaches and referees, and enhanced the experience ⁠of supporters around the world. That spirit of progress must continue.

“Some principles, however, should never change. Integrity. Independence. Good governance. Transparency. Meaningful consultation. Due process. ⁠These are not constraints on progress. They are what make lasting progress possible.”

title: WWE SummerSlam 2026 Night 1 preview, predictions and more
excerpt:
WWE women's champion Liv Morgan talks to Fox News Digital about expectations for this year's SummerSlam.

SummerSlam is one of the biggest WWE premium live events of the summer and, for the second str...
body_text:
WWE women's champion Liv Morgan talks to Fox News Digital about expectations for this year's SummerSlam.

SummerSlam is one of the biggest WWE premium live events of the summer and, for the second straight year, the show will be held across two nights starting on Saturday.

This year’s SummerSlam takes place at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis – the home of the NFL’s Minnesota Vikings. The show will begin at 6 p.m. ET on both Saturday and Sunday nights and multiple championships will be defended over the course of the weekend.

WWE fans can watch the show on ESPN Unlimited.

Read below for a preview and prediction for each match.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL

Fallon Henley, Jacy Jayne and Lainey Reid make their way to the ring during SmackDown at Oakland Arena in Oakland, Calif., on July 24, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

It’s the old school going up against the new school in a six-woman tag team match. The Bellas and Paige will take on Fatal Influence. Reid and Henley captured the women’s tag team titles from Brie Bella and Paige at Saturday Night’s Main Event. Now, with Nikki Bella back in the fold, an epic grudge match is set for SummerSlam.

Prediction: Fatal Influence takes care of The Bellas and Paige.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Solo Sikoa speaks during Monday Night RAW at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif., on July 27, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

LA Knight is still among the most popular wrestlers on the WWE roster and for the second time, he finds himself in a six-man tag team match on a major premium live event. Instead of teaming with the Usos, he’s going up against them. Knight, Solo Sikoa and Royce Keys go up against The Bloodline. Jacob Fatu and The Usos’ attempts to bring Sikoa back to the family have proven feeble thus far. Sikoa has made clear he wants no part of The Bloodline. Knight has been at war with The Bloodline for years while Keys has been dragged into the fight. He knows Fatu better than most and is itching for a fight.

Prediction: The Bloodline takes care of Knight, Sikoa and Keys.

Iyo Sky makes her entrance during Monday Night Raw at American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on July 13, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

Liv Morgan told Fox News Digital earlier this year she was "everyone’s dream match." Whether that was true for Iyo Sky has yet to be seen. Morgan gets her first Women’s World Championship title defense against the Queen of the Ring. Sky won the tournament at Night of Champions, defeating Morgan in the final and then choosing her as her target. Morgan has been the champion since defeating Stephanie Vaquer at WrestleMania 42. The question will be whether she has any ring rust going into the match against Sky.

Prediction: Iyo Sky returns to the top of the women’s division.

Nick Aldis attacks GUNTHER during SmackDown at Oakland Arena in Oakland, Calif., on July 24, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

Nick Aldis was a decorated world champion before injuries forced him toward a different role. He hasn’t appeared in in-ring competition since he was with Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA), which was then-called Impact Wrestling. But his feud with Gunther will culminate in his first match in nearly three years. Gunther has continuously accused Aldis of dropping the ball when it came to him and putting him off to the side. Gunther maintains he’s the best superstar on SmackDown but hasn’t been treated like it. It all came to a head at Night of Champions when Gunther attacked Aldis backstage. The two have been fighting ever since and Aldis was given the green light to fight Gunther at SummerSlam.

Prediction: Gunther wins a hard-fought match.

Oba Femi looks on during Monday Night RAW at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif., on July 27, 2026. (WWE)

Oba Femi put off his King of the Ring title opportunity to take on Brock Lesnar in the trilogy fight. Lesnar upped the ante when he said the match would take place in a Hell in a Cell. It’s going to be one of the biggest fights of the weekend and could very well steal the show. Femi could very well slay "The Beast" one final time. Lesnar could prove that he still has it and never lost a step.

Prediction: Femi wins and gets into the world title picture.

Cody Rhodes and CM Punk speak during SmackDown at Resch Center in Green Bay, Wis., on July 31, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

The tension between CM Punk and Cody Rhodes had been palpable even before WrestleMania 42 when the two champions met in the ring on the go-home SmackDown show. While they were more friends than enemies then, things exploded Friday night when the two men finally exchanged blows. Punk became the champion when he knocked off Sami Zayn for the title and ended his reign after nine days. Rhodes was pinned by Zayn and decided to take his own shot at Punk’s title. Their rivalry finally returns to a WWE ring on Saturday night with the Undisputed WWE Championship on the line.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

title: Is Spain being punished?
excerpt: Earlier this week, at least 57 migrants died while trying to cross the border from Morocco into Ceuta, one of two Spanish enclaves located on the African mainland. In a span of just 24 hours, tens of ...
body_text:
Earlier this week, at least 57 migrants died while trying to cross the border from Morocco into Ceuta, one of two Spanish enclaves located on the African mainland. In a span of just 24 hours, tens of thousands of people entered Ceuta in what Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez denounced as a “violation of territorial integrity”.

Many of the migrants interviewed in news reports claimed they had been encouraged to undertake the journey by social media posts.

Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, wasted no time in taking to X to whine that “Spain, which never misses an opportunity to lecture Israel, has declared a state of emergency in Ceuta following the crisis over its immigration policy.”

Indeed, the Sanchez government has been increasingly critical of Israel, labelling it a “genocidal state” and cancelling major arms deals accordingly. In 2024, Spain recognised the State of Palestine.

Now, in the aftermath of the Ceuta episode, Israel – a country where hypocrisy might as well be declared an official state policy – has jumped at the chance to call the Spaniards out for alleged hypocritical behaviour. In his X post, Danon went on to argue that “maybe before [Spain] continues lecturing us, it’s time it explained to the world why it still maintains colonial enclaves in Africa.”

Of course, you can’t get much more hypocritical than complaining about “colonial enclaves” when your own country is perpetrating not only a straight-up genocide of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip but also a brutal colonial occupation that has given way to a de facto annexation of the West Bank.

Then again, Israel has never had a very good command of reason and logic, preferring instead to propagate an inverted reality according to which the Palestinians being slaughtered en masse are the terrorists and the people doing the slaughtering are the victims.

Along with the enclave of Melilla, Ceuta is claimed by Morocco. And unlike Spain, Morocco is in good relations with Israel. In 2020, the country joined the Abraham Accords, becoming the fourth Arab nation to normalise relations with the Israelis through this agreement.

In response to Danon’s tantrum on X, Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente wrote: “Well, everything is getting to be pretty clear” – presumably a reference to current speculations that Israel had a hand in the mass influx of migrants into Ceuta as punishment for Spain’s transgressions, which include opposition to genocide.

The speculation has been fueled by public statements by Israeli officials and by pro-Israel commentators. In an article published in March, former Pentagon official Michael Rubin opined that “Moroccans should gather, send bulldozers to the border, and then enter Ceuta and Melilla unarmed to raise the [Moroccan] flag.”

And in a dispatch for the Israeli Ynet News website, Amine Ayoub – a fellow at the neoconservative Middle East Forum – proposed that Israel should “help Morocco reclaim” Ceuta and Melilla. In Ayoub’s view, the timing for such an operation was particularly ripe on account of the fraught relationship between the US and Spain, with the Spanish government having been annoyingly uncooperative in the US-Israel war on Iran.

When the war was launched in late February, Spain denied the US use of its military bases. The following month, reports emerged that the US had suggested suspending Spain from NATO.

Noting that the Abraham Accords had introduced a “framework for reconfiguring Middle Eastern and North African alliances in ways that serve American and Israeli interests simultaneously,” Ayoub wagered that “helping Morocco recover Ceuta and Melilla would serve that framework and punish a NATO member that has repeatedly chosen obstruction over partnership at the alliance’s most critical juncture.”

In the very last sentence of his intervention, Ayoub arrived at the real reason for Israeli “help” to Morocco: “It is strategic investment in the partner that, across the Strait of Gibraltar, holds the key to one of the world’s most vital maritime chokepoints.”

Whether Israel is indeed involved in this week’s events in Ceuta remains to be seen. But it suffices to recall that the country has never exactly shied away from underhanded meddling in other people’s affairs.

For his part, US President Donald Trump utilised the “invasion” of Ceuta as proof of the Sanchez government’s incompetence – and as a warning of what will happen in the US if the Democrats are voted back into power: “It’s terrible. Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in.”

Israel would no doubt have preferred a slightly different takeaway from the US leader – perhaps one claiming strategic Ceuta to be Moroccan territory. But apparently the urge to engage in xenophobic fearmongering took precedence in Trump’s brain this time around.

And as Israel continues bleating about Spain’s double standards and otherwise striving to shift the focus away from its own colonial atrocities and genocidal policy, it’s safe to say Israeli hypocrisy knows no borders.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja among 11 confirmed dead after avalanche in Pakistan
excerpt:
World-renowned climber had been leading expedition on Broad Peak when avalanche struck

A world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers c...
body_text:
World-renowned climber had been leading expedition on Broad Peak when avalanche struck

A world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.

Nirmal Purja was killed leading an expedition of 10 other people on the world’s 12th-highest mountain when an avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday.

Elite Exped, the company Purja co-founded, said in a statement: “Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak.

“We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive.”

Purja made history in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world’s peaks over 8,000 metres in just over six months. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, in winter.

“Records are made to be broken,” the former Gurkha and UKSF member told the Guardian in 2019. “Someone one day will come along and be stronger. People are only limited by their imagination. If you don’t dream then you won’t do it. Human beings are capable of doing amazing things.”

The expedition included five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said Karrar Haidri, the vice-president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan.

Elite Exped also confirmed the deaths of other expedition members, including his climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta), a Nepali citizen, and Nima Sherpa.

“Our deepest thoughts, prayers and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and loved ones,” the Elite Exped statement said. “No words can erase the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects their privacy as they grieve,”

On Friday, rescuers had said that four bodies had been found and efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Among the victims were Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, and a US climber, Mallory Geis.

Trackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camps two and three on the west ridge of the 8,047-metre mountain, the most popular ascent route.

The British adventurer Bear Grylls said the news of Purja’s death was “heartbreaking for so many climbers around the world who had a relationship with this remarkable and unique man”.

In the 2023 documentary Finding Michael, Purja and Grylls, were enlisted to recover the body of Michael Matthews, the youngest Briton to climb Everest who disappeared on the mountain in 1999.

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of them in the special forces. In 2018, he was awarded an MBE by the queen for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

He also drew plaudits for twice risking his life to help others. The first time was while descending from Annapurna, when he led a rescue of fellow climber Chin Qui Kin, who had been separated from an accompanying expedition and left without food, water or oxygen for 40 hours. He later died in hospital.

Less than a month later, Purja and his team rescued two climbers from a height of 8,400m, sacrificing their own supplementary oxygen to the climbers in need.

“For me it’s not about ego,” he previously told the Guardian. “It’s about principles. You can’t call yourself a climber and not help in that situation.”

title: Bipartisan pair of senators urge Rubio to release aid to African women, children at risk of Ebola
excerpt:
The CDC is coordinating the 'safe withdrawal' of at least six Americans exposed to a deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo after the WHO declared a global health emergency.

Sens. ...
body_text:
The CDC is coordinating the 'safe withdrawal' of at least six Americans exposed to a deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo after the WHO declared a global health emergency.

Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., are urging the State Department to release hundreds of millions of dollars in aid to help women and infants affected by an Ebola outbreak in East Africa.

In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday, the senators urged him to use $608 million in congressionally-approved international family-planning funds and distribute $1.7 million in already purchased family-planning supplies.

The supplies — which the senators implied included condoms, hormonal contraception, post-rape care medicine and hemorrhage medicines — are being stored at a facility in Geel, Belgium, according to the letter.

The senators said that if the supplies aren't used, their understanding is that they will be "destroyed."

Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska and Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., wrote a letter on Thursday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio asking the administration to release congressionally-appropriated funds to help women and infants at risk of contracting Ebola. (Ida Marie Odgaard / Annabelle Gordon)

EBOLA TREATMENT CENTER SET ON FIRE IN CONGO AFTER RESIDENTS CLASH WITH AUTHORITIES OVER VICTIM'S BODY

"Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic material mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging," the lawmakers wrote.

"By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus," they added.

The senators also asked the State Department to issue a "humanitarian exception" to support the United Nations Population Fund's existing health clinics in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Psychologists speak with Nyota Safi, a patient who recovered from Ebola virus disease, at the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Centre in Bunia, Ituri, in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo on July 13, 2026. (Benediction Murhabazi / AFP via Getty Images)

SUDAN'S FORGOTTEN WAR LEAVES MILLIONS HUNGRY AS GLOBAL ATTENTION REMAINS ELSEWHERE

As of July 29, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) had reported 3,532 Ebola cases in the DRC and 1,556 deaths, representing a mortality rate of roughly 44%.

In neighboring Uganda, there have been 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, according to the CDC.

Murkowski and Shaheen told the State Department that the virus's rapid spread "leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives."

Health workers start simulations on admission of suspected cases and evacuation of those deceased during a training by medical charity, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in Kenya on July 10, 2026. (Tony Karumba / AFP via Getty Images)

VACATION HOT SPOT FACES NEW CDC TRAVEL WARNING AS OUTBREAK CASES CONTINUE CLIMBING

"The cost of [the] United States response is approaching $1 billion," they wrote. "Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent."

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio attends the ASEAN Post-Ministerial Conference with U.S. on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay, Metro Manila, Philippines, on July 22, 2026. (Eloisa Lopez/Pool Photo via AP)

The earliest known case in the latest Ebola outbreak involved a health worker in the DRC’s Ituri Province who developed symptoms in late April and later died, though the World Health Organization (WHO) believes transmission may have begun as early as March.

The WHO was first alerted to the outbreak on May 5 after four health workers died within four days. Ten days later, investigators confirmed that the illness was caused by Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Sophie Cunningham sends blunt message to booing, trans flag-waving WNBA crowd after drilling shot

The Sophie Cunningham train rolled on through liberal Portland Friday night, and it didn't slow down for anyone.

And that includes all the boo-birds in the crowd who waved a trans flag every time Sophie touched the ball!

Cunningham and the Indiana Fever took down the Fire, 112-98, but nobody is here for the Xs and Os from the big win. Let's be honest.

STORM CO-OWNER SUSPENDED AFTER INCIDENT WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS AS STAR BREAKS SILENCE ON CONTROVERSY

Instead, you're here to see how Cunningham did ...

Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever looks on during the first half against the Seattle Storm at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle, Wash., on July 28, 2026. (Getty Images)

The left's most-feared athlete finished with 13 points on 4-of-6 shooting, including 3-of-5 from beyond the arc. She finished with the second-highest +/- of any player on the court (+18). Some player named Caitlin Clark led the way with a +23.

Anyway, Cunningham faced a ton of nonsense from the onset, mainly from the crowd. Shockingly, those in California don't seem to agree with her very sane take that men don't belong in women's sports (novel concept), and they greeted her with boos every time she touched the ball.

"Sophie Cunningham knocks down the three and then lets the crowd hear about it!"

That's right. She did. With a big, fat "L" right to their booing faces after drilling the shot. Lordy. What a feeling that must be, especially in a place like Portland.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham reacts after making a three-point basket against the Portland Fire during the first half at Moda Center in Portland, Ore., on July 31, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Side note: How funny is it that Sophie Cunningham's first two games after sending the country into a spiral for saying men don't belong in locker rooms were in SEATTLE and then PORTLAND? The WNBA Gods must just despise her.

Speaking of those Portland fans ... Just look at how they spend their Friday nights:

Imagine buying tickets to a sporting event just to purely go there and wave a trans flag and boo one specific player the entire night. What a life. What a calling.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham reacts to game play against the Portland Fire during the first half at Moda Center in Portland, Ore., on July 31, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Sadly, Cunningham didn't give them much ammo. She missed two shots all night, and the Fever won their fifth straight game.

title: Most Australian teens still online three months after under-16 ban
excerpt: More than eight in 10 Australian teenagers are still using social media, skirting the government’s three-month-old landmark ban on the platforms for under-16s because ‌tech firms have failed to implem...
body_text:
More than eight in 10 Australian teenagers are still using social media, skirting the government’s three-month-old landmark ban on the platforms for under-16s because ‌tech firms have failed to implement effective age checks, the country’s internet regulator has found.

In a study published on Friday, eSafety also found most children aged between 10 and 15 were using social media just as frequently in March as they had before the ban came into force on December 10 last year, while parental awareness of their habits decreased.

“Most under-16s who had social media accounts before commencement were able to either retain them or create new ones at the three-month ⁠mark, with social media platforms’ failure to implement effective age assurance measures cited as the main reason,” eSafety said in a statement.

Australia introduced the world-first ban because of concerns about the effect of social media on the mental and physical health of children and young people. Its implementation is being closely watched by many nations that have since sought to introduce their own curbs.

Before the ban, nearly 86 percent of children surveyed reported using at least one age-restricted platform. Three months later, that figure remained above 81 percent, the report said.

About 58 percent of teenagers reported using social media daily, barely down from roughly 60 percent before the ban, it found.

The report showed minimal change in “sports and physical activity, arts and music, spending time with friends and family, and attendance at community events”.

About half the children who retained their accounts said platforms had not checked their age, the most common reason they were able to stay on the services. Others said their accounts listed them as aged 16 or older or ‌that age-checking ⁠systems had incorrectly determined they were older.

Australia’s government mounted a defence on Saturday of its ban after Andrew Leigh, assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, was confronted with the regulator’s findings.

He argued the ban had already reshaped the national debate. The ban has been “an important game changer in the conversation among parents”, Leigh said in televised remarks.

“We’ve had millions of accounts shut down,” he said.

“We never expected that this would have 100 percent compliance. We don’t get 100 percent compliance out of minimum drinking age laws, but it’s still appropriate that we have that law on the books.”

title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
excerpt:
Nirmal Purja became known internationally following a 2021 Netflix documentary

Renowned mountaineer and former British Army soldier Nirmal Purja is among those killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in...
body_text:
Nirmal Purja became known internationally following a 2021 Netflix documentary

Renowned mountaineer and former British Army soldier Nirmal Purja is among those killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said.

Sharing the news on social media, Elite Expeditions said it confirmed with "profound sadness and immense heartbreak" that Purja had died in Thursday's avalanche.

It also said that none of other nine members of the expedition had survived.

Purja, a Nepali-born climber, was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019.

Pakistani officials had previously announced that the bodies of three climbers from the expedition  - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - had been recovered.

Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said on social media that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

"The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.

Rescue teams in Pakistan had been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit after an avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

The 43-year-old became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

He said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, Purja said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," he wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised that if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

title: D4vd hearing details high hopes and brutal end of girl at heart of murder case
excerpt:
Texts reveal that singer and Celeste Rivas Hernandez had been in touch stretching back to when she was 11 years old

The rising pop singer D4vd and 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez were in the thro...
body_text:
Texts reveal that singer and Celeste Rivas Hernandez had been in touch stretching back to when she was 11 years old

The rising pop singer D4vd and 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez were in the throes of a clandestine relationship months before her mangled and decomposing body turned up last September stuffed in an impounded car registered to the musician.

D4vd, born David Anthony Burke, is set to stand trial for murder, child sexual abuse and mutilation of human remains in connection to the teenager’s death.

Los Angeles county prosecutors accuse Burke of stabbing Celeste to death and subsequently severing her limbs as he sought to prevent her from revealing their sexual relationship, which began when he was 18 and she was 13 in November 2023.

Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The ghastly discovery of Celeste’s remains sent social media sleuths, particularly those in corners of Discord where Burke had carved a niche as an online gamer before pivoting to music, racing through the singer’s past videos and content for any clues concerning his ties to Celeste.

The clearest picture yet of a rocky, off-on relationship emerged during a recent preliminary evidentiary hearing, where prosecutors presented text messages that the two exchanged stretching back to 2022, when Celeste was 11.

At times, Burke regaled the girl with dreams of an idyllic future: her moving into his home, getting married in Italy and having children together.

The fact that she was a minor and had been reported missing by her family, however, cast a shadow over those plans.

“i can’t wait to move in tg without the cops bitching baby,” Burke allegedly wrote in June 2024 to her, Courthouse News reported. Months prior, in February, police officers visited him at a residence in West Hollywood after finding his number in the teenager’s phone log as they sought her whereabouts. When police informed Burke of her age, he shared she told him she was 18.

Texts indicate that he wanted the sexual nature of their relationship to be a secret. She had asked him in July 2024 if anyone knew they had intercourse. “Nope and I would like to keep it that way before we get married,” Burke replied.

Their relationship hit a few rough patches. The teenager expressed a desire for a more serious connection. “All we do is have sex and just hang out man i want more than that for myself,” she reportedly said.

In January 2024, after Celeste had become pregnant with Burke’s child, she had an abortion, which she later regretted. “I don’t like talking about it because it gets me really upset, but I’d do anything to have it back,” she reportedly wrote to Burke in August 2024.

“Let’s end that there,” he replied. “I don’t like talking to u when you’re upset,” adding later that while the abortion “saddened” him, he did not “dwell on it”.

The night before prosecutors say Burke killed Celeste in April 2025, they had a heated argument over text about his relationship with another woman. The teenager allegedly threatened to end his career.

Prosecutors had also presented evidence of Burke having a cushy recording label deal, which they suggested gave him motive to allegedly silence Celeste.

“What was presented by our office over the course of the last week is a small but illustrative fraction of the evidence investigators have accumulated that proves defendant Burke is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of the brutal murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez,” the Los Angeles county district attorney, Nathan J Hochman, said in a statement. “This has been a parent’s worst nightmare, hearing the ghoulish details of how their child was killed, dismembered and left as trash.”

It remains unclear what strategy Burke’s attorneys will employ at trial. They did not reply to a request for comment on the case proceeding forward.

During the preliminary hearing, the defense team cast doubt on a medical examiner ruling Celeste’s death to be a homicide.

Defense attorney Marilyn Bednarski asked Grant Ho, a doctor who performed Celeste’s autopsy, if his report could rule out that the teenager could have been holding an instrument that caused her stab wounds.

Ho said he could not, but that the teenager’s autopsy did not indicate self-harm.

Prosecutors presented forensic testing that found blood probably originating from Celeste in Burke’s former residence.

A second defense attorney, Blair Berk, questioned a Los Angeles police criminalist about why other items in the house were not tested for DNA, noting that multiple people lived in the home.

Burke, who remains in custody without bail, will be arraigned in court on 31 August. His trial date has not been announced.

Hochman said in a Thursday appearance on NewsNation he will confer with Celeste’s family as well as Burke’s lawyers before deciding whether to pursue the death penalty.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Property owner advocacy groups push back on Mamdani's 'Rental Ripoff Report,' public database of landlords
excerpt: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces backlash after rolling out a new ‘Pied-à-Terre’ tax and publishing a searchable database of property owners, raising concerns over privacy, economic impacts an...
body_text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces backlash after rolling out a new ‘Pied-à-Terre’ tax and publishing a searchable database of property owners, raising concerns over privacy, economic impacts and the treatment of homeowners and investors.

Organizations that advocate on behalf of property owners called out New York City’s democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani in blistering statements to Fox News Digital.

Mamdani campaigned on freezing rents for New Yorkers and appears to have delivered on his crackdown on landlords, upsetting local property owners. He recently released a "Rental Ripoff Report," which makes the case that residents in the nation's largest city are paying too much rent while not receiving enough in return and offers 23 proposals to address the issue.

His administration also sparked controversy by publishing a searchable database identifying affluent property owners who could be subject to the city's proposed pied-à-terre tax, a move critics say could expose them to harassment and public safety risks.

The database, released by the city's Department of Finance, allows users to search properties and view the names and addresses of owners whose non-primary residences could be subject to the proposed tax. A spokesperson for the department said publication of the property roll was required by state law.

MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'

Multiple property owner advocacy groups have criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's recent policies. (Barry Williams/New York Daily News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

The Real Estate Board of New York (REBNY) President James Whelan told Fox News Digital that Mamdani was addressing the problem in a counterproductive way.

"The Mayor's report focuses on symptoms, not causes," he said. "New Yorkers are paying record-high rents because there is not enough housing, and many of the reported conditions are concentrated in heavily rent-stabilized buildings that are facing significant operational and financial challenges."

"Rather than addressing these issues directly, the administration continues to paint property owners with a broad brush, unfairly characterizing an entire industry," Whelan continued. "Seven months into this administration, it is time to prioritize policies that will truly make New York more affordable by increasing housing supply and preserving existing housing."

In response to the searchable database, he warned that many smaller property owners will be caught in the crossfire of what he described as a clumsily directed policy.

"By publishing a database of properties that might be subject to this tax before the tax has even been enacted, City Hall has only added to the confusion surrounding this proposal," Whelan said. "What this database really demonstrates is that the second-home tax is far broader and more complicated than its supporters have suggested."

"Policymakers should take a hard look at the many homeowners who could be swept in despite not fitting the profile of the ultra-wealthy residents this tax was supposedly designed to target," he added.

NEW YORK CITY LANDLORDS WARN AMERICAN DREAM IS SLIPPING AWAY UNDER SOCIALIST RENT POLICIES

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's searchable database identifying affluent property owners has drawn widespread criticism. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Ann Korchak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York (SPONY), condemned Mamdani’s influence on politics in a statement to Fox News Digital while discussing his campaign.

"From the start of his mayoral campaign, Mamdani put a target on the backs of property owners," she said. "Small owners are the backbone of the city’s affordable housing stock. We are part of the solution, not the problem, yet he ignores our frontline experience when planning the future of housing."

"Mamdani repeatedly doubles down on making us the villains, using political stunts like ‘rental rip-off hearings’ and using City Administration officials to go door-to-door to organize tenants while on the taxpayer dime," Korchak continued. "They are not tenant organizers, they’re city officials who represent all New Yorkers — including thousands of small owners."

She added that the hearings were cynical political theater.

"The rental rip-off hearings process was no more independent and objective than last month’s Mamdani-appointed Rent Guidelines Board delivering the rent freeze that the Mayor demanded," Korchak said. "These hearings were political theater to make a case against us. The findings were decided before the hearings concluded, just as the rent freeze was predetermined as we learned from the board member who resigned because of the rigged process."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rise is seen as part of a larger shift within the Democratic Party toward the far-left in terms of both cultural and economic policies. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

She went on to warn that Mamdani’s policies will inevitably punish small businesses and immigrants.

"Mamdani’s housing agenda is stacked against us," Korchak told Fox News Digital. "His rent freeze sets us up for failure. The rents are frozen, but our operating costs and expenses — insurance, utilities, energy, repairs, labor — continue to skyrocket."

"Many rent-stabilized buildings are already at the edge of the economic cliff, and when our buildings fall into disrepair because of his policies, Mamdani will illegally take private buildings from mom-and-pop, immigrant, multi-generational owners and convert them into socialized housing or give them to his hand-picked nonprofit housing providers," she added.

Korchak concluded by warning that widespread damage will be done by his policy agenda.

"Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax is another nail in the coffin," she said. "Creating fear and financial pressure on modest, multi-generational owners, who have poured their life savings, sweat equity and heart and soul into their properties, will destroy the fabric of neighborhoods."

"His list is a database that proves he is targeting property ownership as a whole," Korchak added. "No one is safe."

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News’ Amanda Macias, Alec Schemmel, Andrew Mark Miller, and Kiera McDonald contributed to this report.

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

title: Kelsey Grammer admits surprising reason 'Frasier' almost never happened
excerpt:
Kelsey Grammer reflects on starring in "Young Washington" and explains why he believes the Founding Fathers' vision still offers guidance for America's future.

Kelsey Grammer is revealing the surpris...
body_text:
Kelsey Grammer reflects on starring in "Young Washington" and explains why he believes the Founding Fathers' vision still offers guidance for America's future.

Kelsey Grammer is revealing the surprising twist that turned "Frasier" into one of television's most successful sitcoms.

The actor recently appeared on "Planet Tyrus," where he revealed he nearly starred in a different show after "Cheers" before one conversation changed everything.

Grammer spent nine seasons portraying the Boston psychiatrist on "Cheers," where the character evolved from Diane Chambers' love interest to one of the bar's most memorable regulars.

KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS

Kelsey Grammer starred as Dr. Frasier Crane on NBC's "Frasier" for 11 seasons, from 1993 to 2004. (Gale Adler/Paramount)

"It’s funny, I had visions," the star explained. "I’d been offered another show. They said, ‘We want to do a show with you when "Cheers" is over.’ They said, ‘We think you could actually carry a show on your own.’ I said, ‘Great.’ So we actually started doing it with the same writers that ended up on 'Frasier.' We wrote a completely different story, and they wrote a script. I thought it was kind of funny."

Kelsey Grammer as Dr. Frasier Crane and Ted Danson as Sam Malone. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

"I went out for dinner with John Pike, who was the president of Paramount at the time," the 71-year-old shared. "... I said, 'Have you read the script?' He said, 'Yeah. And I think a sitcom should be funny. ... This is what you guys have come up with? I don't like it. I think you should play Frasier.'"

"It was John Pike who said, 'Play Frasier.’"

WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER SHARES THE KEY TO ACHIEVING THE 'AMERICAN DREAM'

"I said, ‘OK, I see what you’re saying. Build an audience. I am kind of funny in the character. He can’t be married anymore, and he can’t have kids,’" Grammer said.

"He did have a son. ... My thing about sitcoms is if there's a child in it, the child growing up every year becomes the most interesting thing about the show. ... Becoming a young woman or becoming a young man is the only really interesting thing that's going on in front of you. So I got rid of that, had him come in once in a while."

From left: Bebe Neuwirth as Dr. Lilith Sternin, Trevor Einhorn as Frederick Gaylord Crane and Kelsey Grammer as Dr. Frasier Crane appear in "The Apparent Trap," episode 9 of "Frasier." (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

Grammer said moving Frasier from Boston to Seattle helped separate the spinoff from "Cheers." It also gave a believable reason why his young son, Frederick, wasn't part of the show full-time instead of making the psychiatrist seem like a "deadbeat dad."

"[I] just had to be a man trying to find his way," said Grammer.

"Whose support payments were on time," Tyrus joked.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Emmy winners Kelsey Grammer and David Hyde Pierce join fellow "Frasier" cast members Jane Leeves, Peri Gilpin, John Mahoney and Dan Butler for a group hug backstage at the 50th Annual Emmy Awards on Sept. 13, 1998, in Los Angeles. (Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images)

"Frasier" premiered on Sept. 16, 1993, and ran for 11 seasons before ending on May 13, 2004. The sitcom won 37 Primetime Emmy Awards and drew 25.2 million viewers for its series finale, becoming one of television's most acclaimed comedies.

In 2023, Grammer reprised his iconic role in the "Frasier" revival on Paramount+, which followed the psychiatrist's return to Boston. The series ran for two seasons before Paramount+ canceled it in 2025.

Noticeably absent from the reboot was John Mahoney, who played Grammer’s on-screen father, Martin Crane. Mahoney died in 2018 at 77.

Actor John Mahoney died on Feb. 4, 2018, at the age of 77. (Margaret C. Norton/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images)

"John was a remarkably fun guy," Grammer told Fox News Digital in 2021. "He was always kind and sweet and lovely. But the ironic thing about him — when I was directing him once on the show, I said, ‘John, let’s put the dog Eddie in your lap.’ And he says, ‘No, no.’ I said, ‘What’s going on?’ ‘He always bites me. He always growls at me. He scares me, and I don’t like it.’ So I thought, ‘Oh, this is weird. I had no idea.’"

Kelsey Grammer attends the "Frasier" SAG Screening Event on Sept. 9, 2024, in West Hollywood. (Randy Shropshire/Getty Images for Paramount+)

"So they had to put a little sardine oil on his hands, so the dog would lick something instead of trying to growl at him or bite him. This love for Eddie that existed on the show really wasn’t real. It was just an on-camera love. They fought each other, and he was really funny about his relationship with the dog."

"... Every time I spoke to him, we just had a great time," Grammer continued. "We spent time in New York together off-screen, and I saw him in Chicago, and I saw him in Ireland once. He was just a wonderful guy."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Pictured from left: Kelsey Grammer as Dr. Frasier Crane, Moose as Eddie, John Mahoney as Martin Crane and David Hyde Pierce as Dr. Niles Crane. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

At the time, Grammer said he was eager for what the future held, both personally and professionally.

"You know what? Life always inspired me," he said. "Life and the variety of experience is what inspires me. People inspire me; I love people. I mean, it’s odd that I ended up on a show that was based in a bar. My favorite places on Earth are bars. I’ve had the best experiences, met the most interesting people in bars around the world. And so, what keeps me going personally is that there is always another experience I haven’t known."

Kelsey Grammer attends a special screening of Paramount+'s "Frasier" Season 2 at Bluma Appel Theatre in Toronto, Ontario, on Sept. 19, 2024. (Mathew Tsang/Getty Images)

"... I'll go right up to the edge before it starts to get dangerous," he joked. "But I love it. I love riding horses, I love shooting guns, I love just exploring all the things that people can do and all the things that a character can do and show you. By virtue of the fact that you've played it, you've actually kind of lived it."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: BROADCAST BIAS: Networks go from hiding Fauci diaries to defending him from Republicans
excerpt:
Description: The CSD thinks the media was wrong, science was wrong, Dr. Fauci was wrong— and, for millions of families and businesses, it will never again be right.

An easy way to demonstrate that th...
body_text:
Description: The CSD thinks the media was wrong, science was wrong, Dr. Fauci was wrong— and, for millions of families and businesses, it will never again be right.

An easy way to demonstrate that the broadcast networks have a deep-seated Democratic Party bias is to evaluate how they cover congressional committee investigations. If a committee is assembled to destroy Republican reputations, everything it does is newsworthy. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s January 6 Committee was Exhibit A. It was "perfect," in that it had no Republican counterweight on it.

If a committee is trying to hold Democrats accountable for government overreach, the networks avoid it like … a deadly bat virus. On July 25, Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul released more than 1,100 pages of COVID-19 czar Dr. Anthony Fauci's personal diary (from his government computer) spanning 2019 to 2022.

Two days later, "CBS Evening News" broke the network silence with a 24-second report. Then there was nothing for another two days until the morning Fauci was scheduled to appear before Paul’s committee.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

It's not like there was nothing newsworthy in Fauci’s diary entries. For example, he admitted early on that COVID did not emerge from the Wuhan wet markets, but he spent 2020 aggressively denouncing the lab-leak thesis as a fringy conspiracy theory – with much media amplification.

Dr. Anthony Fauci had chummy relationships with several members of the press, including CNN anchors Jake Tapper and Dana Bash, according to his newly-publicized diary entries. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images; )

Surely, the entries the networks hated the most were the references to the fawning friendships he developed with TV anchors and hosts. ABC’s George Stephanopoulos texted, "Thank you, Tony, so impressive" after one interview. He recounted a warm conversation with then-NBC anchor Chuck Todd about how to deal with the cantankerous conservative media.

In July 2020, Fauci gushed that he was forming a friendship with CNN’s Jake Tapper. "Had dinner over Jake Tapper and Jen Tapper’s home in DC. Terrific couple. Friendship building," Fauci wrote. Later that month, Fauci wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" Trump adviser and pediatrician Brett Giroir during a very hostile interview on CNN’s "State of the Union."

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

title: Florida mail carrier accused of snatching pets on route, trapping 100-plus cats and dogs in ‘hoarding’ house
excerpt: Bodycam video shows investigators responding to a Florida home where they rescued more than 100 animals from what police said were "deplorable" conditions in a woman’s home. (Martin County Sheriff’s O...
body_text:
Bodycam video shows investigators responding to a Florida home where they rescued more than 100 animals from what police said were "deplorable" conditions in a woman’s home. (Martin County Sheriff’s Office)

The "worst animal hoarding case" a Florida sheriff has ever seen is now expanding as more animals are being recovered.

Some of the rescued animals already have been reunited with owners who said they’d given up hope of ever seeing them again.

Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, was arrested July 20 after authorities found more than 100 animals held in feces-filled cages in her Stuart home. She’d been "collecting cats" she found along her mail route, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said.

Gail Giustino, 77, has been charged with one count of animal cruelty and one count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)

RIDGLAN FARMS RESCUE BEAGLES FIND NEW LIFE HELPING VETERANS OVERCOME WAR TRAUMA WITH PAWS OF WAR

With no air conditioning or ventilation, the home was "probably 110 degrees" on the late July day when the animals were removed, Budensiek said in a news conference on July 20 outside Giustino’s home.

"We were coming out here thinking maybe 15, 20, 30 cats," he told reporters, as people wearing white hazmat suits carried out cages holding dozens of cats and at least a dozen small dogs. There was "a foot of animal feces" in parts of the house, Budensiek said.

Some of the caged cats were held fast in feces that had hardened like concrete. Staffers had to smash bricks of feces from around the cats’ legs to allow them to move, Sarah Fisher, spokeswoman for the Humane Society of Treasure Coast, told Fox News Digital.

"When we cracked the door…the stench was unreal," Budensiek said. "The air was stifling hot." He went on to say, "She never walks the pets. She never brings them outside of the house. They've been confined to that animal jail really for however long she's been hoarding these pets."

Investigators recovered animals from inside the home of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)

PARTNER OF WOMAN KILLED BY DOGS RECENTLY SAVED NEIGHBOR WOUNDED IN SIMILAR ATTACK: COURT RECORDS

Investigators faced an "overwhelming" smell of "animal urine, feces, and ammonia," an odor that wafted outside the house, authorities said. The "deplorable" conditions inside the house left "no safe path of entry due to excessive debris, animal feces, and urine," investigators reported.

The odor inside the residence was so severe that it "presented a potential health hazard to responding personnel," arrest records show.

Since 2014, local animal control had issued "up to 65 civil citations" to Giustino for the conditions she’s kept animals, the sheriff said.

DOG SAVED FROM ISIS BY ARMY VETERAN 'KIDNAPPED' FROM FAMILY YARD BY LOCAL AUTHORITIES

And code enforcement officers helped her add air-conditioning units, Budensiek said. But investigators found that those units were not working. And "we haven’t been out here checking on her for the last 10 years," he said.

Giustino could have been charged with up to 160 counts of animal cruelty, Budensiek said. Instead, she was charged with one misdemeanor count of animal cruelty and one misdemeanor count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. She was released on a $50,000 bond.

"We truly believe that Gail thinks she's doing the right thing," he said. "But she's doing it the wrong way."

Investigators recovered dogs and cats from inside the house of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)

He said, "The goal of arresting her was to be able to seize the animals, to save them from death and try to get them the help that they need."

They also hoped the process would lead to mental health treatment for Giustino, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.

Giustino started working for the U.S. Postal Service in 1997 and is still employed, said Debra Jean Fetterly, a USPS spokesperson for South Florida.

"We are aware of the situation," Fetterly told Fox News Digital. "The Postal Service does not publicly discuss personnel matters."

Days after the arrest, Martin County officials were able to trap and bring in three of four cats that escaped during the rescue effort at Giustino’s home.

And a friend surrendered five more small dogs Giustino allegedly left in her care, Fisher said. By July 29, the humane society had received 108 animals from Giustino’s home.
