title: Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a bout
excerpt:
Tarona Taafaki makes history in women’s 75kg category

All boxers eliminated in semis receive bronze medals

A boxer has made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the tiny Pacific island nation’s first Comm...
body_text:
Tarona Taafaki makes history in women’s 75kg category

All boxers eliminated in semis receive bronze medals

A boxer has made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the tiny Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight.

Twenty-year-old Tarona Taafaki, ⁠one of five entrants in the women’s 75kg category, received a bye to the semi-finals where she lost on an unanimous points decision to India’s Lovlina Borgohain on Friday. At Commonwealth Games, all boxers eliminated in the semis receive bronze medals.

“I’m very proud and very glad to be able to represent my country on this big stage,” said Taafaki, one of only eight athletes and paraathletes from her country in Glasgow. “Probably 95% of the audience don’t know where my country is, so I feel very privileged to represent Tuvalu.”

Badi Taafaki, her coach and father, said the medal would be celebrated by the 10,000 population of the 10square-mile nation – the world’s fourth smallest – and serve to highlight a climate emergency.

“For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything,” he said. “We’re one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it’s a stepping stone.”

Athletes often train on the island’s airport runway as it is its most stable land mass. However, with sea levels rising, climate experts predict half of the nation’s capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050. “Yes, we train on the runway,” said Taafaki. “When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.”

However, Tarona and her brother Pasoni, who also boxed in the Commonwealth Games, are based in New Zealand where the facilities are better. “When I was growing up, boxing barely existed in Tuvalu,” said Badi. “We didn’t have gloves, so we were forced to fight bare-knuckle, and hit bags filled with sand. My children are very fortunate. They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline. It’s where our genealogy comes from.

“If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change. It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades.

“Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can’t sleep if there’s a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes.”

Taafaki is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia’s Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women’s flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her first bout to England’s Lisa Whiteside.

title: Infantino’s World Cup crisis: UEFA has ‘lost confidence’ in FIFA leadership
excerpt:
European football’s governing body UEFA says it has lost confidence in the sport’s global governing body FIFA under its current leadership.

UEFA voted on Thursday to boycott FIFA if it did not withdr...
body_text:
European football’s governing body UEFA says it has lost confidence in the sport’s global governing body FIFA under its current leadership.

UEFA voted on Thursday to boycott FIFA if it did not withdraw its proposal to sell minority shares in World Cups and other events to private investors.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino announced late on Friday that he would be scrapping his FIFA Future Enterprise (FFE) plan following widespread backlash.

UEFA has welcomed that move in a statement on Saturday, but has gone on to detail its criticism of Infantino.

“We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account,” UEFA’s statement read.

“The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.

“When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of FIFA’s member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: ‘Of course we have to be transparent.’

“He told the assembled stakeholders: ‘The money of FIFA is your money. It’s not the money of the FIFA president. You are the national associations and the money of FIFA has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.’

“On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent.”

UEFA added that it wants to work with partners and stakeholders to propose new ways of distributing resources through the existing FIFA Forward Programme.

“UEFA thanks all the fans, leagues, clubs, players, individuals, associations and confederations that opposed the scheme, alongside the many Prime Ministers, Heads of State and commentators who have demonstrated to the FIFA President that football is not for sale,” the statement added.

“We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in FIFA’s bank account to deliver the kick start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of FIFA. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it.

“This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.”

The move by UEFA to clearly criticize Infantino in the statement heaps pressure on the Swiss-Italian’s presidency – a position he has held since 2016.

Elections are scheduled for March 18, when it was expected that Infantino would be re-elected unopposed – as he was in 2019 and in 2023.

A November 18 deadline had been set for any candidates to stand.

It appears unlikely at this stage that Infantino will be unopposed for his final term, but the question will also be raised as to whether he can continue in his role given the weight of criticism.

Earlier on Saturday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) was the first continental governing body to react to FIFA’s scraping of its plans.

In a letter posted on its website AFC’s president, Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, ⁠said he expects “any initiative that has the ⁠potential to impact global football will be presented and discussed with the Confederations, the FIFA Council, Member Associations and other stakeholders in a timely, ⁠transparent and meaningful manner”.

“The future of global football must always be shaped through proper ⁠consultation, collective dialogue and respect for ⁠the established governance structures of our game,” he said.

Sheikh Salman was defeated by Infantino in the 2016 FIFA elections to replace Sepp Blatter as president.

The 60-year-old is likely to be among the frontrunners should a challenge for the presidency form, as will be Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, who is also a member of UEFA’s executive committee and a member of the FIFA Council.

title: Nancy Guthrie sheriff says investigators may have more video evidence as they review thousands of clips
excerpt:
In a wide-ranging interview, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos discusses new developments in the investigation, setbacks, cooperation with the FBI and why he believes the case will be solved.

TUCSON, A...
body_text:
In a wide-ranging interview, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos discusses new developments in the investigation, setbacks, cooperation with the FBI and why he believes the case will be solved.

TUCSON, Ariz. — The sheriff overseeing the investigation into the suspected abduction of Nancy Guthrie has released two purported notes that may have been sent by one of her kidnappers as he urged anyone with information to come forward and appeared confident that investigators remain on the right track — revealing that investigators are reviewing "tens of thousands" of videos.

Saturday marks six months since the 84-year-old mother of "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie was taken from her longtime home in the Catalina Foothills on Feb. 1.

Savannah Guthrie on Saturday shared an emotional Instagram post marking six months since her mother was abducted, saying her family has "lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair" while pleading for anyone with information to come forward. "We will never stop looking for answers," Guthrie wrote, urging anyone who knows something to contact investigators anonymously and help "bring her home."

While there have been no arrests in the case and no suspects have been publicly identified, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos told Fox News Digital he's optimistic that investigators will crack the case.

NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF 'TODAY' HOST'S MOM

Nancy Guthrie disappeared from her Tucson, Arizona home on Sunday, Feb. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of NBC; Fox News)

"We're not even close to these leads being dried up," he said. "We'll continue to work them, and even if they all dried up and we had nothing else to go on, we have a cold case unit."

Google comes up because they were the ones that first came out with the development of that one photo that was released. And it was critical, right? This is who we believe is the guy. It's the only piece of evidence we have that says, here's a picture of him right now. Does that mean other evidence doesn't exist, video or otherwise? No, I think it does. I think it's out there — and maybe we have some of that."

In a wide-ranging interview Thursday, the sheriff discussed new developments in the investigation, setbacks, cooperation with the FBI and why he believes the case will be solved.

Task force members are still going through a large number of video and may have more images of the suspect, the sheriff said.

"We have so many thousands of pieces of video, literally tens of thousands, that what happens daily is the team looks at these videos and really they're just kind of compartmentalizing them," Nanos told Fox News Digital.

Investigators are still examining the video for clues and sorting them in a way that they can be quickly reassessed later if new context or evidence emerges, he said.

NANCY GUTHRIE UPDATE: DNA COULDN'T BE PROFILED FROM CRIME SCENE HAIR SAMPLE, SHERIFF SAYS

Savannah Guthrie and her mother, Nancy Guthrie, are pictured Thursday, June 15, 2023. (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images)

"We take them and, hey — here's a red car. Give me all the red cars; let's compartmentalize them," he said.

That's done because down the line, someone may get arrested in a red car similar to one that police can already place near the crime scene.

"Now we can go back to those videos and say, 'Aha — this is the same red car,'" Nanos said. "That kind of thinking."

He declined to discuss specific evidence, but investigators have previously been seen canvassing the surrounding neighborhoods, major intersections and commercial areas for video that could help in the case. The FBI also removed home security cameras from Guthrie's roof and backyard back in February.

Months after Google and the FBI teamed up for the groundbreaking recovery of Nest doorbell video that shows the only known images of a suspect in the case, Nanos said other major companies around the country are also helping out.

"It may be Google today, it could be, I don't know, pick another large company that says, 'Hey, sheriff, you know, we work at this and I think we might have something that can help there," he said.

Google, which helped recover cached imagery from a backend system, is just one example, he said.

"Google comes up because they were the ones that first came out with the development of that one photo that was released. And it was critical, right? This is who we believe is the guy. It's the only piece of evidence we have that says, here's a picture of him right now. Does that mean other evidence doesn't exist, video or otherwise? No, I think it does. I think it's out there. And maybe we have some of that."

The sheriff said companies have been reaching out with specialized technology and expertise that may help investigators.

"So I like to think that we have some of the best minds in the nation, if not the world, that are trying to solve this case," he said.

Nanos has downplayed suggestions of meaningful friction between his office and the FBI during the investigation, telling Fox News Digital the detectives and FBI agents on the case are working together on a Guthrie task force assembled from members of the long-standing Southern Arizona Violent Crime Task Force.

Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos gives an update on the investigation after the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie on Feb. 5, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

"You have the videos of those first days of press conferences," he said. "Who's standing there with the sheriff? I mean, it's like right after we get done with the crime scenes, we come out, day one or two, whatever it is, there's a press conference. In fact, in the first four days, there's two press conferences. And who's on the stage with the sheriff? Not just the FBI special agent in charge of Tucson, but the special agent and in charge of all of Arizona."

Additionally, he said local members of the FBI's violent crimes task force were called to the scene on day one and described a close, ongoing working relationship between sheriff's detectives and the FBI, with daily coordination between the agencies.

"My team that is assigned to the FBI office here locally, they meet every day with the FBI, with their managers, with my supervisors and command staff," Nanos said.

He said local members of the FBI's joint task force have been part of the case since "day one" and remain involved six months later.

Investigators couldn't obtain a DNA profile from a hair sample recovered inside Nancy Guthrie’s home, Nanos said, but rapid advances in technology mean other evidence could yield new leads. And the hair itself could still be used to compare to a suspect if one is ever identified.

A drone view of Nancy Guthrie's house after the disappearance of the 84-year-old mother of U.S. journalist and television host Savannah Guthrie, who went missing from her home in Tucson, Arizona, U.S., Feb. 5, 2026. (Evan Garcia/Reuters)

"It came back ... there's no DNA," Nanos said. "But does that mean the hair isn't that of the suspect? We won't know that till we have the suspect's hair. You don't just destroy it."

Nanos indicated the hair was only one part of the broader DNA work underway, though he did not specify how many other samples are being tested. Fox News Digital has previously reported that there was also a mixed sample collected from the home, and sources said early on that a cutting from Guthrie's bedding had also been sent to a crime lab.

Deputies examine a flyer taped to Nancy Guthrie's mailbox on Sunday, Feb. 22, 2026. They were called to the scene after volunteer searchers and several streamers walked onto Guthrie's property with a shovel. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"Anything we can grasp onto with DNA is a part of this investigation," he said.

That includes investigative genetic genealogy research, which is used to generate leads from a family tree.

New evidence could quickly turn the focus of investigators back to people who have been previously cleared, the sheriff said.

A member of the Pima County Sheriff's Department stands in front of the front door of the house of Nancy Guthrie, the missing mother of "Today" show host Savannah Guthrie, Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Tucson, Ariz. (Ty ONeil/AP Photo)

NANCY GUTHRIE CASE: SHERIFF SAYS NO ONE IS PERMANENTLY RULED OUT AS DETAINED MAN PREPARES LAWSUIT

"From what we have in front of us, the evidence, the DNA, the whatever, the videos. Yeah, I think you can eliminate them," Nanos told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview Thursday. "And so that elimination happens. But it's like any [criminal case], because you're eliminated doesn't mean you didn't do it. It doesn't mean that we can't get more information."

New evidence could put anyone back in the investigation’s focus, Nanos said.

"I think I early on said, 'Look, there is no suspects. The family is not suspects. They’re not," he told Fox News Digital. "Now, does that mean that ends it forever? No. What happens if next week somebody calls and says, ‘Hey, a family member did this, and here’s how I know it’? You know that always opens a door."

Investigators believe someone may be able to help identify the masked man seen in Guthrie's Nest doorbell video.

"We believe, just as the family does, just as Savannah does, somebody knows something," Nanos said. "We need that person to call us."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

His office also released a pair of notes that may have been sent by one of Guthrie's abductors. While authorities haven't yet confirmed the notes are legitimate — they haven't ruled them out either. And Guthrie's daughter, Savannah Guthrie, has said she believes they may be real.

The sheriff's department said the notes share a "unique linguistic style" and could have been written by the same person. Investigators are asking for the public's help identifying that person.

"As with the unidentified male depicted in the video, we believe these distinctive linguistic characteristics may be recognizable to someone who knows or has interacted with the notes' writer," authorities said. "A friend, family member, coworker, classmate, or acquaintance may recognize these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible."

A source familiar tells Fox News Digital that two photos of the suspect in the Nancy Guthrie doorbell video were taken on different days. (FBI)

Anyone with information is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI or, to remain anonymous, call 520-88-CRIME.

The sum of all rewards in the case is over $1.2 million — none of which has been claimed.

title: DoJ appears to ignore New Mexico deadline for key Epstein ranch files
excerpt:
State attorney general set 31 July deadline for documents relating to abuse of girls at Epstein-owned Zorro ranch

The US Department of Justice (DoJ) appeared to ignore a Friday deadline set by Raúl T...
body_text:
State attorney general set 31 July deadline for documents relating to abuse of girls at Epstein-owned Zorro ranch

The US Department of Justice (DoJ) appeared to ignore a Friday deadline set by Raúl Torrez, the attorney general of New Mexico, to share information about the abuse of girls at a remote ranch formerly owned by the disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Torrez’s office asked the DoJ in February for unredacted files after he reopened a dormant criminal investigation into activities at Zorro ranch, a remote 10,000-acre property in desert scrub outside New Mexico.

It set a 31 July deadline for the department to share relevant records. As it approached on Friday, the justice department did not respond to a request for comment.

The Guardian reported in February that recent releases of the so-called Epstein files included thousands of mentions of the ranch, and numerous photographs of men and young girls there. A succession of survivors had previously given testimony about abuse they were subjected to.

However, unlike other properties prominent in Epstein’s sex-trafficking conspiracy in Palm Beach, New York, and his private Caribbean island, no federal search of the ranch was ever confirmed to have taken place.

Torrez set a deadline of Friday for federal prosecutors from the justice department, and the US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York (SDNY), which led the original Epstein investigation, to allow access to whatever documents they had.

Despite promises of cooperation from Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, and Jay Clayton, former US attorney for the SDNY, now director designate of national intelligence, Torrez said only 31 pages were ever handed over.

They were mostly old news clippings and heavily redacted pages of little use to state investigators, he said.

Torrez said in a 14 July letter to Blanche he would “pursue all available legal remedies without further notice” if the 31 July deadline passed, having made “repeated, documented, good-faith efforts to obtain the unredacted investigative records in the USDOJ’s custody”.

The same week, in an interview with Albuquerque ABC News affiliate KOAT, Torrez said: “I’m not taking anything off the table. I’m not ruling out a lawsuit.”

Epstein died in jail in New York in August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex trafficking charges. The fight for documents relating to his activities at Zorro ranch, which he bought in 1993 from the estate of the Democratic former New Mexico governor Bruce King, became something of a cat and mouse affair after Torrez’s reopening of an inquiry first launched by his predecessor Hector Balderas in February 2019.

According to the attorney general, the southern district of New York called him in July to announce that it would not cooperate.

But Clayton, in his confirmation hearing in the US Senate last month, told Martin Heinrich, Democratic senator for New Mexico: “My folks, I think as we speak, are seeking dialogue with the attorney general to see if we can reach an accommodation”. Clayton noted that the documents were subject to certain “protective orders”, namely redactions to hide the identities of victims.

Blanche, accused in February by Democrats of a “full-blown cover-up” of the Epstein files, told his own confirmation hearing last month that he was “continuing to work” with the New Mexico department of justice.

But Torrez said he had heard nothing further, either from Blanche, or the SDNY.

Meanwhile, the US attorney’s office for the district of New Mexico, in a statement to the Guardian, said it had “substantively responded” to Torrez’s request on 30 June by emailing the 31 documents.

Some, a spokesperson said, were communications directing Torrez to the SDNY. The New Mexico US attorney’s office “did not lead or handle the Zorro Ranch investigation and therefore neither collected nor retained any investigative materials”, the statement said.

Torrez did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on Friday. He told MS Now’s the Briefing with Jen Psaki on 23 July that he was annoyed by months of stonewalling from Blanche, Donald Trump’s pick for attorney general, whose confirmation is in peril.

“It appears that the administration has been really focused on the management of communications around the Epstein case, rather than acting in a way that demonstrates a commitment to getting to the truth and getting to accountability,” said Torrez.

Especially frustrating, he told MS Now, was the conduct of the SDNY after the first, Balderas-ordered investigation was shelved. Torrez said: “We stood down that investigation at the explicit request of the southern district of New York, and so to have them fail to honor their agreement and then not give us access to this file is extremely unusual, and it’s complicating our ability to advance this criminal investigation.”

Blanche “has the authority right now, with the stroke of a pen, to grant us this access, to let us, our investigators and prosecutors, come and take a look at the files, identify co-conspirators, witnesses, corroborating evidence, identify new potential leads,” Torrez added.

“Every day that goes by that that doesn’t happen is another day that we’ve delayed delivering justice for the survivors.”

title: 100 days until midterms and Democrats are winning because they actually have a message
excerpt:
Alexandria Hoff reports on the growing influence of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) as big-name donors back their candidates.

With 100 days until the midterms, one thing has become surpris...
body_text:
Alexandria Hoff reports on the growing influence of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) as big-name donors back their candidates.

With 100 days until the midterms, one thing has become surprisingly clear.

Democrats know exactly what election they want to run.

100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

I’m not talking about policy. Republicans have plenty of issues that resonate with voters.

A grocery store stands along a street in Brooklyn, N.Y., on July 13, 2026. The Urban Institute released new data that found more Americans are using credit cards and other means to cover grocery bills as food prices continue to rise, along with other necessities. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

I’m talking about something much simpler.

LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN

After three decades studying how people make decisions, I’ve learned that people don’t vote issue by issue. They don’t carry around a mental spreadsheet comparing tax policy, border security, energy production and education reform.

They look for one idea that helps them make sense of everything else.

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH

They’ve taken a complicated election and reduced it to one word:

After three decades studying how people make decisions, I’ve learned that people don’t vote issue by issue. They don’t carry around a mental spreadsheet comparing tax policy, border security, energy production and education reform. They simplify.

Whether or not you agree with their solutions isn’t the point. From a communications perspective, they’ve done something incredibly powerful: they’ve given voters a lens.

Every new headline about rising costs reinforces the same story.

That’s what great messaging does. It doesn’t just communicate. It organizes.

Republicans, meanwhile, have no shortage of winning issues.

Those are all important conversations. Many poll extremely well.

But they’re still individual conversations.

Republicans, meanwhile, have no shortage of winning issues.

That’s the difference between having a message and having a menu.

As someone who studies persuasion, I can tell you that clarity almost always wins.

Republicans’ closest thing to a national message is that Democrats have become too extreme. That they’re too far left, too ideological, too willing to let government expand into every part of American life.

That message energizes Republicans. It persuades some independents, too.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has promised a 30% discount on a core basket of groceries at city-backed stores, raising questions from economists about how the savings would be financed. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Most Americans aren’t waking up asking whether Washington has embraced democratic socialism.

They’re asking why groceries still cost so much.

They’re wondering why buying a home feels out of reach.

They’re looking at insurance bills, child care costs and monthly budgets.

Republicans’ closest thing to a national message is that Democrats have become too extreme. That they’re too far left, too ideological, too willing to let government expand into every part of American life.

Democrats have decided that every road leads back to that conversation.

Republicans are still asking voters to connect the dots across half a dozen different conversations.

But with only 100 days left, the biggest advantage Democrats have isn’t necessarily on the issues.

It’s that they’ve decided what the election is about.

And in politics, the party that defines the election usually starts with the upper hand.

The next 100 days won’t simply determine who wins the House or Senate. They’ll determine which story voters carry with them into the voting booth.

Because elections are rarely won by the party with the longest list of arguments.

They’re won by the party that gives people the simplest way to understand the moment they’re living through.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM LEE HARTLEY CARTER

Lee Hartley Carter is a communications strategist and public opinion expert. She's the founder and CEO of Carter Intelligence Group and author of "Persuasion: Convincing Others When Facts Don't Seem to Matter" (TarcherPerigee, September 3, 2019). Follow her on X on @lh_carter.

title: What’s old is new again: Trump-style conservative is back as PM of European nation
excerpt:
Janez Janša secures parliamentary backing and begins a new term in office. (Reuters)

ŠKOFJA LOKA, Slovenia: The Republic of Slovenia, the central European nation known for being the birthplace of Fir...
body_text:
Janez Janša secures parliamentary backing and begins a new term in office. (Reuters)

ŠKOFJA LOKA, Slovenia: The Republic of Slovenia, the central European nation known for being the birthplace of First Lady Melania Trump and LA Lakers star Luka Dončić, is undergoing a radical shift in politics as the country comes to terms with its new larger-than-life prime minister.

Prime Minister Janez Janša recently scraped together a coalition that did away with the country’s leftist leader, Robert Golob.

In what is his fourth term, Janša has begun what many see as Trump-like policy corrections. He has reversed Golob’s anti-Israel policies by announcing his intent to move the Slovenian embassy to Jerusalem, freezing Slovenia’s recognition of a Palestinian state and revoking a 2025 ban on military trade with Israel.

EUROPE'S 'GREEN IDEOLOGY' CLIMATE AGENDA RISKS CRUSHING ITS INDUSTRY, ENVIRONMENT MINISTER WARNS

Right-wing Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) leader Janez Jansa addresses the media after his investiture vote as Slovenia's Prime Minister at the National Assembly in Ljubljana on May 22, 2026.  (Jure Makovec / AFP via Getty Images)

Janša also believes in strong U.S. relations. During an America 250 event hosted by the U.S. Embassy in Ljubljana, and with the First Lady's father, Viktor Knavs, in attendance, Janša described how America was the beacon for Slovenian independence. "We imagined America, the United States of America, as the ideal embodiment of that free world... That Slovenia, too, would become the home of the brave in a land of the free."

Domestically, he says his new government will reverse what he called the Golob government’s "inefficiency" and turn Slovenia into "a country of opportunity, prosperity and justice, where each responsible citizen will feel safe and accepted."

He has announced plans to reverse many anti-business policies, cut government red tape, support private education and healthcare, reform the pension system, decrease the size of government and invest in infrastructure projects, including a plan to build a second reactor at Slovenia’s Krško nuclear power plant.

Despite some policy disagreements, Janša was a close ally of former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. He has expressed support for Ukraine, traveling to Kyiv during his last term as prime minister in March 2022 with the then-Polish and Czech Prime Ministers in an early showing of EU solidarity against the Russian invasion and he recently returned to Kyiv to mark Ukraine Statehood Day as part of the Ukraine–Southeast Europe Summit.

WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED

File: A sign which reads 'Welcome to the Hometown of the First Lady' in Slovenian, is pictured on November 27, 2016 in Sevnica, Slovenia. Born in Slovenia, Melania Trump was raised in the town of Sevnica, by her father, a car salesman, and her mother, a pattern maker at a textile factory. The former model will become the second foreign-born First Lady of the United States when her husband Donald Trump is sworn in as President during a ceremony in Washington DC on January 20, 2017.  ( Jack Taylor/Getty Images)

He supports increased military aid to the country and increased sanctions against Russia. And like Orbán, Janša was staunchly anti-immigrant during the huge Europe migration wave in 2015, when "Balkan Route" migrants practically marched through Slovenia on their way to other parts of Europe.

Janša often praises many of President Trump’s immigration policies. Although no reforms have yet made it through the Slovenian parliament, shortly after taking office, Janša joined 18 other EU leaders in signing a letter calling for "a fundamental change in immigration policy" and practice.

They called for reducing irregular migration, combatting human smuggling more effectively, increasing deportations, and strengthening cooperation with third countries. Janša said Slovenia is "finally joining" other countries calling for these reforms, writing, "The end is approaching for social tourism, overlooked people smuggling and the importation of voters for the European left."

'YOU'RE DESTROYING YOUR COUNTRIES': IS EUROPE FINALLY HEEDING TRUMP'S WARNING ON ILLEGAL IMMIGRATION?

And, like Trump, Janša has his critics. He has been called "the greatest threat to Slovenia's sovereignty and democracy."

An aggressive user of X, where he comments on politics and criticizes his opponents in late night posting sprees, Janša has had battles with the country’s media, with many accusing him of undermining its independence.

Janša has also served time in jail, having been convicted and imprisoned in a case he called politically motivated.

Now serving a fourth non-consecutive term as prime minister— or predsednik vlade—he strangely lost the election that eventually put him back in office in June.

On two occasions, Janša and his party lost an election, yet he still became the prime minister. Think of it as losing the popular vote yet winning the Electoral College.

FILE: Residents of Sevnica, hometown of Melania Trump, wife of Republican presidential elect Donald Trump, hang a US flag as they celebrate the victory of Donald Trump in the race for the White House in Sevnica, Slovenia on November 9, 2016. Republican Donald Trump has won the US presidency with at least 290 electoral votes, securing more than the 270 he needed to succeed Barack Obama.  (Jure Makovec/AFP Via Getty Images)

Slovenes went to the polls on March 22 after a tumultuous four-year term for then-Prime Minister Robert Golob and his far-left coalition partners. Polls that had initially forecast a landslide victory for Janša tightened quickly in the run-up to election day. Golob’s Gibanje Svoboda, or Freedom Movement, party would "win" by taking 29 seats of the 90-seat legislature with 28.7% of the vote. That was a net loss of 12 seats from the 41 seats and 34.5% of the vote the party won in 2022.

Janša’s Slovenska demokratska stranka, or Slovenian Democratic Party, the party he has led since 1993, took 28 seats with 27.9% of the vote. The same 29-28 outcome as in 2008, when Janša also "lost" yet was able to form a governing coalition.

MELANIA TRUMP HELPS REUNITE FIFTH GROUP OF UKRAINIAN, RUSSIAN CHILDREN WITH FAMILIES

After a month of trying, Golob was unable to form a new ruling coalition. Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar said she would not nominate anyone for prime minister as no one was able to get the 46 votes needed in Parliament.

Enter Janša, who many analysts call a master coalition builder. After two weeks of discussions, his future government would end up receiving 51 votes in a secret ballot of the National Assembly: 48 from his coalition and their partners, two from the representatives of the Italian and Hungarian minorities in Slovenia… and, surprisingly, one from an anonymous member of the opposition.

Then Slovenia's opposition leader and nationalist former Prime Minister Janez Jansa and his wife Urska cast their ballots at a polling station during the general election in Arnace on March 22, 2026.  ( Jure Makovec / AFP via Getty Images)

Janša has been involved in Slovenian politics since before there was an independent Slovenia. In 1988, he was arrested, tried "in camera" in a military court, and imprisoned by the Yugoslav People’s Army in what became known as the "JBTZ affair". He was alleged to have shared military documents with journalists. After public outcry at the time, Janša was released after serving six months of an 18-month sentence.

In 1989, Janša helped form the Slovenian Democratic Union, one of the first opposition parties in the then-Socialist Republic of Slovenia. After Slovenia’s first free elections in May 1990, Janša was named minister of defense, helping lead Slovenia’s 10-day war of independence against Yugoslavia in the summer of 1991.

In June 2013, the Ljubljana District Court ruled Janša and two others had sought about €2million (about $2.3 million) from a Finnish firm, Patria, to help it win a 2006 military supply contract. Janša was sentenced to 2 years in the same prison in which he began his 1988 imprisonment. He called the case politically motivated and, again, he was released after serving 6 months. The conviction was unanimously overturned by the Constitutional Court in April 2015.

Janša is expected to come to the U.S. to address the United Nations General Assembly in September. It is not known if he will meet with President Trump and the First Lady.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Brazen social media fraud schemes wreak havoc as Trump official issues stark warning for 'fraudfluencers'
excerpt: The Trump administration's anti-fraud task force has launched a nationwide crackdown on unemployment benefit fraud, beginning in Massachusetts. Officials announced 15 arrests, highlighting the issue o...
body_text:
The Trump administration's anti-fraud task force has launched a nationwide crackdown on unemployment benefit fraud, beginning in Massachusetts. Officials announced 15 arrests, highlighting the issue of illegal immigrants allegedly stealing US citizens' identities to claim SNAP, disability, and Social Security benefits. This initiative aims to aggressively prosecute those stealing from critical programs.

EXCLUSIVE: The rise of a new type of fraudster has a top Trump administration investigator sounding the alarm as new — albeit brazen — schemes for ripping off hard-working American taxpayers emerge.

The Department of Labor (DOL) Inspector General is warning of a growing cottage industry of online scammers, dubbed "fraudfluencers," who boast their skill in exploiting government programs and facilitate fraud on behalf of others. Typically, the scammers take a cut of the fraudulently obtained benefits.

"This isn’t just a crime — it’s a deliberate and public betrayal of every hardworking American who plays by the rules," DOL Inspector General Anthony P. D’Esposito told Fox News Digital. "Fraud is not a trend or content; it’s theft of taxpayer dollars, and it will be prosecuted."

Former Rep. Anthony D'Esposito, R-N.Y., speaks during a news conference announcing the formation of the bipartisan Aviation Safety Caucus outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2024. D'Esposito is now the Department of Labor's Inspector General. (Bonnie Cash/Getty Images)

EXCLUSIVE: WOMAN WHO STOLE $1.7M MEANT FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS GETS PRISON TIME AS DHS CRACKS DOWN ON FEMA FRAUD

In one case, a California Employment Development Department (EDD) contract employee named Britteny Egland openly used her social media to invite others to participate in her schemes. She offered to help her followers take advantage of taxpayer-funded programs they weren't qualified for by using insider information and stolen identities to file fraudulent unemployment insurance, grant and rent relief applications.

Egland had nearly 10,000 followers on Instagram and over 1,500 followers on X at the time of the posts. Her actions exhibit a growing cottage industry of online schemers who brazenly solicit others to team up and commit fraud.

She went on to steal $2.8 million from government coffers.

"NEW OR REGULAR CLAIMS ONLY," a typical post from the fraudfluencer, who used the handle @Britisshh on X, reads. "IF YOU DID PANDEMIC EDD THIS ISN'T FOR YOU! EVEN IF YOU HAVE A REMAINING BALANCE IT WILL NOT WORK."

An advertisement posted online by "fraudfluencer" Britteny Egland soliciting clients to steal from taxpayer-funded programs. (Department of Labor Office of the Inspector General)

EXCLUSIVE: FBI ADDS ALLEGED COVID FRAUDSTER ACCUSED OF TAKING $5M FROM KIDS' MEAL PROGRAM TO MOST WANTED LIST

"IF YOU HAVEN'T DID EDD DURING THAT PERIOD LET'S RUN IT UP. 10-30K," the post continued, before offering for her to "check a claim" for the price of $150.

Egland prompted users to "get with the winning team" by defrauding the U.S. government, but warned potential clients against asking her too many questions because she was unable to address the influx of messages.

"IT'S A LOT OF MONEY ON THE FLOOR! PLEASE DON'T BE STUPID AND MISS OUT," another post from the perpetrator said. "NOBODY WENT TO JAIL OR OWE BACK FOR ANYTHING - LITERALLY - THE WHOLE WORLD IS SCAMMING THE GOVERNMENT AND ALL THESE PROGRAMS."

In a third post, the scammer offered her services in defrauding a $20,000 grant program, saying that she would take $5,000 and give the rest to her client.

An advertisement posted online by "fraudfluencer" Britteny Egland soliciting clients to steal from taxpayer-funded programs. (Department of Labor Office of the Inspector General)

VANCE ANTI-FRAUD TASK FORCE SUSPENDS 447 HOSPICES IN LOS ANGELES OVER MORE THAN $600M IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

The law eventually caught up with Egland. In June 2025, she pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

Egland was sentenced 60 months in federal prison, 36 months of supervised release and ordered to repay the full $2.8 million she stole.

"What makes this increasingly dangerous is the growing effort by fraudsters on social media to glamorize and normalize stealing from their own communities — turning theft into entertainment and betrayal into a lifestyle," said D'Esposito.

"My office, working in close coordination with Vice President Vance’s White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, has zero tolerance for those who cheat the system. We will pursue these cases aggressively, seek prison sentences, and ensure real accountability."

An advertisement posted online by "fraudfluencer" Britteny Egland soliciting clients to steal from taxpayer-funded programs. (Department of Labor Office of the Inspector General)

Investigators are increasingly seeing fraudsters use social media to normalize theft, advertise their methods and build audiences around criminal behavior.

An Atlanta man named Jonathan Dupiton, who had a podcast with the motto "F.R.A.U.D is Dope," was convicted in April and sentenced to seven years in federal prison for using stolen identities to brazenly obtain $3.8 million in fraudulent unemployment insurance benefits from the same California EDD program.

In 2022, a Memphis rapper called "Nuke Bizzle," whose real name is Fontrell Antonio Baines, was sentenced to 77 months in federal prison after exploiting Pandemic Unemployment Assistance provisions from the CARES Act, meant to help struggling Americans during the COVID-19 pandemic.

An advertisement posted online by "fraudfluencer" Britteny Egland soliciting clients to steal from taxpayer-funded programs. (Department of Labor Office of the Inspector General)

Baines bragged about his $788,000 in ill-gotten gains in a music video posted to YouTube.

"The criminal mindset hasn’t changed — only the platform has," said D'Esposito, a former NYPD detective. "I’ve seen criminals make mistakes. Today’s ‘Fraudfluencers’ make those mistakes in high definition. They steal from taxpayers, boast about it on social media, and leave a digital footprint our investigators can follow."

D'Esposito and the White House Fraud Task Force was created, in part, to crack down on taxpayer funds being paid out to fraudsters and to end the widespread abuse of government programs.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Fifa leadership
excerpt:
Gianni Infantino has been the president of Fifa since February 2016

Uefa says it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's Fifa leadership as the fallout from the scrapped controversial investment pl...
body_text:
Gianni Infantino has been the president of Fifa since February 2016

Uefa says it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's Fifa leadership as the fallout from the scrapped controversial investment plan intensifies.

On Saturday, Infantino said Fifa would no longer proceed with the proposal to sell stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors.

Uefa - which governs European football - had earlier voted to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead, and other governing bodies also voiced their opposition.

On Saturday, Uefa said it welcomed the decision to withdraw the plan, describing it as "a victory for the whole game".

It also accused Infantino of failing to deliver on promises, quoting a speech he gave when campaigning to become Fifa president in 2016.

The fallout from the plans means Infantino is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.

"The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," Uefa's statement read.

"When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: 'Of course we have to be transparent.'

"He told the assembled stakeholders: 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'

"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent."

Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

Uefa had been highly critical of the proposals since they were first reported in the media on Tuesday.

In a powerful, lengthy statement released several hours after Fifa announced it had scrapped the plans, Uefa said:

It "cannot keep going on" with "secret schemes of fast-track timescales cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game"

Those responsible for the plan should be identified and held to account

It would devise a plan "with its associations and in close co-operation with other confederations" to make sure this "cannot occur again"

And it would work with partners to "propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing Fifa Forward programme"

It also accused Infantino of "failing to use associations' money for the benefit of the game".

"We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in Fifa's bank account to deliver the kickstart that the grassroots and the wider game need," the statement added.

"But we don't need to sell off the family silver to pay for it.

"This is a victory for the whole game.  But it must not be the end of the story.

"The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in Fifa has only just begun."

Fifa has yet to respond to Uefa's statement.

Any hope Infantino might have had of tiptoeing away from the scene of his World Cup private-investment wreckage having sustained only minor damage to his reputation has been obliterated.

Uefa has gone straight for the Fifa president.

The Asian Football Confederation couched its condemnation of Infantino - and, make no mistake, it is livid - in creative terms.

But Uefa's statement is one of the most ferocious - possibly the most ferocious - ever aimed at the head of world football.

Words such as "shabby" and "secret schemes" speak for themselves.

It is fair to ask why football's powerbrokers didn't step in before now. There have been plenty of instances in the past few months alone when people have felt Fifa's president seemed to be acting against the benefit of the wider game.

Uefa has now taken aim at Infantino with a thunderous barrage of criticism, condemnation and vicious questioning.

The damage to Infantino is severe and it doesn't appear anyone is coming to help.

The proposal - first reported in the media on Tuesday - was met with widespread criticism, with Uefa voting on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.

European football's governing body said the World Cup "cannot be treated as an investment product".

Two other major confederations then spoke out against the plans.

Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

On Friday, Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.

Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors would have been able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it was made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros (£20.5m)per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

In the document, the World Cup was described as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, was said to be "under-monetised".

There was no mention of the women's game.

Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE, had it been approved.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

A report in the New York Post, which broke the story of the Fifa plan withdrawal, quoted an unnamed source saying the situation had become a "brand nightmare" for Kushner.

title: Death toll in Ceuta border crisis rises to 67 as Spanish government announces plans for barrier – Europe live

Tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to the Spanish enclave this week

There has been an update by the Spanish government on the Ceuta border crisis, with officials saying the death toll has risen to 67. The government also announced plans to install a containment barrier extending from the breakwater into the sea to deter further crossings after tens of thousands of migrants entered the Spanish enclave from Morocco this week, AP reported.

In this feature, my colleague Jason Burke reports from Le Porge, where he explores the extraordinary efforts of those on the frontline, from firefighters and soldiers to volunteers, as they fight to contain a “megafire” that has devastated thousands of hectares of land.

Hello, and welcome to our Europe live blog. Nine people have been killed in Ukraine after Russia launched a barrage of missiles and drones at the capital Kyiv overnight, Ukrainian authorities have said.

Twenty-two people were also injured in the attack, which the Russian defence ministry described as a “massive strike” against “Ukrainian military-industrial complex facilities and logistics centres in Kyiv”. Andrii Sybiha, the Ukrainian foreign minister, said Russia was “intensifying its air attacks and terror against civilians”.

It came just two days after an onslaught of Russian missiles killed 10 people and injured more than 50 others across Ukraine, as Moscow looks to exploit Kyiv’s shortage of western-supplied air defence systems.

The scale of the problem was laid bare by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said Kyiv managed to shoot down just one of the 27 ballistic missiles fired in the overnight attack because stocks of interceptor missiles for US Patriot systems had been depleted.

double quotation markOvernight, the Russians launched 35 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, as well as 185 attack drones of various types. Kyiv was the primary target, but strikes also hit the Dnipro, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Poltava regions. Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot systems. And it is this shortage of ballistic missile interceptors that only encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives.

He appealed to allies to urgently supply more Patriot interceptors, saying every additional missile saved lives and that shortages were leading to more civilian casualties.

Yesterday, he said he spoke to the US vice-president, JD Vance, and discussed a meeting with the president, Donald Trump, earlier this week in Washington, which Zelensky described as “positive and productive”.

More than 300 firefighters were battling a fast-moving wildfire near the coastal Greek resort of Porto Germeno, about 45 miles (70km) north-west of Athens, as strong winds continued to fuel the blaze and complicate firefighting efforts. Greek authorities said the fire had spread to the shoreline, with officials confirming to AFP that homes had been damaged. It is one of several wildfires burning across Europe, with France and Spain also battling major outbreaks as extreme heat, prolonged drought and the climate crisis create increasingly fire-prone conditions.

France and Italy have bolstered border controls after about 60,000 people crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco. The crisis has turned increasingly deadly, with at least 57 people killed attempting the crossing, according to reports, prompting Spain to deploy troops to help regain control of the border. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, blamed trafficking gangs for orchestrating the surge, accusing them of exploiting vulnerable migrants by encouraging the dangerous crossings.

title: Knickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless panties isn’t as outrageous as it seems
excerpt:
Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say

The news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Sum...
body_text:
Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say

The news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Summers crotchless knickers on their website has been greeted – as might be expected – with outrage online, being described as everything from “tawdry” to “S & M”.

But it could be this is just the latest evolution in what the UK’s biggest underwear retailer has available for the smalls drawer. In recent years, the store has sold vastly different options through its own products, ranging from full-brief knickers to thongs, period knickers and those that can be used by women who wear stomas. The introduction of other brands in clothing came five years ago, with underwear included. Ann Summers – which is selling bras and chemises as well as knickers on the M&S website – lines up alongside lingerie brands including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein.

Catherine Shuttleworth, the chief executive of retail consultancy Savvy, sees it as part of wider strategy. “They’ve started introducing brands to bring them into sectors that probably isn’t their core,” she says. “And this is another one. It’s just a little bit more eye-catching.”

Shuttleworth describes M&S underwear as a “national obsession” and there’s little doubt the store remains a must-visit for anyone restocking their underwear drawer. If its long-term popularity might have meant it was perceived as a bit mumsy for younger people, that has changed recently. In 2024, the store reported that people under 30 made up a third of underwear sales – double that of 2023.

Shuttleworth says the introduction of Ann Summers could be about continuing to engage this demographic. “They are always innovating for every stage of your life,” she says. “And I think this is a gap in their category. Ann Summers is a byword for sex, isn’t it?”

This echoes the message coming from the retailer itself. In a statement, an M&S spokesperson said: “Our ‘brands at M&S’ strategy is all about giving customers greater choice through carefully selected third-party brands that complement our existing M&S offer. Ann Summers is one of the latest brands to join [M&S online], helping broaden our underwear and nightwear offer.”

There is also, of course, the publicity factor. “It doesn’t really matter whether they sell any crotchless pants or not, we’re all going to be talking about it,” says Shuttleworth. “You might also go online to look. You might not buy those, but you’ll think: ‘I could do with replacing my pants.’”

M&S has sold underwear since the 1920s and fitted bras since 1947. It was the first retailer to sell pre-shrunk cotton underwear in 1965, and by 1976 knickers were the biggest export – nearly 4m pairs were sold internationally every year. Fashion dictated different styles – from the “hip-hugger” styles in the 60s to thongs, which reached the apex of popularity in the mid-00s.

In 2016, the store sold 60m pairs of knickers a year, with Brazilian knickers replacing the thong. The style, which reveals some of the wearer’s bum, made up 10% of those sales. By 2021, thongs were back, thanks to the popularity of low rise jeans. According to the retailer’s website, the No 1 bestseller now is a five-pack of white full briefs.

Lorraine Topper, a researcher at The Underpinnings Museum, argues the reaction around the crotchless knickers is disproportionate – because the store does stock sexier styles along with basics.

“M&S have always followed fashion with regard to their lingerie designs,” she says. “For some reason, it’s the multipack of full briefs that sticks in people’s heads when you talk about their underwear, rather than, for example, the beautiful lace designs from the Rosie Exclusively range.”

She describes the outrage as “a fuss over nothing … Open-crotch underwear for women was the norm before the 1920s so this type of garment isn’t quite as scandalous as we might first think.”

title: WATCH: Booker continues to reject SAVE Act despite bombshell NJ voter roll scandal
excerpt: Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., is arguing that passing the SAVE Act would not have stopped the 6,600 noncitizens in New Jersey from casting votes, calling for proper prosecution to be done at state level. ...
body_text:
Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., is arguing that passing the SAVE Act would not have stopped the 6,600 noncitizens in New Jersey from casting votes, calling for proper prosecution to be done at state level. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital

Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., argued the discovery that roughly 6,600 noncitizens were mistakenly eligible to vote in New Jersey does not justify passing President Donald Trump’s SAVE America Act, insisting the error is unrelated to a lack of federal voter ID requirements.

"Nothing in the SAVE Act would have prevented a clerical error like we've seen in Texas and Oregon and New Jersey," Booker said. "We’ve got to protect our voting systems."

New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced last week that the state removed roughly 6,600 noncitizens from its voter roll who were eligible to vote in the 2024 presidential election. Sherrill blamed the issue on a "serious software error" in New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle System.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS CONFRONT NJ GOVERNOR OVER 6,600 NONCITIZENS REGISTERED TO VOTE IN ALLEGED SOFTWARE FAILURE

Mikie Sherrill, governor of New Jersey, speaks in the Assembly Chamber of the New Jersey State House in Trenton, New Jersey, US, on Tuesday, March 10, 2026. (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The scandal comes to light as Trump has been hounding Senate Republicans to pass the SAVE Act, with some GOP members not in favor of passing the legislation and Democrats overwhelmingly opposing it.

"[The SAVE Act] would stop millions of Americans from voting," Booker said about Trump’s efforts to pass the legislation.

Booker argued that Sherrill and the state are actively looking into what led to noncitizens being eligible to vote, as Sherill said she immediately ordered an investigation and for all noncitizens exposed to be taken off voter rolls upon finding out.

"We take this very seriously in New Jersey," Booker said. "People are stepping up."

DEMOCRATS CONCEDE NJ VOTER-ROLL FAILURE WAS ‘HORRIBLE’ — BUT REJECT BROADER FRAUD FEARS

Sen. Cory Booker joined civil rights and voting rights advocates at a rally outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2025, to reintroduce the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"We have a governor that's saying this is unacceptable. We're gonna make sure that we get to the bottom of it. People need to be held accountable."

Booker has been vehemently against passing the SAVE Act, referring to it as a "massive voter suppression bill." Democrats opposing the legislation argue that requiring all voters to provide in-person citizen documentation will halt millions of Americans from being eligible to vote in elections.

Despite his opposition to the SAVE Act, Booker told Fox News Digital that election requirements "should always have proof of citizenship for voting." But he argued this should be handled at the state level, even in federal elections.

WATCH: ELISSA SLOTKIN SAYS SAVE AMERICA ACT WOULD MAKE IT 'HARD FOR ANY DEMOCRAT' TO WIN AN ELECTION

"The states, as the Constitution says, should handle their voting when there's problems or violations of the law. People should be prosecuted."

There is currently no national standard for identifying or reporting these errors in voting systems, like what was seen in New Jersey. This makes it nearly impossible to truly analyze how widespread the issue is. Republicans in favor of the SAVE Act argue the legislation would help resolve and expose these issues.

"We're going to handle the problems in New Jersey, but I hate how it's being weaponized by some people to advance schemes that actually would hurt Americans," Booker said about the SAVE Act.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: WATCH: Democrats admit when they'd eliminate the filibuster as SAVE Act fight heats up
excerpt: Fox News Digital pressed Democratic and Republican senators on whether they'd eliminate the Senate filibuster as President Donald Trump pushes for its termination to pass the SAVE America Act. (Credit...
body_text:
Fox News Digital pressed Democratic and Republican senators on whether they'd eliminate the Senate filibuster as President Donald Trump pushes for its termination to pass the SAVE America Act. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

As President Donald Trump intensifies his push to eliminate the Senate filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act, lawmakers are exposing familiar fault lines over when the chamber's 60-vote rule should, and shouldn't, apply.

Democratic senators avoided endorsing an outright elimination of the filibuster. Some defended exceptions for certain legislation, with several arguing it should stay in place while Republicans push to pass the SAVE Act through the Senate.

"I would want to know what specific measure it covered," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I'm in favor of eliminating the filibuster for specific measures, not across the board."

TRUMP'S VOTER ID BILL CATCHES UNLIKELY BREAK AS MCCONNELL REMAINS SIDELINED

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., weighs in on eliminating the Senate filibuster as Republicans push to pass the SAVE Act. (Eric Lee/Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"When we wanted the Voting Rights Act passed, I was willing to do it," Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash said.

"It depends on constitutional issues," she said. "If there are people that are overriding the Constitution and not following the Constitution, that would be an area where I would think about [eliminating the filibuster.]"

Democrats previously pushed to create exceptions to the filibuster for legislation including voting rights bills after Republicans repeatedly blocked those measures during President Joe Biden's administration.

As the SAVE Act stalls in the Senate, Trump has repeatedly urged Senate Majority Leader John Thune and other Senate Republicans to eliminate the filibuster to pass the election integrity bill.

"I think we have to be really careful," Sen. Angela Alsobrooks said. "The filibuster is what’s preventing President Trump from his SAVE Act."

Trump took to Truth Social urging Thune not to allow the Senate to leave for August recess until lawmakers either pass the Save Act terminate the filibuster. He also insisted that Senate Democrats would do it to advance their own legislation if they regained the majority.

WATCH: ELISSA SLOTKIN SAYS SAVE AMERICA ACT WOULD MAKE IT 'HARD FOR ANY DEMOCRAT' TO WIN AN ELECTION

Senate Republicans are eyeing a Democratic proposal from years ago to change the Senate's rules to ram President Donald Trump's nominees through Senate Democrats' blockade. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I think that the Democrats would absolutely eliminate the filibuster," Sen. Roger Marshall said. "Every Democrat senator that's here now, that was here when they had the chance, voted to end it."

Marshall explained that his position switched on this, with him now having newfound support for eliminating the filibuster as he claims the Democratic party has become unwilling to cooperate.

"Democrats don't want to cooperate," Marshall said.

He continued, "They want to do everything they can to make life miserable in America, thinking it's going to help them politically. Always putting their political goals ahead of what's best for America."

TRUMP DEMANDS THUNE KEEP SENATE IN SESSION UNTIL SAVE AMERICA ACT PASSES

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., acknowledged the same argument that Thune has defended himself to the president for not passing the SAVE Act: the votes in the upper chamber are not there to remove the filibuster.

"[Trump] knows the votes aren’t there to do what he wants to do, in the way he wants to do it," Kennedy said. "The House has passed a budget resolution to get reconciliation started. We can pass the SAVE Act with the right… the correctly crafted bill."

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is working to craft that bill to pass certain elements of the SAVE Act through the budget reconciliation process — dropping the need for Senate Democrats to vote in favor of the bill to get it passed to Trump.

"There comes a time when you got to stop talking and just vote," Kennedy said.

" I'm ready to vote, and I'm gonna vote yes. And I'll stay here as long into August or September as I need to for us to get our work done."

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: FIFA World Cup plan fallout: AFC reacts as Infantino scraps investment push
excerpt: Asian Football ‌Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa has ⁠welcomed FIFA’s ⁠decision to walk back plans to sell a stake in the World Cup and stressed the need ⁠to discuss ...
body_text:
Asian Football ‌Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa has ⁠welcomed FIFA’s ⁠decision to walk back plans to sell a stake in the World Cup and stressed the need ⁠to discuss all such moves with transparency in the future.

FIFA’s plan was to raise up to $4.2bn by ⁠selling about a 20 percent stake to private investors in a new unit that would run FIFA events, including the World Cup.

The proposal, first announced on Tuesday, had faced a storm of ‌opposition from regional confederations, including the AFC, which said they were blindsided by the announcement.

Following the backlash, FIFA President Gianni Infantino said world football’s governing body had scrapped the plans after listening “carefully to all the views”.

In a letter posted on the AFC’s website on Saturday, Sheikh Salman ⁠said he expects “any initiative that has the ⁠potential to impact global football will be presented and discussed with the Confederations, the FIFA Council, Member Associations and other stakeholders in a timely, ⁠transparent and meaningful manner”.

“The future of global football must always be shaped through proper ⁠consultation, collective dialogue and respect for ⁠the established governance structures of our game,” he said.

On Thursday, Sheikh Salman, in a letter to member associations, had said the way the FIFA proposal had been made was “totally unacceptable“.

The Kuala Lumpur-based AFC is one of FIFA’s six confederations and is responsible for running ‌regional ‌club and national team competitions across continental Asia, the Middle East and Australia.

title: ‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in Westminster
excerpt:
Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds

Parliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as ear...
body_text:
Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds

Parliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as early as midday despite alcohol-related scandals, a report has revealed.

Drinking is commonplace and some MPs have had their stomachs pumped after consuming so much alcohol that they ended up in hospital, one disclosed.

Alcohol is “embedded” in how Westminster works, driven by loneliness among MPs, socialising in order to meet ministers, and drinks being served at daytime and evening events.

Those are the findings of a survey of 190 MPs and their staff which shows that Westminster’s drinking culture endures, despite rising concern and a string of incidents, including an MP’s researcher allegedly having had her drink spiked in Strangers’ bar in parliament and the revelation that the Labour MP Neil Coyle was at one time drinking up to 200 units of alcohol a week – the equivalent of 10 pints a night. The spiking led to a police investigation and the temporary closure of Strangers’ bar.

The report, by the Institute of Alcohol Studies (IAS) thinktank, said: “The findings suggest that Westminster remains a highly unusual workplace where alcohol is embedded in professional life, networking, lobbying and socialising in ways that would be exceptional in most other UK workplaces.

“Participants described alcohol as being available throughout the working day, frequently provided for free, and often intertwined with career advancement.”

Twenty-four MPs, 58 Westminster staff and 108 constituency office personnel shared their experiences and views. One MP, describing how readily available alcohol was at Westminster, said: “Going to a meeting at noon and alcohol’s available. Of course, I’m not used to that in my old job.”

The free alcohol at events on the parliamentary estate, which organisations arrange to help them lobby MPs, emerged as a particular issue.

Another MP said: “Where else in a work environment would you go, unless it was the works Christmas do, and there was free alcohol there for you? It just wouldn’t happen in real life.”

A third said: “You can start drinking here from 12 o’clock onwards and go around and consume large amounts of alcohol, and it’s relatively freely available.”

A fourth described events as a “legitimised opportunity to drink alcohol”, while a fifth said this routine provision of alcohol helps to create a “casual attitude to drinking”.

Hannah Spencer, the Green party MP elected at the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, received a mixed reaction from MPs when in April she labelled Westminster’s drinking culture “unprofessional and worrying” and said it led to cases of “questionable and dangerous behaviour”. She remarked that “you can smell the alcohol when people are in between votes”.

42% of the MPs interviewed had been offered an alcoholic drink at a work meeting or event on a weekly basis during the previous six months; 13% said that occurred daily.

22% had concerns about a colleague’s drinking.

Parliament’s long and unusual working hours, the loneliness many MPs experience being away from home, the pressures of the job and socialising in order to advance their careers can all act as catalysts for drinking.

The report added: “The availability of alcohol was seen to encourage unhealthy behaviour in general, from affecting colleagues’ sleep and stress levels to potentially normalising high-risk drinking, with one MP referring to colleagues having had their stomachs pumped in hospital and going back into Westminster the following day.”

Some MPs said the findings should prompt Westminster to rethink its attitude to alcohol. The Labour MP Cat Smith said: “We wouldn’t accept a surgeon operating after a drink or a driver getting behind the wheel – so why should we accept legislators voting on the laws of the land after one?

“If we’re serious about being a professional workplace, we have to ask hard questions about practices like late night votes that sit alongside on-tap bars.”

Beccy Cooper, who was a public health consultant before entering parliament as a Labour MP in 2024, said the report was a wake-up call. In a foreword to the report, she suggested that parliament should draw up its first formal workplace policy on alcohol.

She added: “Two findings stood out to me. Almost one in 10 respondents reported a negative experience because of someone else’s drinking at work and 70% either didn’t know, or weren’t sure, how to raise a concern about a colleague’s drinking.

“That combination – real, measurable harm and no clear route to address it – is exactly the kind of gap we need to address.”

Katherine Severi, the IAS’s chief executive, said Westminster should limit the provision of free alcohol to evening events as part of a renewed drive to make it a more modern workplace, which many MPs and staff support. “Very few professions these days would allow free alcohol from midday, or regularly host outside organisations sponsoring events where drinking is the norm during working hours,” she added.

The report also said that the commercialisation of parliament as an events venue contributed to MPs’ drinking.

In 2023, parliament’s independent complaints and grievance scheme said alcohol was a “frequent factor” in its investigations into alleged misconduct at Westminster. In its findings of 30 investigations it undertook between 2021 and 2022, it added that drinking in parliament’s array of bars was “leading to intimidating behaviour like shouting and swearing”.

In July 2023, Daniel Greenberg, the parliamentary standards commissioner, said alcohol had led to “behaviour problems” at Westminster and suggested the sale of alcohol on the state be kept under review.

A parliament spokesperson said everyone working there had been reminded to use alcohol responsibly, but hinted that immediate changes were unlikely. “Any changes to parliament’s provision of alcohol would ultimately be a matter for members to decide on. The estate is a unique working environment that includes public access and events,” they said.

“Parliament’s behaviour code makes clear that everyone should be treated with respect at all times, and those who choose to drink alcohol on the estate must do so responsibly.”

Westminster’s efforts to promote more responsible drinking include greater provision of no- and low-alcohol products and venue staff’s right to refuse to serve anyone who is, or looks likely to become, intoxicated.
