title: Trump says US has ‘understanding’ with Israel on Hamas disarmament deal
excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump has claimed that Israel is “very happy” about the newly announced deal with the Palestinian group Hamas, even though the country has yet to agree to its terms.

Fr...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has claimed that Israel is “very happy” about the newly announced deal with the Palestinian group Hamas, even though the country has yet to agree to its terms.

Friday’s statement came as Trump led a cabinet meeting at Maryland’s Camp David, a presidential retreat.

The US president explained that the deal may go through “ups and down” as the situation remains “complex”, but he presented a rosy picture overall.

“We do have an understanding with Israel. Israel’s very happy about it. Israel helped us with it,” Trump said of the agreement.

Hours earlier, Hamas had confirmed it agreed to the first step in a deal to bring Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza to a complete end.

Israel, however, has remained largely silent on the arrangement, which would include Hamas surrendering its weapons to a Palestinian committee in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.

At least one Israeli official, far-right Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, has called the plan “unacceptable to Israel”. He called its provisions “tantamount to agreeing to Hamas organising for the next massacre”.

In an interview with CNN, the Israeli ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, nevertheless maintained that Trump would “absolutely not” be disappointed with Israel’s eventual response.

Still, he, too, questioned details of the agreement, saying Israel would only support a deal that assured that “Hamas will not have the capability to even touch this weapon again.”

Trump, meanwhile, painted a far more positive picture of Israeli sentiment as he spoke to reporters.

“It’s a great breakthrough. Nobody’s ever thought that would be possible to disarm Hamas,” he said.

The preliminary agreement, announced following a meeting of mediators from Egypt, Qatar, Turkiye and the US, could indeed represent a major turn in Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, during which at least 73,341 Palestinians have been killed in the enclave.

Both sides signed a ceasefire agreement as part of a 20-point US-backed plan in October of last year. The future of its full implementation has been unclear amid near-daily Israeli violations. At least 1,214 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire began.

A so-called International Board of Peace has been launched to oversee the deal, with Trump as its chair, and a political organisation called the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza has been appointed to eventually oversee daily administrative operations in the besieged enclave.

But wider questions over Israel’s eventual withdrawal from Gaza, the surrendering of Hamas’s weapons, the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), and a redevelopment plan for Gaza have remained unanswered.

The latest plan also remains on unsteady footing. Under the deal, Hamas is set to prepare an inventory of weapons over 14 days, with extensions possible.

The ISF and a new Palestinian police force would then oversee the transfer of those weapons to a Palestinian National Committee, which will be tasked with storing and monitoring the weapons.

Under the deal, Israeli forces would incrementally withdraw from Gaza during the process. The military has remained in Gaza since the October ceasefire agreement, occupying more than 70 percent of the enclave as it expanded Israel’s “Yellow Line” of control.

Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera correspondent Rosiland Jordan explained that there are no specific deadlines related to Hamas’s transfer of weapons and the withdrawal of Israeli forces.

That process would only begin after the “changing the security situation on the ground”, which itself involves several rounds of Israeli approval.

Earlier this week, the Israeli cabinet initially approved the entry of some ISF forces into Gaza. It will also vet the new police force.

“It has indicated that this change in the security posture or ‘demilitarisation’, as the Board of Peace has called it, will take some time,” Jordan said.

“It’s not going to be until that takes place that you really will see a blossoming, as it were, of a new type of political governance inside Gaza. They don’t want to put a deadline on it, but they say this is the process of how this will take place.”

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Harlan Ullman, the chairman of the Killowen Group advisory firm, cautioned that any agreement remains fragile. Success will be contingent on the response of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces consequential elections in October.

“This is a very fragile agreement. It needs to be nurtured,” he said. “There are many, many aspects that can come apart, but I hope that Trump’s optimism is justified.”

title: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In breaks 73-year record to become longest-running UK No 1 single
excerpt:
Duetting stars surpass record set in 1953, when crooner Frankie Laine hit the top with I Believe

Sam Fender and Olivia Dean have scored the longest running UK No 1 single in history with Rein Me In, ...
body_text:
Duetting stars surpass record set in 1953, when crooner Frankie Laine hit the top with I Believe

Sam Fender and Olivia Dean have scored the longest running UK No 1 single in history with Rein Me In, beating a record that has stood since 1953.

Back then, the UK singles chart had been running for less than a year and contained just 12 songs when I Believe, a bombastic ballad by US crooner Frankie Laine, hit No 1 and spent a total of 18 weeks on the chart.

There have been other songs that have come close to beating him since, such as Bryan Adams’s (Everything I Do) I Do It For You, which spent 16 weeks at the top in 1991, and Wet Wet Wet’s Love is All Around, which had 15 weeks in 1994. Both were gooey power ballads launched off the back of major movie placements – and both prompted just as much exasperation as celebration with every passing week at No 1. More recently, Drake’s One Dance had a 15 week stint at No 1 in 2016, and Ed Sheeran’s Shape of You scored 14 weeks in 2017.

But Fender and Dean have clung on to clock up an amazing 19 weeks at the summit – made all the more impressive by chart rules introduced in recent years to prevent this length of run from ever happening.

On hearing the news, Fender said he was “completely lost for words. Thank you so much to Olivia Dean and the fans for making this song the juggernaut that it is.”

Fender wrote Rein Me In for his album People Watching, which was released in February 2025. He released five other singles from the album prior to Rein Me In, including the title track, which seemed like it would be the biggest hit, reaching No 4 and hanging around the Top 100 for 43 weeks.

That title song is an obvious anthem: high tempo with strident guitars, euphoric synths and a Springsteen-esque sense of grandeur. Rein Me In, on the other hand, is a gentler and less obviously commercial proposition, rooted in Fender’s love of British folk and given a slower, rollicking rhythm. The beautiful music belies a bleak, heart-rending story of someone who spins into alcohol and drugs, “working myself up to a nice warm bliss”, after self-destructively ending a relationship.

“I’m talking about substance abuse and drinking too much to get the reason back, the reason for going through your day,” Fender has said. “It’s loosely based on my own life, this song, but also, I always kind of take parts of my own life and put it into characters and embellish it, ‘cause all good stories deserve embellishment. The ‘rein me in’ part kind of [means] your friends are gonna rein you in from drinking too much and going off the rails because you’re heartbroken and you’re dealing with it in a bad way.”

The song went from album track to hit single after being re-recorded with a new verse by Dean, who has had her own huge solo success in tandem with Rein Me In, thanks to her hit second album, The Art of Loving. Her verse voices the woman who Fender’s protagonist walked away from, singing to him: “You’re so afraid of that heart inside your chest.”

Released in June 2025, the new version of Rein Me In took 36 weeks to reach No 1, and has been on and off the top spot since February, interrupted by short spells from Harry Styles, Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Taylor Swift before wresting the No 1 place back each time. This week, the song held off competition from Shakira and Burna Boy, who remain at No 2 with their official World Cup song, Dai Dai.

Rein Me In has also managed to buck a rule introduced in 2017 called “accelerated decline”, which was created to make more songs flow through the UK charts, sweeping away older ones that had been sticking around. Once a song has been on the charts for 10 weeks, if its streaming numbers drop three weeks in a row, the value of its streams are then halved – generally causing a precipitous drop down the charts, even if it remains popular in real terms.

Rein Me In’s relatively up-and-down, slow burn path to the top has helped it avoid that fate, along with its sheer songwriting quality and emotional impact, which has given it appeal right across the tastes of British pop fans.

Jo Twist, chief executive of the UK music industry’s leading trade association, the British Phonographic Institute (BPI), said: “In an evolving world where we all consume music globally, it’s a truly remarkable feat for Rein Me In to resonate with fans in such a profound way. The British public have taken the song to their hearts, and we should all be proud and celebrate this special moment in our music heritage.”

The duet version of Rein Me In also won song of the year at the 2026 Brit awards.

Adams’s (Everything I Do) I Do It For You still has the longest consecutive run at No 1: its 16 weeks were unbroken, before being dethroned by U2’s The Fly.

There was another British record broken this week on the albums chart, as Charli xcx becomes the first British female artist to have two No 1 albums in the same year. Her new album, Music, Fashion, Film, reached the top just five months after her previous one, her soundtrack to Emerald Fennell’s film adaptation of Wuthering Heights.

When Sam Fender and Olivia Dean launched their re-recorded version of Rein Me In last summer – Dean appearing on stage to perform the song during Fender’s run of British stadium shows – it seems highly unlikely either of them thought they were sitting on a record-breaking single that would still be lodged at No 1 a year later.

Rein Me In certainly doesn’t have the obvious blockbusting qualities of previous long-term chart toppers such as Everything I Do (I Do It for You), Bohemian Rhapsody, or Meat Loaf’s I’d Do Anything For Love (But I Won’t Do That). It’s got a singalong chorus, but even by the standards of Fender’s more anthemic Springsteen-inspired material – Seventeen Going Under or Hypersonic Missiles – it’s understated; a sweet tune with a vaguely country-ish lilt. The guitar part sounds like a banjo and the piano has a metallic “tack” sound, familiar from saloon-bar players in old westerns.

Even so, it’s the kind of track that works well in a climate dominated by streaming. It’s pretty, mellifluous, well-written, and sounds amiable in a way that is at odds with its subject matter. It sits somewhere between genres – a bit folky, a bit rocky, a bit country, plus a hint of soul thanks to Dean’s vocal – and it bears repeated listening because it’s not so striking that anyone would tire of it quickly.

Perhaps its shelf life was extended by the fact that the balance between the two artists who made it has gradually shifted over the last year. In summer 2025, Fender was giving a mid-ranking British singer some stadium-level exposure, but with the release of The Art of Loving – a huge global hit, bolstered by a string of massively successful singles, the billion-streaming Man I Need among them – Dean’s career rocketed. A song that began life very much as Sam Fender featuring Olivia Dean has, over the course of its success, gradually become something else: a collaboration between two huge stars.

title: Mahershala Ali on Marvel’s cursed Blade reboot: ‘If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it’
excerpt:
Two-time Oscar winner was to take on role of vampire-hunting antihero but said project is no longer happening

The two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali has confirmed that his Blade reboot is no longer...
body_text:
Two-time Oscar winner was to take on role of vampire-hunting antihero but said project is no longer happening

The two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali has confirmed that his Blade reboot is no longer going forward.

The star of Moonlight and Green Book had been attached to play Marvel’s vampire-hunting antihero in 2019. The role had originally been played by Wesley Snipes in three films between 1998 and 2004.

The reboot was then trapped in development hell with various directors and screenwriters attached.

“If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it,” Ali said in a new GQ interview.

He later added: “I feel ready to move on from the Blade questions. Those questions are for them. They didn’t want to do it, so they should answer that question.”

His comments come after the Marvel head, Kevin Feige, said he felt like a “gigantic loser” for not getting the project off the ground.

The film was at one stage set to be directed by the Mogul Mowgli film-maker Bassam Tariq. Ali and Tariq have since worked together on the revenge thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which is premiering at this year’s Toronto film festival.

Ali said he “didn’t feel great about the fact that things finished the way that they did” with the Blade reboot. He had provided his voice for the character in a post-credits sequence in 2021’s underperforming Marvel adventure Eternals.

Ali also added on the Blade collapse: “The best way I can answer this question is, when I look at what is for me, is it was either this or that – and I’ll take this. No offence to them. I’ve been doing this professionally for pushing 30 years now, and one thing I’ve learned is that what is for you is for you and what is not is not. For whatever reason, that project is not for me.”

Since winning two best supporting actor Oscars in 2017 and 2019, Ali’s movie roles have included Jurassic World Rebirth and Leave the World Behind as well as providing his voice in the Spider-Verse series. When asked about his lack of other big screen roles since, he said that “some of how quiet I’ve been is not really of my own choosing”.

Ali’s voice will soon be heard in much-anticipated stop-motion animated adventure Wildwood alongside Carey Mulligan and Angela Bassett as well as in the delayed third Spider-Verse adventure.

title: Florida woman’s autopsy report reveals extent of alligator attack
excerpt:
Brittany Clark struggled for her life before dying from brutal injuries in rare attack, autopsy report confirms

A woman who was killed in a rare alligator attack while swimming with her boyfriend in ...
body_text:
Brittany Clark struggled for her life before dying from brutal injuries in rare attack, autopsy report confirms

A woman who was killed in a rare alligator attack while swimming with her boyfriend in Florida struggled for her life before dying from the brutal injuries inflicted on her by the animal, newly released autopsy results confirmed.

The report containing the results of Brittany Clark’s autopsy, published on Thursday, also contained new details about the extent of the 28 June mauling that unfolded in Seminole county’s Little Big Econ state forest.

Clark, 31, and her boyfriend – identified in the 11-page autopsy report as Chance Allison – were swimming in the Econlockhatchee River when an alligator attacked her, local officials had previously said.

Allison desperately tried to free Clark from the alligator’s mouth, according to a Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission (FWC) spokesperson. Nonetheless, the attack led to the “near complete traumatic amputations” of Clark’s left arm at the shoulder as well as her right forearm, the autopsy report said.

The autopsy report also said that Clark had teeth marks from the attack on her left shoulder blade and collarbone.

Clark died from her injuries as emergency responders brought her to a hospital, the FWC had said. The autopsy report noted that it was Allison who identified her body at Orlando regional medical center that same day.

The Orange county associate medical examiner Jenaye Mack subsequently conducted the autopsy and determined Clark died from the multiple blunt force injuries that she received from the alligator. Mack also ruled that Clark’s manner of death was an accident.

The FWC said officials removed two alligators – 12ft and 13ft in length, respectively – from the river and euthanized them. DNA testing conducted on those alligators linked the longer of that pair to Clark, the FWC later announced.

Alligator attacks on humans are rare in Florida, according to the FWC, which compiles reports of encounters with the state’s estimated 1.3 million gators. The agency in 2022 reported an average of about eight unprovoked alligator bites annually – and only 26 fatalities from those attacks since 1948.

Clark’s online obituary said she financially supported herself by working as a heavy construction equipment operator, and she had attained the role of foreman before her death.

“She was ready to settle down, start her own family and begin new adventures,” the obituary added.

Clark’s survivors included her parents and two siblings, according to the obituary. A celebration of life honoring her was scheduled for 26 July at a ranch in Geneva, Florida.

title: Trump blasts Spain migrant surge as 'catastrophe,' warns US could face worse if Democrats regain power
excerpt:
President Donald Trump pointed to the situation in Spain as a warning about illegal immigration, saying the U.S. would face an even larger influx if Republicans lose the midterm elections.

President ...
body_text:
President Donald Trump pointed to the situation in Spain as a warning about illegal immigration, saying the U.S. would face an even larger influx if Republicans lose the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump said Friday during a Cabinet meeting that scenes of migrants flooding into Spain's enclave of Ceuta from Morocco looked like a "catastrophe," but that the U.S. could see worse in the future if Democrats regain power.

"You know, I saw Spain yesterday, and I watched the catastrophe that took place. It looks like an invasion of a country by hundreds of thousands of people. And that same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don't get elected," Trump said Friday at Camp David. "Except worse, much bigger, much easier to get into. Despite the fact that we have built thousands of miles of wall, which I said we were going to do. But if we didn't have that, forget it. But we have the safest border in the world. If we're not in office, our country will be invaded at levels that made Spain look small time."

"And when I watched it, I said, boy, I said, ‘I'm going to say it because I knew you were going to be at Camp David.’ And I say, ‘That's going to be a talking point for the midterms, because when you look at what happened to Spain, they don't know what to do.’ And it's happening again today," the president continued. "They're coming in by the tens of thousands. It’s just invading the country. And what that is weak law, bad management, but very liberal law. They passed a couple of laws and people read, you know, people are smart. They read from other countries, and they swam that 3-mile swim or however they got in."

"But nobody's seen anything like it. That will look good compared to what's going to happen to the United States," Trump also said. "The biggest thing, the worst thing that Biden did is allowing 25 million people into our country, because many of those people are criminals. They're murderers," Trump also said. "A lot of them are gone now. We got them out. But they allowed people to come into this country that you can't allow to come into a country."

WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED

President Donald Trump, center, joined by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, left, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, listens during a Cabinet meeting, on Friday, July 31, 2026, at Camp David. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

Trump made similar comments to Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich earlier Friday morning.

"It’s terrible. Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in," Trump said.

"If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life," he warned.

U.S. border security has remained a key plank of the president's campaign and policy focus throughout his political career.

An English translation of a Friday Spanish-language post on X from Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said, "The Government will guarantee the safety of the residents of Ceuta, intensifying the presence of the Security Forces and Corps on the city's streets." The post also included a video of him delivering remarks in Spanish.

FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY

Map depicting Spain, Morocco, and Spain's Cueta, which borders Morocco. (2026 EarthStar Geographics, OpenMapTiles, OpenStreetMap contributors)

Ceuta, which is located along the northwestern African coast and borders Morocco, is not attached to mainland Spain.

"Additionally, we will deploy a physical containment barrier in the sea to facilitate repatriation at the border, in compliance with the Supreme Court ruling. We will expedite the repatriation files of the migrants who arrived irregularly. And we will maintain cooperation with the Moroccan authorities to continue fighting against the mafias that traffic in human beings," the prime minister's post added.

Around 60,000 migrants had ventured from Morocco to Ceuta over the past 24 hours, Cueta President Juan Jesús Vivas said on Friday.

SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD

Spain's interior ministry issued its own figures not long after Vivas spoke, estimating that some 50,000 individuals came from Morocco since Thursday, adding that half had already gone back to Morocco.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: WATCH: Fauci walks away when pressed on Fifth Amendment, pandemic regrets
excerpt: Dr. Anthony Fauci was confronted outside his home with questions on potential regret pleading the Fifth 111 times in his Senate hearing, and his handling of COVID-19 policies. (Credit: Nicholas Ballas...
body_text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci was confronted outside his home with questions on potential regret pleading the Fifth 111 times in his Senate hearing, and his handling of COVID-19 policies. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Dr. Anthony Fauci declined to answer Fox News Digital's questions outside his home Thursday, walking away when asked whether he regretted pleading the Fifth Amendment during a contentious Senate hearing or his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Do you regret the way you handled the hearing, pleading the Fifth so much?" Fox News Digital asked Fauci.

Fauci’s silence came one day after he declined, on the advice of his attorneys, to answer questions before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and medical advisor to several U.S. presidents, testifies under subpoena about his role in the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a U.S. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., July 29, 2026. (REUTERS/Nathan Howard)

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said in his opening statement.

The former White House COVID adviser was questioned over his response to the pandemic and his policy decisions, and was accused of funding gain-of-function research in Wuhan, China.

Paul argues Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth Amendment was unsupported because Biden pardoned him and said the committee will vote next week on a resolution to hold him in contempt of Congress.

CAN FAUCI HIDE BEHIND THE FIFTH? GAME-CHANGING BIDEN PARDON MAY NOT PROVIDE COMPLETE COVER, EXPERTS SAY

Sen. Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky and chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, speaks during a hearing in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Anthony Fauci declined to testify in a Senate committee hearing on his role in the US response to COVID-19, invoking his 5th Amendment rights. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"The Fifth Amendment is to claim immunity from self-incrimination," Paul said on "The Will Cain Show" on Wednesday. "But if you've already been given immunity, you can't self-incriminate unless you lie."

Fauci also stayed silent when asked if he regrets the decisions he made as the public’s health leader during the pandemic.

"Is there anything you would do different on COVID sir?" Fox News Digital asked after Fauci refused to answer questions about his Senate hearing.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Dr. Anthony Fauci walks away after Fox News Digital questioned him outside his home over pleading the Fifth during his Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Senate hearing on Wednesday. (Nicholas Ballasy/Fox News Digital)

Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era diary entries before the hearing, arguing they revealed discrepancies between Fauci’s private notes and public statements.

One entry documented an early discussion in which several scientists considered whether features of the virus could have been deliberately inserted. Fauci subsequently publicly favored a natural origin.

Fauci also said publicly that he was not responsible for rallying schools to shut down during the pandemic. But he wrote in his diary that he influenced both New York and California government officials to lock down their state’s school systems.

Paul, with the support of other GOP senators, has announced that he is seeking contempt charges against Fauci following his refusal to answer questions in Wednesday’s hearing.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker guarantees Democratic nominee in 2028 will be anti-Israel

body_text:
Far-left streaming personality Hasan Piker predicted in an interview with CNN's Donie O'Sullivan that there was a 0% chance the Democratic Party's 2028 candidate will be pro-Israel.

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said there was a 0% chance the Democratic nominee would be pro-Israel in an interview posted Thursday.

CNN's Donie O'Sullivan asked Piker if he would endorse the Democratic candidate in 2028 if they are pro-Israel in a way that he disagrees with, if he's focused on "defeating fascism" in America.

"Surely shouldn't you get on board with whoever the main candidate is?" O'Sullivan asked.

FETTERMAN CALLS ZOHRAN MAMDANI A 'CLOWN' OVER PUSH TO ARREST NETANYAHU IN NEW YORK CITY

"Luckily, I don't think I'll have to make that calculation at all because there is 0% chance that whoever the elected Democrat is that wins the primary will be pro-Israel in any way, shape or form. You'll see," Piker responded.

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker is facing renewed scrutiny after viewers spotted a framed newspaper front page from Sept. 12, 2001, in his background. (Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

The far-left streaming personality was recently asked about his preferred candidate for Democrats in 2028.

When asked to choose between Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., as his preferred candidate, Piker immediately selected the New York congresswoman.

Polling has shown support for Israel collapse among Democrats, and far-left candidates have won primaries across the country this year with anti-Israel platforms.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

"AOC. It's not even a question," Piker said during a Zeteo interview.

Piker made the choice at the end of a rapid-fire exercise that began with California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel. The list later included former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Khanna.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, speaks to members of the media following a vote at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Piker has come under renewed scrutiny over a recent addition to his visual background during his streams.

ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

Viewers noticed what appeared to be a framed copy of the front page of a newspaper with an image of the Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the Twin Towers in New York City.

The earliest livestream reviewed by Fox News Digital showing the newspaper in the background was broadcast on July 13. The front page appears to be The New York Times' Sept. 12, 2001, edition, which was headlined, "U.S. Attacked: Hijacked Jets Destroy Twin Towers and Hit Pentagon in Day of Terror." The X account DSA Watch posted a clip of Piker's stream, where he discussed the newspaper front page framed on the wall behind him.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"You might have noticed something, some changes behind me. I finally framed the cutie Cinderella newspaper from 9/11, the morning of 9/12… the newspaper that covered 9/11. It's now officially sitting behind me," he told viewers earlier this month.

Hasan Piker, a streamer and creator, appears during day two of Web Summit Vancouver 2026 at the Vancouver Convention Centre in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, on May 13, 2026. (Sportsfile via Getty Images)

Piker was widely criticized after saying that "America deserved 9/11" during a stream in 2019. After facing immense backlash, Piker said in an interview that he "obviously" did not mean that America deserved the attacks and accused critics of disregarding "the actual truth of what I was talking about," explaining the viral quote as a critique of U.S. foreign policy.

Fox News' Rachel Wolf contributed to this report.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

title: Bryan Kohberger claims family joined plea talks as he seeks to withdraw guilty plea: court docs
excerpt: A judge approved Bryan Kohberger's request for a new lawyer in his attempt to secure a new trial, despite his previous guilty plea for murdering four University of Idaho students in 2022. Legal analys...
body_text:
A judge approved Bryan Kohberger's request for a new lawyer in his attempt to secure a new trial, despite his previous guilty plea for murdering four University of Idaho students in 2022. Legal analyst Mehek Cooke discusses the high bar for overturning a guilty plea, while the victim's family expresses the pain of reliving the tragedy.

Bryan Kohberger says his family was involved in plea discussions as he seeks to undo his guilty plea, newly released court documents obtained by Fox News Digital reveal.

The convicted killer, who pleaded guilty to stabbing and killing four University of Idaho students in 2022, recently filed a petition for post-conviction relief seeking to withdraw the guilty plea he entered last year in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty.

In his handwritten petition filed on Monday, he wrote that "members of Kohberger's immediate family" were present during attorney-client discussions.

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER SAYS FAMILY READY FOR TRIAL AFTER BRYAN KOHBERGER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

Kohberger claims that he was "convinced to falsely confess," claiming his high-profile defense team of Anne Taylor, Elisa Massoth and Bicka Barlow didn't tell him about "exculpatory discovery" — evidence mentioned in the recent "Broken Plea" book but never vetted in court.

IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

In a message to the New York Times, Kohberger claimed that "justice was not served" and that it was "circumnavigated by a broken plea."

Bryan Christopher Kohberger is seen in a booking photo after his arrest on Dec. 30, 2022, in Pennsylvania. (Monroe County Correctional Facility via Getty Images)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Broken Plea" is the title of a recent book about the case that shed new light on what the defense may have looked like at trial — and his use of the term surprised author Chris Whitcomb, who says he had never spoken to Kohberger.

Whitcomb told "Crime & Justice" podcast host Donna Rotunno on Thursday he has never communicated with Kohberger or any member of his family, and Whitcomb has no information on whether Kohberger or any of his family members read the book.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

As for his petition, Kohberger claims his attorneys misrepresented what Idaho’s death row would be like.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

He alleges one attorney told an elaborate story about personally "touring an actual 8-foot-by-8-foot death-row cell," which Kohberger said was "fabricated."

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S MOTHER CALLED HIM 'MY ANGEL' AND INSISTED POLICE MADE A 'REALLY, REALLY BAD MISTAKE': BOOK

People leave the Ada County Courthouse after the Bryan Kohberger sentencing Wednesday, July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (Drew Nash/AP Photo)

He said this information was communicated to him and his family and was used to frighten or pressure him into accepting the plea deal.

On Wednesday, Ada County District Judge Steven Hippler granted Kohberger's request for court-appointed counsel, directing the Idaho State Public Defender to appoint a new attorney to represent him in all post-conviction proceedings.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Kohberger's former defense team.

title: Trump rejects Iran blame for Minnesota cyberattack, points finger at 'corrupt' political foe
excerpt:
President Donald Trump blamed state officials for the reported attack on 30 water plants, saying Iran "has bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

President Donald Trump dismissed speculation...
body_text:
President Donald Trump blamed state officials for the reported attack on 30 water plants, saying Iran "has bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

President Donald Trump dismissed speculation that Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting dozens of water systems in Minnesota, blaming instead the state’s "corrupt governor," Tim Walz, and the state he runs.

"I just want to mention that we heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack, and they blame it on Iran," he said at the start of a Cabinet meeting Friday at Camp David, Maryland.

"I don't think so. I think I blame it on Minnesota because they're grossly incompetent," Trump said. "There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, oh, is Iran? Iran should be so lucky. Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

Trump’s dismissal puts him at odds with a preliminary assessment reportedly shared by U.S. and state officials and comes days after federal agencies warned that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting the same kinds of systems. Iranian involvement and poor cybersecurity are not mutually exclusive: previous Iranian-linked attacks on U.S. water facilities exploited internet-connected equipment protected by default or nonexistent passwords.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBES MINNESOTA OVER 'TRANSGENDER DOLLS' IN SCHOOLS, BUT STATE DISPUTES STORY

President Donald Trump addresses the nation to give an update on Iran. (Alex Brandon/Pool via Reuters)

Trump has repeatedly attacked 2024 vice presidential candidate Walz over widespread fraud in Minnesota’s state-administered social services programs.

Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee, abandoned his bid for a third term in January amid mounting scrutiny of his administration’s handling of the schemes. Walz has not been accused of participating in the fraud.

A water tower is seen Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Plymouth, Minn. A cyberattack targeted operating technology at more than 30 water systems in Minnesota, including Plymouth's, earlier this week, state officials said. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)

Minnesota IT Services said the "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems" Sunday and Monday, but the Minnesota Department of Health is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage."

U.S. and state officials and others familiar with the incident told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack.

Minnesota IT Services said it has not determined yet whether a "specific actor" was responsible for the attack and the probe remains active.

The attacks disrupted automated operations in several communities.

Malicious software temporarily shut down controls for the well and water treatment plant in Braham, while Plymouth and South St. Paul shifted some operations to manual control. Officials reported no known threat to drinking water.

Federal agencies warned just days before the Minnesota attacks that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting the computerized controls used by water systems, power facilities and local governments. The agencies said the campaign had already disrupted operations at some facilities and caused financial losses. Investigators assessed that the hackers were seeking to cause disruption inside the U.S.

Iran has targeted American water infrastructure before.

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz speaks during a debate at the CBS Broadcast Center Oct. 1, 2024, in New York City. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

In 2023, hackers affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps breached programmable controllers at several U.S. water and wastewater facilities, according to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The hackers generally exploited equipment that was exposed to the internet and still used default or nonexistent passwords. The affected utilities moved some operations offline, and no drinking water was compromised.

In an earlier case, the Justice Department charged an Iranian hacker with repeatedly accessing the control system of a small dam in Rye, New York, in 2013. Prosecutors said the intrusion would have allowed him to operate the dam’s sluice gate remotely, but the gate had been manually disconnected for maintenance at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment.

Fox News' Gregory Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

title: HIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say experts
excerpt:
Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

New innovations in HIV prevention could dram...
body_text:
Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

New innovations in HIV prevention could dramatically reduce the number of new HIV cases around the globe, but US foreign aid cuts will mean that those that most need the new medication will be unable to access it, according to experts at the Aids 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

One year ago, the World Health Organization recommended that governments around the world prioritize expanded access to lenacapavir, an injectable version of the HIV prevention medication PrEP that requires only two injections annually. PrEP, which also comes in the form of daily oral medications and bimonthly injections, is 99% effective in preventing sexually transmitted HIV for people who take it consistently.

In its announcement, the WHO noted that access to lenacapavir is limited outside clinical trials. But the organisation recommended that governments around the world prioritise scaling up availability of the injectable medication, because it could be gamechanging for populations that face considerable barriers to access for the medications that are currently available.

For people who face poverty or stigma, or who live in rural areas that are far away from healthcare services, accessing a daily pill or an every-other-month injection can be close to impossible. Lenacapavir would provide strong protection against HIV while only requiring patients to access healthcare twice annually. A mathematical modeling study from the WHO and the United Nations estimated that widespread availability of lenacapavir could prevent 41% of new HIV infections in South Africa, Zimbabwe and western Kenya.

Notably, when the WHO recommended global investment in lenacapavir for HIV prevention in 2025, the Trump administration was already in the process of dissolving USAID, which provided 73% of donor-funded resources for HIV prevention globally, according to a study in the Lancet Global Health. As of July 2026, multiple reports show that investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically around the world.

“We have these major achievements in prevention. On the other hand, we are facing these major funding cuts that are affecting deeply the delivery not only of these new prevention technologies but also decreasing the number of people engaged in care, engaged in prevention services,” said Beatriz Grinsztejn, president of the International Aids Society, during a press conference at the Aids 2026 Conference.

Grinsztejn is also an infectious disease physician and researcher at the HIV prevention organisation Fiocruz in Rio de Janeiro.

The funding cuts not only affect the availability of medications themselves, but also the ability of organisations to reach the people who need them.

“When funding cuts came, one of the big things that’s been impacted is peer outreach workers, which are crucial to reaching people who use drugs, to building trust with people who use drugs and engaging them with services,” said Ailish Brennan, a policy analyst at Harm Reduction International.

People who inject drugs are at a particularly high risk for contracting HIV, especially if they do not have access to clean syringes. A report from the International Network of People Who Use Drugs found that organisations were most likely to respond to the loss of funding by cutting outreach services.

Brennan said that many harm reduction and HIV prevention organisations around the world were having to shut down locations, including mobile locations, which can mean clients at risk for HIV lose trust in the organisation.

“But also just if they have to travel further they lose their local point of contact, and ultimately this means the innovations that we’re seeing, the long-acting injectables that have so much hope and opportunity, are not going to reach the people who need them most,” Brennan said.

At the press conference, Grinsztejn noted that even before the dissolution of USAID, much of Latin America had been left out of agreements with US-based pharmaceutical companies to make innovative HIV prevention more affordable.

Gilead Sciences provides generic versions of long-acting medications to low- and middle-income countries for far below sticker price, but justifies excluding countries such as Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and Argentina by classifying them as “upper middle-income countries”. HIV advocates dispute this justification, partly because people in these countries played a key role in clinical trials to test these medications.

“We do have prevention technologies that are our dream,” Grinsztejn said during the conference, adding that it should be possible to fulfill the UNAIDS long-held goal of eliminating AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

Grinsztejn then added: “From my personal perspective, I think that it’s really hard that we will get to the targets given the current scenario.”

title: India’s monsoon in danger as El Niño predicted to bring hot and dry global conditions, experts warn
excerpt:
El Niño forecast to strengthen from August to October, resulting in higher temperatures and more extreme weather

India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of ...
body_text:
El Niño forecast to strengthen from August to October, resulting in higher temperatures and more extreme weather

India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned.

The El Niño system will strengthen from August to October, which will bring higher temperatures globally, with increasing rainfall in some regions while other suffer drought, according to new data and forecasts released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Friday.

Marine heatwaves have already shocked scientists this year and are set to intensify: the WMO said temperatures were likely to exceed 2.9C above normal in several regions.

The risk of a weakened monsoon, which brings the rain on which Indian farmers rely, was highlighted as the forecast gave an “enhancement in the probability for below-normal rainfall”, which would produce increased drought, floods and wildfire risk around the Indian Ocean basin. Drier conditions are also likely across parts of equatorial Africa to the west of the Horn of Africa, across the south and east of Australia, large parts of South America and in North America.

Higher than normal rainfall is expected in southern Europe, central Asia and the Horn of Africa and south-eastern South America.

Extreme weather has already caused havoc around the world this summer, with record-breaking heatwaves beginning in May in the UK, and wildfires across France and Spain that have destroyed villages and caused hundreds of thousands of people to be displaced.

Scientists have warned this year of the development of an El Niño, a weather system in the Pacific that frequently affects temperatures and rainfall around the world. Some El Niño years in the past have been relatively mild, but scientists have said that this year’s has been supercharged by the climate crisis.

Warmer waters – earlier in the year than usual and with water temperatures still increasing – have led to predictions of a “super El Niño” forming. The WMO does not use this term, but has warned that the weather system developing is likely to be significantly stronger and more intense than usual. Friday’s forecasts were the organisation’s latest update, covering August to October.

Celeste Saulo, the secretary general of the WMO, called on governments to make preparations to help people affected by the heat, drought and potential floods that are likely in the months ahead.

“El Niño is one of the most closely monitored climate phenomena in the world,” she said. “But forecasts in themselves do not prevent hazards, people do. This El Niño, developing against the backdrop of unprecedented ocean heat and rising temperatures, provides governments and communities with a window of opportunity to anticipate risks and act before impacts unfold. The decisions we make today will shape the impacts we experience tomorrow.”

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, warned of the impacts on Friday and called for governments to take action on fossil fuels. “Two months ago, I warned that El Niño was arriving on our doorstep. Now it is inside the house, and turning up the heat,” he told reporters in New York.

“The Pacific waters driving it have never been this warm this early in an El Niño, and temperatures are still increasing,” he said. “[This year] risks shattering every seasonal record, and driving even more severe effects worldwide. We are in uncharted territory.”

He warned particularly of the risks to workers. “Heat is claiming lives on a growing scale, day after day, in every region of the world. It is also putting an enormous share of the global workforce at risk, exposing billions of people to dangers and often life-threatening conditions,” he said.

Separately, studies have shown that the extreme weather Europe is experiencing and the increasing likelihood of drought and wildfires, have been “supercharged” by the climate crisis.

title: NFL analyst Tony Romo placed on leave by CBS Sports following drunk driving arrest in Wisconsin

Tony Romo, arrested a week ago on charges related to operating a vehicl...
body_text:
Fox News national correspondent Kevin Corke reports on Tony Romo’s refusal to take a breathalyzer test on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Tony Romo, arrested a week ago on charges related to operating a vehicle while intoxicated, has been sidelined from his role as the top NFL analyst at CBS, the network announced Friday morning.

"Tony Romo is on leave from his role at CBS Sports until further notice," CBS Sports said in a statement.

It is unclear to what degree the leave was negotiated with Romo – whether he agreed or even requested it so that he could manage the legal and personal ramifications of his arrest.

Tony Romo mugshot from arrest. (Fox News Digital)

TONY ROMO ARRESTED IN MILWAUKEE FOR ALLEGED OWI OFFENSE: REPORT

It is possible Romo wanted this. It is also possible it was foisted upon him by his employer, who saw putting Romo on air during this time as a bad strategy.

The network is replacing Romo with former Houston Texans defensive lineman J.J. Watt as its lead analyst. Watt will work with play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on the No. 1 CBS announcing team.

The first CBS game scheduled this NFL season is a preseason matchup between the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles on Aug. 28. That primetime game begins at 8 p.m.

CBS Sports play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz (left), analyst Tony Romo (center) and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson at a press conference at the Super Bowl LVIII Media Center at the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino on Feb. 6, 2024. (Kirby Lee/USA TODAY Sports)

NFL EMPLOYEES' TROUBLING DRIVING INCIDENTS MOUNT

CBS is poised for an extended Romo leave, according to an industry source who added that Watt has been told his addition to the No. 1 announcing team is indefinite.

Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office deputies stopped Romo on Interstate 43 after observing what their report described as unsafe passing. Authorities said Romo displayed signs of impairment, performed poorly on field sobriety tests and refused a preliminary breath test.

Deputies also reported finding an open bottle of alcohol inside Romo's vehicle. Romo was cited for first-offense OWI, unsafe passing and having an open intoxicant in a motor vehicle before being booked and later released pending a September court appearance.

In this Nov. 9, 2014, file photo, Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo acknowledges spectators after a 31-17 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars in an NFL football game at Wembley Stadium in London. (Tim Ireland/AP)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Romo, 46, became CBS Sports' lead NFL game analyst on April 4, 2017, the same day he announced his retirement from the NFL after the Dallas Cowboys released him.

CBS immediately announced that Romo would replace Phil Simms, who had served as the network's No. 1 game analyst since 1998. Romo was paired with Nantz and Wolfson on CBS's top NFL broadcast team.
