Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

title: ‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth Games
excerpt:
CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time dances

The 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow have already provided plenty of highlights. But fans a...
body_text:
CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time dances

The 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow have already provided plenty of highlights. But fans across the world have been dazzled by one particular breakout star: the “mop man”.

When a cleaner came out at half-time during a netball match to wipe down the court before the restart, everything appeared normal. But as the cleaner swept, and the first bars of Queen’s I Want to Break Free rang out in the venue, he went from sweeping to a standing split.

A full dance routine set to the 1984 hit then followed, much to the surprise and delight of the audience at the OVO Hydro. The crowd watched him do the worm, splits and front handsprings. He has since entertained crowds during breaks in play at a number of other events and clips of his performances have gone viral online.

The man behind the mop is CJ Miller, 25, from Livingston, West Lothian, a trained dancer who was hired by the Games to keep crowds entertained during intermissions.

He considers himself more of an introvert than his cleaning alter ego. “I’m an anxious and paranoid queen,” said Miller. “And I’m so grateful for the turn of events. It’s been a lovely 50 minutes of fame. I wish I’d had a haircut before it happened.”

Miller was initially told he would be part of a flashmob at the Games with other dancers. “Then it was, ‘oh, here’s a mop. Here’s the song.’ It wasn’t until the Tuesday before the Games I found out it was gonna be Boo Boo the Fool here, on his own,” Miller laughed, pointing to himself.

When choreographing the routine, Miller was inspired by “the concept of a volunteer … a cleaner that had been possessed by the music and just exploded.”

But the character soon took on a life – and fanbase – of his own. “People have messaged being like, ‘Thank you for making me smile, I really needed that today.’”

For Miller, the universal charm of his performance comes from “the sheer stupidity, the sheer bonkersness of it all”. “It just made people feel like it’s OK to mess around,” he said. “Sometimes, people need to be reminded to just take a break. Just take a minute to smile at someone else being so bloody ridiculous.”

Miller’s performance was soon picked up by broadcasters and newspapers around the world. There was particular praise for the unexpected chemistry with his dance partner: Doris the mop.

“Phil [Goodlad] from the BBC had named the mop Doris – so I didn’t even name the bloody mop!” said Miller. “He asked me, and I went: ‘The mop is a mop, Phil.’ And he was like: ‘I think it looks like a Doris.’ I went: ‘Brilliant. It’s Doris the mop now, Phil, spectacular.’”

Did he have a name in mind for his other dance partner, the vacuum? “It was a Vax vacuum, so I think the vacuum should be called Vaxtina – like Xtina. You can write that one down.”

Going into the Games, Miller felt nervous about performing in front of a sports crowd for the first time. “Basketball, for me, was a scary one. I was like: ‘I don’t think the basketball crowd are going to want to see my flamboyant ass, giving them a dance to Freddie Mercury. And I was wrong. The basketball crowd were incredible.”

“It was a lesson for me to check my own prejudice,” he said. “It doesn’t excuse the point of view I had of sports fans, and that has been changed now from the immense support I’ve received from the sports fans at the Commonwealth. Thank you for proving me wrong, sports fans.”

Going forward, Miller is soon to join Newcastle College as a dance tutor and continue building his career as a choreographer. But will the world ever see more of mop man?

“I think it would be fun,” said Miller, who has been approached by one company about taking his performance further. “If I were to do it again, let’s get some other professions in there,” said Miller. “Referee, waiter, bloody construction worker. Let’s get inventive with it.”

While mop man’s performances may have come to an end, Miller hopes viewers can be inspired by his character’s self-confidence and sense of whimsy. “Be messy, fail, screw up,” he said. “That’s what makes us human. Get your mop and shake your ass, you know what I mean?”

title: Keep your eyes trained on this Big Ten sleeper to make some conference noise in 2026
excerpt:
Joel Klatt revealed the top five games that will decide the Big Ten in the 2026 season.

With Big Ten Media Days wrapping up on Thursday, talking season is officially in the books, and if I may be so ...
body_text:
Joel Klatt revealed the top five games that will decide the Big Ten in the 2026 season.

With Big Ten Media Days wrapping up on Thursday, talking season is officially in the books, and if I may be so bold, thank GOD!

Now we can finally look ahead to the start of college football season, and with that, the picture of 2026 as a whole starts to come into focus.

Speaking of the Big Ten, after looking through the conference's predicted order of finish, I have zeroed in on one dark horse that my shock a ton of people this coming season.

ONE OF THESE EIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS WILL BE HOISTING THE NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP TROPHY IN 2026

I have been seeing the USC Trojans getting a lot of love as a "sleeper" in the Big Ten conference, and while I really like how 2026 is shaping up for Lincoln Riley and the Men of Troy, they were picked to finish fourth by the media.

I wanted something a little more exciting, and after scrolling a little deeper down the list of teams, I think I may have found my Big Ten sleeper.

All the way down at seventh – not a doormat but certainly not a favorite either – you'll find the Washington Huskies, and I absolutely love what they have going on heading into the season.

INDIANA'S CURT CIGNETTI ROASTS THE SEC AS ESPN STARTS THEIR PROMOTIONAL CAMPAIGN ALREADY: 'WE DON'T WHINE'

Demond Williams Jr. of the Washington Huskies passes against the Oregon Ducks during the first half at Husky Stadium on Nov. 29, 2025 in Seattle, Washington. (Steph Chambers/Getty Images)

For Washington, it starts at the top with head coach Jedd Fisch.

This might be my bias showing, but Fisch was my top pick for the Florida Gators when it became obvious that Lane Kiffin was heading elsewhere. I believe he's one hell of a coach, but the numbers back this up, as well.

Fisch's previous stop before arriving in Seattle was with the Arizona Wildcats, and in year one he inherited a mess of a program, bottoming out at 1-11.

INDIANA COACH CURT CIGNETTI BECOMES UNSTOPPABLE THANKS TO LATEST DEVELOPMENT ON RECRUITING TRAIL

Year two was appreciably better at 5-7, but still nothing to write home about.

In year three, however, Fisch and the Wildcats were the talk of college football, shocking everyone with a 10-3 record and putting players like QB Noah Fifita and wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan on the map.

Head coach Jedd Fisch of the Arizona Wildcats walks the sidelines during the second half of the NCAAF game against the Washington Huskies at Arizona Stadium on Sept. 30, 2023, in Tucson, Arizona. (Christian Petersen/Getty Images)

Surprisingly, Fisch didn't stick around for another year with Fifita and McMillan in Tucson, opting to take over for the newly departed Kalen DeBoer at Washington.

The cupboard was left pretty bare for Fisch when he touched down in the Pacific Northwest, as the new Huskies head coach had to replace 20 of his 22 starters from the team that went to the national championship game just a season prior.

Fisch showed his chops once again, guiding the Huskies to a 6-7 record and a berth in the Sun Bowl despite having to patch together an entire team from scratch.

After a 9-4 season and a bowl win in 2025, it's safe to see why I'm so optimistic about the Huskies given Fisch's track record of ascending each subsequent season.

Washington didn't take a ton of players in the transfer portal, and while some might view that as a negative, I think it's a sign of things stabilizing for the team.

The Huskies rank in the top 15 nationally in returning production at 65%, just a tick under Oregon and UCLA for tops in the Big Ten and certainly a far cry from his first season in Seattle.

The biggest reason for optimism among those returning starters is quarterback Demond Williams Jr.

Washington Huskies quarterback Demond Williams Jr. (2) warms up prior to the LA Bowl against the Boise State Broncos at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The game took place on Dec. 13, 2025. (Jayne Kamin-Oncea/Imagn Images)

After spot duty and a few starts in 2024, Williams blossomed into a legitimate threat both through the air and on the ground and was one of the most coveted players in the transfer portal before he opted to return to Washington for his junior year.

Other talented returning starters include offensive tackle Drew Azzopardi and safety Alex McLaughlin, both of whom are generating plenty of buzz in the preseason.

The schedule sets up very nicely for the Huskies, too, as they play five of their first six games within the friendly confines of Husky Stadium and won't leave the Pacific Time Zone until mid-October.

They also avoid Ohio State and Michigan while they get both Indiana and Penn State at home this year.

Jedd Fisch of the Washington Huskies speaks during the Spring football press conference at Husky Stadium on March 27, 2024 in Seattle, Washington. (Alika Jenner/Getty Images)

If you need a Big Ten darkhorse to ride with in 2026, I suggest you look no further than the Washington Huskies.

They have the coaching, the returning production at key positions, and the schedule to be a real threat this coming season.

Buy stock in Fisch and company now, because it won't be getting any cheaper.

title: Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza
excerpt:
There are many reasons why it might not work.

At the same time, it is potentially a rare chink of light in a bleak picture. Hamas has never agreed to disarm before now. Handled carefully and well, th...
body_text:
There are many reasons why it might not work.

At the same time, it is potentially a rare chink of light in a bleak picture. Hamas has never agreed to disarm before now. Handled carefully and well, there is a chance now to make diplomatic progress.

A bargain lies at the heart of the new proposition for Hamas to disarm in Gaza.

The idea is that as Hamas hands over its weapons, Israel pulls out of the 70% of Gaza that it occupies.

That may sound simple, but the realities of politics, war, zero trust, the deaths of thousands and the destruction of Gaza make the process very complicated.

Life in Gaza is catastrophic for well over 2 million Palestinian civilians who are living in desperate conditions.

For most, Israel has destroyed their homes and their livelihoods. Israel killed more than 70,000 Palestinians during the war, and more than 1,000 more since the ceasefire, according to the Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN. Unicef says that Israel has killed more than 20,000 children since 7 October 2023, with at least 1,000 babies among the dead and wounded.

Much of Gaza is rubble. It is not just the damage caused by Israel Defense Forces (IDF) military operations. There has also been an organised, officially sponsored project to destroy communities and smash infrastructure. Civilian demolition contractors from Israel have been contracted to finish the job started by IDF bombs.

Many Palestinians believe Israel wants to force them out, by making life so insupportable and appalling that they will leave if they get the chance. Leaders and senior officials inside Jordan and Egypt also believe that powerful individuals in the Israeli government are working to create the conditions for the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians, most likely across their borders.

On the Israeli side, there is a strong sense in the Jewish majority of 80% or so that Hamas will remain a potentially deadly threat until it is totally disarmed and stripped of any vestige of power.

On 7 October 2023 Hamas and other Palestinians attacked Israel, killing almost 1,200 people, around two thirds of whom were civilians including children, and taking 251 people into Gaza as hostages.  Many Israelis believe Hamas would do that again if it had the chance.

Follow live: Hamas agrees to Trump's plan to disarm in Gaza, official tells BBC, with Israel yet to comment

Hamas says it has agreed to disarm after Trump announces Board of Peace plan

The diplomatic process that produced the agreement with Hamas does not operate in a bubble. Making the plan work depends on broader issues too.

Israel has a general election at the end of October. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is behind in the polls and fighting not just for his political life and legacy but potentially for his liberty. While he remains in office, his long running trial on corruption charges that could carry a jail sentence has been slowed to a crawl. That would change if he lost power.

Netanyahu faces pressure at home and abroad. Domestically he does not want his political opponents to be able to accuse him of being soft on Hamas. Internationally the only address that matters to him is in Washington DC.

The US also has elections looming with midterms in November. President Donald Trump cannot a win in the war on Iran, so he needs one in Gaza. If Trump's Republican party loses badly, the power he relishes using will drain away. Trump will blame Netanyahu if he decides he is preventing the victory he wants and needs.

One of Netanyahu's boasts to Israel's electorate is that he can handle the Americans, including Trump, better than any of his rivals. A Trump tirade before election day in Israel scuppers that proposition.

Netanyahu is an expert at playing for time when faced with a big challenge. He will try to juggle pressure at home and pressure from the Oval Office until election day.

Hamas is also under severe pressure. Most of its senior men and thousands of its fighters were killed by Israel. The IDF still assassinates senior Hamas figures when it gets a chance. As I write, a flash from the IDF on my phone says it has killed a commander of a Palestinian militia who it says took hostages on 7 October 2023.

Many Palestinians blame Hamas for the consequences of its decision to attack Israel on 7 October. Hamas also faces challenges from powerful families and by militias funded and backed by Israel.

It is trying to rebuild grass roots support. This was how the BBC's Gaza correspondent Rushdi Abu Alouf put it to me: "For months, Hamas increasingly shifted part of its focus back to social and political outreach, expanding Quran memorisation programmes and charitable activities aimed at children, teenagers and young people, while taking advantage of the severe humanitarian crisis and the growing dependence of so many families on aid."

Khalil al Hayya, the newly confirmed political leader of Hamas, was a crucial player in the decision to drop objections to the framework. Egypt and Turkey did much of the hard diplomatic work to get him there.

Hamas concessions are linked to Israel agreeing to pull back in Gaza. Israel is on record as demanding full Hamas disarmament as a pre-condition for withdrawal.

Bowen: Hamas diminished, but still part of the picture

Only a step-by-step agreement, starting small and building confidence, has a chance of working. Trump will have to stay engaged, which is far from certain with a war with Iran among a planet full of other challenges.

Just keeping the process going will require sustained diplomatic engagement and no sudden shocks that make meditation impossible.

That will be difficult. The occupied West Bank is on the verge of an explosion of even worse violence. Figures gathered by ACLED, a group that monitors armed conflict, says that 2026 is on track to become the most violent year in the West Bank since it began monitoring the territory a decade ago.

Jewish settlers have been allowed by the IDF and encouraged by extremists in the Netanyahu government to run riot, attacking and sometimes killing Palestinians and driving them off their land.

Palestinians have been organising themselves to resist. Some opponents and critics of Netanyahu believe that he wants a major crisis on the West Bank to justify a tough response before the elections and remove any pressure to pull back in Gaza.

Netanyahu and prominent ministers in his cabinet have said repeatedly that there will never be a Palestinian state.

Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, is committing the government to decisions aimed at increasing Jewish settlement and killing off the prospects of an independent Palestine. Smotrich is an extreme religious nationalist who has been sanctioned by major Western countries and banned from entering the UK, France, other leading European nations, as well as Australia and New Zealand. Israel condemned those decisions as antisemitic.

A process that does not give Palestinians a political horizon and a route to self-determination will not work, condemning another generation to lives dominated by war.

Diplomatic failure would not benefit Palestinians or Israelis. It would play into the hands of those on both sides who believe their conflict has no solution other than defeating their enemy.

If Hamas disarmament plan holds, it could mark first credible step to ending Gaza war

Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families

title: Liberal court stuns with ruling that hands Trump major immigration win
excerpt: DHS Chief Counsel James Percival said a group of federal district judges—not the judiciary as a whole—are repeatedly blocking deportations and Temporary Protected Status rollbacks despite SCOTUS rulin...
body_text:
DHS Chief Counsel James Percival said a group of federal district judges—not the judiciary as a whole—are repeatedly blocking deportations and Temporary Protected Status rollbacks despite SCOTUS rulings, calling it "naked political activism."

A liberal-led federal appeals court handed President Donald Trump two immigration victories Wednesday, reversing separate district court orders that had delayed the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for migrants from South Sudan and Ethiopia.

The judgments from the First Circuit Court of Appeals come after U.S. District Judges Brian Murphy and Patti Saris issued back-to-back orders temporarily blocking the Trump administration's termination of TPS for Ethiopia and South Sudan, respectively, late last week. The rulings drew sharp criticism from legal experts and Trump administration officials, who called the judges "rogue" and argued their decisions defied the Supreme Court.

The three-judge First Circuit panel consisted of Judges Julie Rikelman and Seth Aframe, both appointed by President Joe Biden, and Judge Joshua Dunlap, who was appointed by President Donald Trump.

BIDEN JUDGE BLOCKING ETHIOPIAN DEPORTATIONS DESPITE SCOTUS RULING CLASHED WITH ICE BEFORE

President Donald Trump during an announcement in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

In nearly identical rulings, the majority liberal panel found that the lower court judges' orders conflicted with the Supreme Court's decision in Mullin v. Doe, which held that courts cannot block TPS terminations based on non-constitutional claims.

"Mullin held that 'the TPS statute's judicial-review bar applies to all non-constitutional claims' challenging the Secretary of Homeland Security's determination with respect to the termination of a TPS designation," the judges wrote.

Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan told Fox News Digital that the First Circuit correctly applied the precedent established by the Supreme Court.

"These are clear wins for President Trump following his big win at the U.S. Supreme Court, explaining that district courts are not supposed to second guess TPS terminations, and even as this plays out, we're moving towards the end of this litigation because district courts should not be hearing these disputes, and that's what the Supreme Court said," Wessan told Fox News Digital.

U.S. President Donald Trump takes questions from the media during a bilateral meeting with President of Lebanon Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office of the White House on July 21, 2026 in Washington, DC. U.S. District Court Judge Patti Saris attends the opening ceremony for the Justice Stephen G. Breyer Community Learning Center on Courts and the Constitution at the federal courthouse in Boston, Massachusetts, U.S., March 25, 2025. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images; Brian Snyder/Reuters)

SUPREME COURT'S LATEST IMMIGRATION RULING WILL CAUSE AMERICANS TO 'DIE AND SUFFER' ATTORNEY WARNS

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson welcomed the rulings as "a win for the rule of law and common sense."

"Temporary Protected Status is exactly that—temporary," the spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent."

The lawsuits were brought by African Communities Together, a New York-based immigrant advocacy organization that serves as the lead plaintiff in both cases, alongside individual TPS recipients from Ethiopia and South Sudan. The plaintiffs argue DHS unlawfully ended the protections in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution, alleging the agency failed to properly assess conditions in the two countries and that the decisions were motivated by racial discrimination.

Murphy and Saris temporarily blocked the Trump administration from terminating TPS last week, issuing procedural orders to preserve the status quo while they considered whether the plaintiffs should be permitted to amend their complaints to pursue renewed constitutional claims.

DHS EVISCERATES MEDIA FOR ‘ABSOLUTE ABSURDITY’ OVER CONCERN ABOUT ‘WORST OF THE WORST’ ACTIVIST JUDGES LIST

While the Supreme Court's decision in Mullin v. Doe foreclosed most statutory challenges to TPS terminations, it left open the possibility that courts could consider claims alleging constitutional violations.

U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy has temporarily blocked key Trump administration decisions to terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) (United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary/ REUTERS/Nathan Howard)

However, Wessan said the district judges were operating outside the "legal bounds" by blocking the TPS terminations before any constitutional claims had been established.

"If they want to let the plaintiffs amend their complaint, they're allowed to do that, but in the meantime, TPS is over," Wessan told Fox News Digital.

The First Circuit's decisions mark the latest setback for Murphy and Saris after the Trump administration accused both judges of effectively sidestepping the Supreme Court's June ruling. After Murphy's order, DHS General Counsel James Percival wrote on X that the district judge was engaged in "mutiny against the Supreme Court," while he described Saris' ruling as "open defiance" of the justices' decision.

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Murphy and Saris for comment.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Murdaugh defense says newly disclosed reserve DNA samples should go to Othram before state analysis
excerpt: Fox News correspondent Steve Harrigan reports on the Alex Murdaugh double murder retrial kicking off in Lexington, South Carolina. Defense attorneys are pushing for a re-examination of DNA found under...
body_text:
Fox News correspondent Steve Harrigan reports on the Alex Murdaugh double murder retrial kicking off in Lexington, South Carolina. Defense attorneys are pushing for a re-examination of DNA found under Maggie Murdaugh's fingernails, arguing new methods could reveal evidence previously unavailable. Murdaugh, currently serving time for financial crimes, seeks to wear civilian clothes to prevent juror prejudice.

Alex Murdaugh's attorneys say prosecutors recently disclosed that previously unprocessed reserve DNA samples remain in the murder case, fueling a renewed effort to have an independent laboratory analyze the evidence before South Carolina investigators conduct additional testing.

Defense attorneys wrote allowing the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) to conduct additional short tandem repeat, or STR, testing first could consume or degrade the remaining DNA before Texas-based Othram Inc. has an opportunity to analyze it.

In a memorandum filed July 30, obtained by WSAV in Savannah, Georgia, and reviewed by Fox News Digital, Murdaugh's attorneys asked a judge to release the reserve DNA samples to Othram before SLED conducts any further testing.

MURDAUGH DEFENSE PLANS ALTERNATE SUSPECT PUSH AS DNA QUESTIONS LOOM OVER RETRIAL

The filing argued the sequence of testing was critical because Othram's single nucleotide polymorphism, or SNP, testing requires DNA that has not already been depleted or degraded through prior analysis.

Disgraced South Carolina lawyer Alex Murdaugh was convicted in March of murdering his wife, Maggie, and youngest son, Paul, on his hunting estate in June 2021. (Andrew J. Whitaker/The Post And Courier via AP, Pool, File)

"Because SNP testing requires a genetic sample that has not been depleted or degraded by prior analysis, the sequence in which the reserve samples from Items 70 and 71 are tested matters," the memorandum states. "SLED's proposed STR retesting risks consuming the very material Othram would need, while proceeding with Othram's SNP analysis first forecloses no STR testing SLED might still wish to conduct afterward."

The memorandum noted prosecutors disclosed "for the first time" that reserve DNA samples from Items 70 and 71 remain unprocessed.

ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER SAGA LANDS RIGHT BACK WHERE IT STARTED BEFORE NEXT LOWCOUNTRY COURTROOM BATTLE

The filing described a July 7 Webex conference involving defense attorneys, prosecutors, SLED forensic scientists and Othram CEO Dr. David Mittelman following a June 29 hearing to discuss the proposed testing.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Alex Murdaugh, convicted of killing his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, in June 2021, sits during a hearing on a motion for a retrial, Tuesday, Jan. 16, 2024, at the Richland County Judicial Center in Columbia, S.C. (Tracy Glantz/The State via AP, Pool)

The defense further argued SLED had "articulated no scientific basis" for repeating testing already performed on the evidence. Attorneys wrote another round of STR testing could permanently reduce the amount of DNA available for independent analysis.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"There is no scientific reason on the current record to consume additional reserve sample material to obtain a second STR result," the filing states. "Absent some articulated basis for believing repeat STR testing will produce new or different information, the only apparent effect of allowing SLED to proceed is to consume irreplaceable sample material before Othram ... has the opportunity to test it."

The defense also renewed its criticism of SLED's handling of forensic evidence, citing previous disputes over blood evidence recovered from one of Murdaugh's T-shirts as further justification for independent testing.

Paul, Alex, Maggie and Buster Murdaugh at a sporting event. Alex, was convicted of fatally shooting his wife and son. (Facebook)

ALEX MURDAUGH'S DOUBLE MURDER CONVICTION UNANIMOUSLY OVERTURNED BY SOUTH CAROLINA SUPREME COURT

The memorandum estimated Othram could complete its analysis within 60 to 90 days at Murdaugh's expense.

Last month, prosecutors urged a judge to reject Murdaugh's latest requests for independent DNA testing and expanded access to electronic case materials while he remains in prison awaiting retrial.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

In the June filings, prosecutors opposed two motions from Murdaugh's legal team: one seeking independent DNA testing tied to evidence recovered from beneath Maggie Murdaugh's fingernails and another requesting permission for Murdaugh to review case materials electronically while incarcerated.

The filings come as Murdaugh prepares for a second murder trial after the South Carolina Supreme Court overturned his convictions in May, finding former Colleton County court clerk Rebecca "Becky" Hill engaged in jury tampering that compromised his right to a fair trial.

Murdaugh was convicted in March 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Colleton County hunting estate in June 2021. The jury also found him guilty of two weapons charges.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

title: Taylor Sheridan's 'Lioness' season 3 is an action-packed saga loaded with violence and carnage
excerpt:
"Landman" star Andy Garcia touted show creator Taylor Sheridan's distinctive talent for dialogue, character development and a unique worldview in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Season three of "...
body_text:
"Landman" star Andy Garcia touted show creator Taylor Sheridan's distinctive talent for dialogue, character development and a unique worldview in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Season three of "Lioness" will shock fans by taking things to unprecedented levels.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN RETURNS TO MOVIES AFTER FIVE YEARS WITH NASA THRILLER, POLITICAL DRAMA

ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'REALLY SEES WOMEN' AS LIONESS SEASON THREE HITS PARAMOUNT+

NEW LIONESS SEASON 3 TRAILER SIGNALS TAYLOR SHERIDAN IS TAKING THE PARAMOUNT+ SERIES TO NEW HEIGHTS

Zoe Saldaña as Joe in Lioness season 3, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. (Lauren "Lo" Smith/Paramount+)

It's no secret that I'm a big fan of Sheridan's work and I love the gritty and dark CIA/military series starring Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman, Michael Kelly and a lot of other incredibly talented actors and actresses.

The lead up to season three of "Lioness" has been boosted by some outstanding trailers and previews promising a new mission for Joe and her hardened team.

Well, I had the opportunity to get an advanced look at several of the early episodes of season three, and I can confidently say the stage is set for season three to be the most explosive one yet.

Season one dealt with a terror target, season two focused heavily on the cartels and a high stakes mission in Iran and season three is taking viewers to a new enemy staring down America:

Nicole Kidman as Kaitlyn in episode 2 of season 3 of Lioness, streaming on Paramount+ in 2026. (Ryan Green/Paramount+)

I am going to keep this review spoiler free because season three is simply too great and too fast paced for me to want to ruin anything.

What I will say is that season three doesn't just keep the same energy as the previous two. It elevates it, and the season one premiere features an action sequence involving the CIA and Delta Force commandos that rivals the season two premiere, which I've said many times is the best action sequence in the history of TV.

It's honestly incredible how plugged in Sheridan is when it comes to the shadowy world of special operations. The tactics, movements, the way dogs are utilized and communication all feel very real. Even the gear the characters carry is about as real as it will ever get.

The action sequence in the season three premiere also reminded me a lot of the tunnel scene in "Sicario." Very similar vibe, but way more violent and action-packed. Did I mention the drones? Yeah, get ready for several terrifying moments that reflect how wars are now fought.

Season three also utilizes multiple timelines, and manages to do something that rarely happens with that technique:

It flows naturally and isn't at all confusing.

Also, Ian Bohen and Elizaveta Neretin are fresh additions to the cast in season three. Bohen plays a Delta Force operator, and Nereten.......well, let's not ruin anything for anybody.

Austin Hébert as Randy and James Jordan as Two Cups in Lioness, episode 2, season 3, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. (Ryan Green/Paramount+)

Overall, Sheridan has created another masterpiece of a season through the episodes I've seen. New villains, new faces and a new level of action and carnage. I can't recommend it enough, and I absolutely can't wait to see what happens the rest of the way. Send me your predictions at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

David Hookstead is a reporter for OutKick.

title: World Cup: FIFA studying impact of expanding to 64 teams for 2030 edition
excerpt:
FIFA is studying whether to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition in a move that could reshape football’s showpiece tournament when it celebrates its centennial.

World footbal...
body_text:
FIFA is studying whether to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition in a move that could reshape football’s showpiece tournament when it celebrates its centennial.

World football’s governing body wants to appoint an independent agency to assess the ambitious expansion plan, which would add another 16 nations to ⁠a tournament that had already grown from 32 to 48 teams in 2026.

“FIFA wishes to appoint an independent agency to determine whether and how expanding the FIFA World Cup from 48 to 64 participating national teams, starting with the 2030 edition, would impact on the tournament proposition,” it said in a research brief seen by the news agency Reuters.

South American confederation CONMEBOL had officially proposed hosting the 2030 World ‌Cup with 64 teams last year, allowing more countries the opportunity to join in the celebrations for the tournament’s centennial edition.

The 2026 edition in the US, Canada and Mexico was the first since 1998 to move away from the 32-team format, adding four more groups and an extra knockout round in the process, resulting in 104 matches over more than five weeks.

The accelerated study comes on the heels of FIFA’s plan to create a $20bn subsidiary to run the World Cup and its other events with external investors, a move that has attracted criticism and a ⁠UEFA decision to boycott FIFA events.

Al Jazeera has contacted FIFA for comment.

UEFA President ⁠Aleksander Ceferin said last year that expanding the World Cup to 64 teams was not a good idea.

The European governing body’s position has not changed since then, while Asian Football Confederation President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa had also voiced opposition, questioning last year where further expansion ⁠might end.

FIFA’s proposed analysis is meant to assess whether the proposed expansion can strengthen the tournament or whether concerns such as competition dilution, calendar congestion, operational complexity and market saturation ⁠outweigh the potential benefits.

The study will examine the potential impact of expanding ⁠the tournament to 64 teams, including the effects on the competition, competitive balance, qualification, player welfare and the international calendar.

It will also estimate the revenues that could be generated from ticket sales, sponsorship and media rights under the proposed format.

“The final recommendation should demonstrate not only whether a 64-team tournament ‌can generate incremental value, but whether that value is sustainable,” the document added.

FIFA said a decision on selecting the agency would be made on August 14 and they would have only four weeks to deliver their analysis by September 11.

The ‌2030 ‌World Cup is being jointly hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain, while Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will host one match each to celebrate the tournament’s 100th anniversary.

FIFA is already facing a dispute with its confederations due to a plan to sell stakes in World Cups and other events to private investors.

title: NSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman finds
excerpt:
Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An elderly public housing tenan...
body_text:
Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An elderly public housing tenant whose home was damaged by sewage overflows will be fully compensated by the New South Wales government after it disposed of her personal belongings without her consent and failed to properly support her insurance claim.

The NSW Ombudsman on Friday published its report after an investigation in which it found Homes NSW acted unreasonably in how it handled the tenant’s contaminated belongings and “failed to provide full and accurate information to the insurer”.

The woman, whose name and suburb were not made public, had lived in the unit for more than 15 years. She reported three successive sewage overflows within three months, which saw raw sewage enter the property.

After the third incident she was relocated, but her belongings remained in the contaminated unit for two months before being boxed up and moved to a vacant property.

The furniture, household items, and family heirlooms were not cleaned nor returned to her, despite Homes NSW telling her “she would be actively involved in the decision to keep or dispose of any items”.

She was later told “she would be adequately compensated” through an insurance claim, according to the report. When the claim was lodged, the insurer denied liability and offered a small “goodwill” payment.

The report found Homes NSW’s failure to provide the insurer with “full and accurate information” which contributed to the rejection of the claim.

The Ombudsman’s recommendations included an apology and full compensation “in accordance with her itemised compensation claim”. It also recommended an additional payment for “the distress and suffering she experienced while trying to resolve her claim over more than five years”.

Homes NSW has accepted all of the recommendations and will implement them by next month, according to the report.

The senior deputy ombudsman for complaints and investigations, Kate Anderson, said the findings and recommendations come after identifying “inadequate policies and procedures in place”.

“There were several points where there was inadequate communication to her about … what next steps were going to follow and then those steps were ultimately not followed,” she said.

Anderson said the case demonstrated the importance of ensuring agencies were able to “listen to their complainants”, particularly when they should “have engaged with this particular individual to reach a conclusion on this complaint far earlier”.

“This individual actually had very good record of the possessions that she had and the respective value of them, which ultimately was not taken into consideration,” she said.

“At all points, people should be treated with courtesy and respect and the situation that materialised here really demonstrated that ultimately by the time it had come to us, the tenant had been trying to resolve it herself with Home NSW for a number of years and hadn’t been able to get an effective resolution.”

A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it “sincerely apologises to the tenant affected” and acknowledged “the distress, inconvenience and impact the situation has had on them”.

Homes NSW has since introduced “a number of changes to how we deliver maintenance and repairs with the aim of improved tenant satisfaction, including establishing an in-house call centre to manage repair requests”, the spokesperson said.

title: These boots are the safest for US wildland firefighters. Fewer and fewer can afford them
excerpt:
The handcrafted leather boots are a century-old tradition – but with money tight, the cost of up to $800 is harder to justify

For 18 years, one of the most important relationships in Luke Mayfield’s ...
body_text:
The handcrafted leather boots are a century-old tradition – but with money tight, the cost of up to $800 is harder to justify

For 18 years, one of the most important relationships in Luke Mayfield’s life was with his boots. As a hotshot – one of the US’s elite firefighting crews sent deep, on foot, into wildfires – Mayfield hiked a thousand miles a fire season in his boots, stood in them 16 hours a day and slept near them on assignments that lasted weeks in terrain no truck could reach.

Like every wildland firefighter, he learned the rituals of their upkeep: how to grease them, how to lace them, how soon before the season to break in a new pair so the blisters came during training instead of on duty.

“For all that, they really are the best boots for the job,” Mayfield says. “It’s crazy to me that that’s the case, considering it’s 2026.”

The boot in question is a very particular object, and it has barely changed in more than a century. Eight inches of full-grain leather, minimum, laced high to protect against cuts and hot ash. A sole rated to take heat that could melt an ordinary shoe. A tall, stacked heel that bites into a slope going up and holds the foot steady coming down.

While there are some newer parts, such as fire-resistant Technora threads that self-extinguish in seconds, the majority of the boot is still made the traditional way: by hand, at a small constellation of family workshops in the Pacific north-west. One of them, White’s Boots in Spokane, Washington, is credited with originating the design in 1939, as a variation of the logger boot they had been making since the early 1900s.

It’s part artisan history, part law; many of the boot’s heritage aspects were built into guidelines the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) released for certification.

Despite the rigorous standards of certification, the boots are not a guarantee. Stand too long in hot ash and the heat eventually conducts through the sole; crews call it hot foot. When he was a young firefighter, Mayfield recalls, the lugs on his boots melted clean off.

In the face of these conditions, the boots were made to be rebuilt rather than replaced. A good pair can last the better part of a decade – but that craftsmanship comes at a price. Fire boots of the highest caliber can cost $800 a pair, with less expensive models in the $300-$500 range.

Those sums would be trivial on the budget sheet of the federal government, but Washington DC is rarely the buyer. In fact, the US’s wildland firefighters are largely responsible for equipping themselves.

Part of that is due to a surprising, and consequential, bureaucratic classification. Until only recently, the US government did not formally consider wildland firefighters to be firefighters at all. On paper, they were forestry technicians.

That designation carried genuine weight. It helped keep the burden of equipping the workforce on the “forestry technicians” themselves; the word “fire” did not appear in their job title and neither, reliably, did the government’s duty to outfit them.

The costs that do get covered aren’t shared evenly, either. How a crew is funded and equipped can vary sharply from one to the next, as a function of which agency or region a firefighter happens to land in. Mayfield says he once ran a hotshot crew with six figures in discretionary spending, while a comparable crew a few hundred miles south, in a different region, made do with a small fraction of that.

All of these issues are contributing to a problem of retention. The US interior department acknowledged in 2025 that compensation “has not kept pace” with the work, with firefighters “finding it increasingly difficult to remain in these jobs”. Until recently, wages ran so low that in 2021 the government moved to ensure a floor of no less than $15 an hour.

Demand on these firefighters is only mounting. The US Forest Service no longer references a fire season; it now speaks of a “fire year”. “What used to be a three-month job can be eight months-plus of fighting fire, away from your family,” Mayfield says.

That churning workforce is still, all things considered, a market. The federal wildland firefighting force has stayed essentially flat for more than a decade; about 11,000 people work at the forest service, with several thousand more across the interior agencies. For the handful of companies that still make fire boots by hand, that is not, whatever the price tag might suggest, a particularly lucrative model.

No one understands that better than the people making the boots. Shuyler Mowe, CEO of Spokane-based Nicks Handmade Boots, founded in 1964, thinks his boots are, if anything, underpriced. “People are always like: ‘Wow, your boots are $600,’” he says. “These should be, like, $2,000!”

Mowe’s thoughts are less a complaint than an accounting. The Technora fire-resistant thread is notably difficult to work with; the leather used in the boot is considerably thicker than any consumer boot and, consequently, more difficult to shape; the boot is left on a mold, called a “last”, shaping the leather more effectively, for longer than is practical at scale.

“It’s a lot of these little things that add up to a completely different product,” Mowe says. Being overbuilt is the point – everything is thicker and heavier than it strictly needs to be, which helps a pair bounce back after multiple rebuilds and last for years. “You’re paying for the institutional knowledge.”

The birthplace of that knowledge is White’s, the company where Nicks’ founder learned the trade before striking out on his own in the 60s. (“The Coke to our Pepsi,” Mowe jokes.) White’s has been making boots since 1853, longer than the US Forest Service has existed.

Making the boots is a work of craft. It takes 2,000-3,000 pairs before someone is any good at hand-welting, says Eric Kinney, White’s president (and a bootmaker of 26 years). “Everyone thinks they can do it until they try it for a while.” In all but a handful of White’s Boots’ 168 years, the company has been run by a bootmaker.

White’s Smokejumper model is still considered the gold standard; it was first worn in 1939 by Francis Lufkin, one of the country’s first smokejumpers – elite firefighters who parachute in to remote wildfires – and bought for about a week’s pay. Nearly a century later, that’s the cost ratio White’s has maintained for their premier line.

“The price has stayed true to that course throughout its history,” says Kinney. “Seven hundred and seventy-five dollars is probably on the low end for a week’s pay, but that’s what we’re selling them for.”

That price has held even as the business model has shifted. White’s once stocked 6,000 pairs of its hand-welted Smokejumper; now, it sells closer to 1,500 a year. Demand has been redistributed across White’s other construction styles, which still move from 10,000 to 15,000 annually, according to Kinney – but the premium, handmade boot that once defined the company is being squeezed.

For many firefighters, the boots are getting harder to justify. A pair built to last a decade only pays off for someone fighting fire hard and long enough to wear it out – and a younger, increasingly transient workforce means fewer feet will be around to do so.

Mayfield himself made that same calculation; by the time he reached hotshot captain, he says, he had blown through two pairs of White’s in a single season, $600 apiece. Fed up, he moved to Nicks. When those also suffered damage years later, he was convinced to try out the boots that his newer crewmates were turning to: a hunting boot at half the price. His feet, he says, felt good immediately, without the need to break in stiff shoe leather. He hasn’t gone back – but he hasn’t gotten rid of his old boots, either.

“I have a fully rebuilt pair of Nicks sitting in my garage,” Mayfield says. “If I were cutting trees down and all that stuff, I would want people in a taller leather boot, because accidents happen. I fully recommend that.”

Mayfield is far from alone. There are now a number of companies making boots like his new pair: lighter hunting-style boots often manufactured in Italy, without a long break-in period. Many of those boots also sidestep NFPA certification, and may be less durable in the long term. That tradeoff matters less to a workforce that often turns over within a few seasons. To adapt, White’s is preparing to release an Italian-made boot of its own. “It’s a great-looking boot, just not our traditional stuff,” Kinney says.

For his part, Kinney is looking to steward the Pacific north-west boot tradition through his tenure. “I’ve probably got seven or eight years left at the company,” he says. “We’re doing everything we can to do it the same way on the high-end, hand-welted stuff. We’ll see what happens in 10 years.”

There has been genuine movement on the government side. In March 2025, after years of temporary patches, Congress made permanent the first major pay raise in decades, and the current administration has since moved to extend hazard pay to more of the work. But reform reached the pay and stopped at the boots.

A stipend meant to cover boots has sat at $500 since 2020. The most basic piece of equipment the job requires – the one thing between a person and hot ground – is still something firefighters buy themselves, made by a shrinking number of highly skilled hands.

title: Monica Lewinsky has one request for critics nearly 30 years after White House scandal
excerpt:
Activist Monica Lewinsky told Fox News Digital that her personal definition of power has evolved over the years.

Monica Lewinsky has evolved since the White House scandal – and she hopes critics one ...
body_text:
Activist Monica Lewinsky told Fox News Digital that her personal definition of power has evolved over the years.

Monica Lewinsky has evolved since the White House scandal – and she hopes critics one day can, too.

Lewinsky, 53, credited time and patience as her saving graces while reflecting on challenges from her past during an appearance on the "All the Cool Girls" podcast.

"I think that coming into my 50s was amazing and just the shedding of worries," she told co-hosts Laura Brown and Kristina O'Neill.

MONICA LEWINSKY'S LINDSEY GRAHAM TRIBUTE DRAWS CRITICISM AND PRAISE FOR PLACING PEOPLE OVER PARTY: EXPERT

Monica Lewinsky reclaimed her own narrative years after a White House scandal. (Monica Schipper)

"I mean that whole … joke about 'I don't give anymore f---s,' and it's like you really start to give fewer and fewer f---s, and you settle into acceptance in a way that has been really reassuring for me."

Unlike the critics, the podcast host moved on from past discretions to reclaim not only her life, but also her own story.

"In terms of the people who still have old, old beliefs, I wish they would get some new jokes because, I mean, 30 years of the same jokes, Jesus," she said. "Or 28 years. We're not at 30 yet."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Monica Lewinsky pleaded for critics to find a new joke nearly 30 years after highly-publicized scandal. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

Lewinsky was 21 years old when she began an unpaid internship at the White House in July 1995. She turned 22 that summer, and her sexual relationship with former President Bill Clinton, who was 49 at the time, began in November 1995.

It was only after she confided in a Pentagon co-worker, Linda Tripp – who secretly recorded their conversations, which were then used in Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton – when the affair became public fodder.

During a January 1998 White House news conference, Clinton famously denied the affair, and stated, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," and Lewinsky subsequently went into hiding due to public humiliation.

Bill Clinton was impeached while serving as the 42nd president. (House Judiciary Committee/Getty Images)

The subsequent impeachment trial against the 42nd president began in January 1999 and ended Feb. 12. While Clinton was impeached by the house, he was acquitted of perjury and obstruction of justice charges.

While the scandal made headlines for years, Lewinsky only truly began reclaiming her identity in the last decade.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I feel really grateful. I'm really grateful, and I'm excited," she said. "It's when I step away and I look at my own story objectively – or as objectively as one can – it is pretty extraordinary to still be here, like physically still here, and to have been able to help shape how people see me more and understand me more and connect with me in ways that are meaningful. It's bonkers."

Monica Lewinsky previously recalled the toll of receiving negative energy from "billions of strangers" over the years. (Robin L. Marshall)

Themes surrounding authority and control have remained a constant in Lewinsky's life post scandal.

"I think of power in two different ways. There's the power that someone has and they use, that impacts other people's power," Lewinsky explained to Fox News Digital earlier this year.

"Then there's the power that someone has in connection to themselves and that's a lot more like strength."

She added, "People often think of resilience as being linear, and it is so much more like a spiral. You will move forward, you'll go back, and move forward ... you'll go back, and I think it's, again, people have to be patient with themselves."

Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

title: Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war
excerpt:
Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East

Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait o...
body_text:
Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East

Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military as Donald Trump gathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort.

Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports.

The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan.

Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties.

In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targeting Hezbollah tunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast.

Lebanese officials accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents.

Trump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, but increasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections.

On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”.

Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began.

Support in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote. 
 Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans.

Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.

title: Why the under on runs looks like the smart baseball play when Pirates visit the Reds tonight
excerpt:
Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Jared Jones was on his way to making MLB history on Wednesday night, but he found himself in the wrong chapter of the book. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

Yeste...
body_text:
Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Jared Jones was on his way to making MLB history on Wednesday night, but he found himself in the wrong chapter of the book. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

Yesterday did not go as expected. I lost one game between the Giants and Padres as Robbie Ray spun a gem in what could be his last start for the squad. Sometimes you run into that, and all you can do is tip your cap to the other team. I'll suck it up and move on, and hopefully get some of that money back here today as we play the Pirates vs. the Reds.

The Pittsburgh Pirates seem to be in a similar cycle this season. They have one step forward and then one back. I suppose the good news is that they aren't going one step forward and two steps backward. They are exactly at .500 coming into today's game, sitting at 55-55 for the year. The final 52 games of the season will tell the story of whether this year is successful or not. Maybe that's harsh, because this still should be a step-forward season, and one they can use for momentum moving forward.

Pittsburgh Pirates starting pitcher Paul Skenes (30) watches from the dugout in the sixth inning of the MLB National League game between the Cincinnati Reds and the Pittsburgh Pirates at Great American Ball Park in downtown Cincinnati on Thursday, Sept. 25, 2025. (Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

I've written about the importance of Pittsburgh being aggressive in using this window for them to make a consistently good team. If they don't, guys like today's starter, Paul Skenes, will start looking for ways off the team. Skenes is 9-9 for the season with a 3.65 ERA and a 1.06 WHIP. This is the worst season of his young career, but all of his numbers are 31st in the Majors or better. He has been worse on the road than at home, but not terrible. This has been a tough month for Skenes; he has allowed 17 earned runs in 27.2 innings of work. He has faced the Reds twice this season and allowed five earned runs in 10 innings of work.

The Cincinnati Reds took a step back this season after making the postseason. They started the season hot out of the gate. This team was 20-11 after April came to an end. Since then, they have gone 30-46. To start May, they lost eight consecutive games and went 4-13 to start the month. To start the second half of the season, they've gone 8-5. Perhaps the All-Star Break is what the team needed to make some adjustments.

Cincinnati Reds starting pitcher Hunter Greene (21) pitches against the Chicago Cubs in the second inning at Great American Ball Park on May 23, 2025. (Katie Stratman/Imagn Images)

There is more than enough time to make a run at the postseason, but they'll need to get some better performances from their pitching staff. The Reds do have some good pitchers, so the adjustments can be made. Today's starter, Hunter Greene, is one of the better young arms in the league, but he has struggled since he came into their rotation in early July. He has allowed 17 earned runs in 21.2 innings this season. In fairness to him, he has two quality starts and two disasters. Pirates hitters are batting .200 against him over 55 at-bats.

We have two aces on the mound, guys who have, or could someday, win Cy Young awards. However, neither has been exactly impressive when it comes to consistency. Skenes has struggled all month. Greene has allowed 14 earned runs in two starts, and three earned runs in his other two. Which version of these pitchers is showing up?

Jake Fraley #27 and Elly De La Cruz #44 of the Cincinnati Reds celebrate after Fraley hit a home run in the second inning against the Atlanta Braves at Great American Ball Park on June 23, 2023 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Dylan Buell/Getty Images)

The Pirates haven't been playing great baseball lately, so it is really hard to back them, even with Skenes on the mound. The Reds have been terrible at home — 24-30. I think the smarter option here is to take the under eight runs. Both teams know the importance of this game, and both starters will know how crucial it is to give their team a chance. Neither team has great numbers against the opposing starter, so I'll back the under eight.
