title: Angry cruise passengers blast major line over surprise daily gratuity hike
excerpt: Gambling influencer Bobby Rivas, known online as "Bluffin Bob," surprises a Virgin Voyages cabin steward with a $5,000 cash tip after winning at the ship’s casino, sparking emotional reactions from vi...
body_text:
Gambling influencer Bobby Rivas, known online as "Bluffin Bob," surprises a Virgin Voyages cabin steward with a $5,000 cash tip after winning at the ship’s casino, sparking emotional reactions from viewers online.

Passengers of Celebrity Cruises are pushing back after the cruise line raised its automatic gratuity charges with little notice, with some guests threatening to remove their payment of the fees altogether and tip crew members in cash instead.

As of July 29, guests who do not prepay the gratuities will automatically pay between $19.50 and $24.50 per person, per day, depending on their stateroom category, according to the Celebrity Cruises gratuity policy on the company's website.

The increase raises the daily gratuity by $1.50 per person across every stateroom category, according to reports.

AMERICA’S TIPPING CULTURE HAS GONE FROM REWARDING SERVICE TO FEE INSANITY

Under the new rates, guests staying in Inside, Ocean View and Veranda staterooms will pay $19.50 per person, per day.

Concierge Class and AquaClass guests will pay $20.50, while those staying in The Retreat will pay $24.50, the policy states.

Celebrity Cruises passengers are pushing back after the cruise line raised its automatic gratuity charges with little notice. (Guvendemir/Getty Images)

The gratuity program is part of crew compensation and reflects industry standards, while guests frequently credit crew members with making their vacations memorable, a spokesperson from Miami-based Royal Caribbean Group — of which Celebrity Cruises is part — told Fox News Digital.

The cruise line also automatically adds a 20% gratuity to purchases including beverages, beverage packages, specialty dining, room service, minibar items and spa and salon services, according to the policy.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

While many passengers said they support the idea of tipping crew members, they criticized the timing of the announcement, saying they were notified on the same day the higher rates took effect.

"Today is July 29. Nice bit of lead time," one Reddit user wrote about what happened. "I might have paid in advance for the savings... but this sucks."

The increase raises the daily gratuity by $1.50 per person across every stateroom category. (jewhyte/Getty Images)

"Not 'We're raising gratuities in a week, you can pay the current rate until then.' It's RIGHT NOW," another user wrote.

Several passengers said the cruise line should simply build gratuities into the advertised fare, rather than charging them separately.

"At this point, they just need to include gratuities in their fare like the luxury lines do," one Reddit user wrote.

Several guests said they planned to opt out of the automatic gratuities and instead hand cash directly to crew members, saying they wanted to ensure the money reached the employees who served them.

Several passengers argued the cruise line should simply build gratuities into the advertised fare instead of charging them separately. (Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I've started removing them and spending the exact same amount or more in direct tips," one passenger wrote.

"At least then I know what I'm paying is going directly to the workers."

Not all reactions were negative, however.

"My stateroom attendants have always been great. I don't mind the gratuity going up," one Reddit user wrote.

"Celebrity could have rolled this out more thoughtfully, though."

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Pakistan coal mine explosion kills at least 11, traps dozens
excerpt:
A coal mine explosion has killed at least 11 miners in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, with dozens of people still missing.

The bodies of the miners were recovered hours after the deadly blast on Th...
body_text:
A coal mine explosion has killed at least 11 miners in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, with dozens of people still missing.

The bodies of the miners were recovered hours after the deadly blast on Thursday, which is believed to have been triggered by a buildup of methane gas, said government mine inspector Ghani Baloch.

Rescue workers assisted by the Provincial Disaster Management Authority and other emergency responders will continue the search until all of the trapped miners are accounted for, Baloch added.

A total of 36 people were in the collapsed part of the complex at the time of the explosion, the province’s chief inspector of mines, Muhammad Atif, said.

Twenty-eight were still missing by late Thursday night, with rescue efforts ongoing at a depth of 4,000 feet (1,219 metres), he told the news agency Reuters.

“We are hopeful to find some miners alive, but chances are low,” he said.

The explosion occurred in Sorange, a remote area near the provincial capital Quetta.

Accidents are common in Pakistan’s coal mining industry, particularly in Balochistan, where many mines lack adequate ventilation, gas monitoring systems and other basic safety measures.

Mineworkers and labour groups have long accused mine owners of failing to enforce safety regulations or provide adequate protective equipment.

Despite the risks and low wages, thousands of miners depend on the coal industry for their livelihoods in Balochistan, which is Pakistan’s largest, but least developed, province, where unemployment and poverty remain widespread.

title: Virginia university says feds did not disclose student’s terror conviction before attack
excerpt:
ROTC cadets at Old Dominion University described stabbing and wrestling the attacker who killed Lt. Col. Brandon Shah during a March 12 shooting in Norfolk, Virginia. (Army ROTC)

The Virginia univers...
body_text:
ROTC cadets at Old Dominion University described stabbing and wrestling the attacker who killed Lt. Col. Brandon Shah during a March 12 shooting in Norfolk, Virginia. (Army ROTC)

The Virginia university where a student with a prior ISIS-related conviction carried out a deadly terror attack in March said federal officials did not notify the school about his criminal history before he was re-enrolled as a returning student.

On March 12, Mohamed Bailor Jalloh reportedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire inside an ROTC classroom at Old Dominion University (ODU), killing an Army veteran instructor and injuring two students before ROTC members fatally subdued him.

Jalloh was previously convicted in 2016 of attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State terror group in connection with a plot to target U.S. military personnel.

However, neither his federal probation officer, the FBI, nor any state or federal agency notified ODU of his conviction, the university said.

VIRGINIA MAN CHARGED WITH SELLING WEAPON USED BY OLD DOMINION UNIVERSITY GUNMAN

Mohamed Bailor Jalloh served in the Army National Guard before carrying out the March 12, 2026, shooting at Old Dominion University. (The Intercept)

"Had ODU known about Jalloh’s criminal history, it is highly likely that ODU would have sought his removal from campus due to the risk he posed, particularly to military-affiliated individuals," the independent report said.

The FBI told Fox News Digital on Thursday that it is not the agency responsible for notifying colleges.

"The FBI does not serve as a notification authority for colleges or universities regarding an individual’s criminal history – that is a shared responsibility across state, local, federal and community partners," the FBI said.

Additionally, the bureau noted that Jalloh's terrorism-related convictions were widely publicized by the Department of Justice in 2016 and 2017, with at least three press releases detailing his case still available on the agency's website.

"Furthermore, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia issued several press releases and publicly available information, including a press release when Jalloh was sentenced in 2017 for attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization," the agency said. "The release remains on the Department of Justice website, and can be found through an internet search with multiple links available."

OLD DOMINION UNIVERSITY SHOOTER IDENTIFIED AS MOHAMED JALLOH, FORMER NATIONAL GUARD MEMBER, ISIS SUPPORTER

ODU said that under Virginia law enacted in 2022, public universities are prohibited from asking applicants about their criminal history during the admissions process.

In compliance with the law, ODU said it removed criminal history questions from its applications, leaving the university dependent on voluntary student disclosures or outside law enforcement notifications.

Under Jalloh’s federal supervised release, his probation officer reportedly had the authority to require him to disclose his criminal record to third parties.

However, no such notification was provided to any university office or campus police, according to the report.

"Given that Virginia law requires universities to rely on student self-disclosure, it is even more important that other law enforcement agencies ensure that information that universities need to know to safeguard their students is shared with universities. This critical failure led to tragic consequences here," the ODU report said.

Jalloh also never voluntarily disclosed his 2016 federal terrorism conviction to ODU, according to the report.

Mohamed Bailor Jalloh was identified as the shooter at Old Dominion University on Thursday, March 12, 2026. (AP Photo)

While Virginia law allows public universities to inquire about criminal history after an applicant is admitted, ODU's policy at the time only sent post-admission background questionnaires to first-time students, excluding readmitted returning students such as Jalloh.

According to the campus report, Jalloh first enrolled at ODU as an undergraduate student in 2007. After being academically suspended in 2010, he was readmitted in 2011 following service in the Army National Guard. He briefly took classes through Spring 2012 before stopping for unknown reasons, and was later convicted on federal terrorism charges in 2016.

He then served eight years in prison before being released in December 2024. Afterwards, Jalloh applied for readmission as a returning student and was re-enrolled at ODU in 2025.

After Jalloh’s case exposed a gap in the university's post-admission screening policies, ODU said it officially expanded its post-admission criminal history questionnaire to include readmitted students alongside first-time students.

Lt. Col. Brandon Shah was identified as the instructor killed in the deadly shooting at Old Dominion University on March 12.  (Old Dominion University)

Additionally, the report said nothing else on Jalloh’s readmission application raised any concerns.

Jalloh’s application reportedly listed a private residential address in Sterling, Virginia, rather than a federal prison address. Two professors who taught him in the months before the attack also reported no behavioral concerns.

The United States Probation and Pretrial Services Eastern District of Virginia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Saudi Arabia announces maritime defence alliance to secure vital waterways
excerpt:
Saudi Arabia and 13 other countries have announced the creation of a maritime military coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
...
body_text:
Saudi Arabia and 13 other countries have announced the creation of a maritime military coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

In a statement published on Thursday, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defence said the Multinational Maritime Defense Alliance was established as a framework to strengthen collective maritime defence cooperation.

The states declared their intent to protect freedom of navigation, securing international trade routes and energy supply routes through the three waterways, which form a strategic maritime corridor linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean.

The move comes as the United States-Iran conflict has become focused on the Strait of Hormuz. The virtual closure of the route, which formerly carried about 20 percent of global oil and gas exports, is weighing heavily on the global economy.

In a recent escalation, the Bab el-Mandeb-Red Sea-Gulf of Aden route has come under repeated attack from Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.

The representatives of 43 countries – out of 51 that were invited – participated in the meeting for the establishment of the alliance.

A European Union delegation was included, the Saudi ministry said. The EU already has a naval protection mission, Aspides, in the Red Sea. It is not clear how the Saudi-led coalition would differ.

Turkiye, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt, Pakistan, Djibouti, Somalia, Bangladesh, Yemen, Sudan and the Comoros are understood to be the other signatories to the alliance.

It is notable that neither the United Arab Emirates nor Oman have signed up, despite having similar security objectives amid the conflict centred on Iran.

“The door remains open for other countries to accede to the coalition’s charter after completing their national procedures,” the Saudi ministry’s statement said.

The participating states share a “conviction that maritime security is a shared responsibility and that cooperation and coordination among states constitute the cornerstone for confronting common and transnational maritime threats”, the statement continued.

It did not say what ships or aircraft each country would contribute. However, activities will include sharing intelligence, information and operational planning, as well as conducting joint exercises and maritime operations.

The alliance is “purely defensive in nature and does not target any state”, it noted.

Saudi Arabia is recognised as a founding member of the alliance and home to its headquarters, though the statement did not specify the exact location.

The Houthi rebel group in Yemen imposed a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia last week, disrupting oil shipments diverted to the Red Sea.

Since the start of the war in Iran in late February, and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh has been able to continue to export most of its oil thanks to the East-West pipeline, which connects oil refineries in the country’s east to the terminal of Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.

Saudi exports have to cross Bab al-Mandeb, which is located between Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, whose western province facing the maritime chokepoint is controlled by the Houthis. That gives the armed group a strategic advantage to target ships in the Red Sea.

Approximately 10 to 12 percent of global maritime trade passes through the strait, including millions of barrels of oil per day. It is also one of only two exit-entry points to the Red Sea, the other being the Suez Canal.

Bab al-Mandeb is only 29km (18 miles) wide at its narrowest point, limiting traffic to two channels for inbound and outbound shipments. Therefore, any disruption taking place in the area could cause a new surge in global energy prices.

title: Danica Patrick stuns America with her double-bikini in Europe, NFL Live tackles black coaches & a sad MLB stat
excerpt:

body_text:
Join Dan Dakich at the Indy 500 for an exclusive interview with racing legend Danica Patrick as she opens up about the tragic passing of NASCAR icon Kyle Busch.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Final two days of July, folks. This is it. Let's end the month strong, and get the busy part of the sports calendar started.

That's right. The BUSY part! Thank goodness. I'm so tired of the WNBA being the only talking point right now in sports. Yes, I know baseball is also going on — and we've got a trade deadline coming up — but you know what I mean.

It's exhausting. I'm as guilty as anyone, but I'll admit, I've sort of been worn down by that insufferable league this week. We've got a football game in one week. Let's focus on that. Please?

Welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Danica Patrick gives everyone an update on her summer trip in Europe. Thanks goodness. I was wondering!

Danica Patrick attends the 54th Academy of Country Music Awards at MGM Grand Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas, Nev., on April 7, 2019. (FilmMagic)

What else? I've got NFL personality Kay Adams sending up the bat signal that FOOTBALL is officially back, maybe the most depressing baseball stat of all time, Vic Fangio making the Big Js in Philadelphia SWEAT, and let's check in with the new and improved NFL Live in the post Ryan Clark era!

Wait till you see how they covered Day 1 of NFL training camps.

OK, grab you a slice of cheesecake for National Cheesecake Day, and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

I think I'd put cheesecake right up there with any and all desserts. It's so versatile. You can drizzle it with just about anything, and get away with it.

Anyone here been to a Cheesecake Factory lately? I think I've been only once or twice in my life. You just don't see them down here in Florida, at least where I am.

That being said, it does remind me of the famous Vince Young story from his rookie year where he allegedly spend $15,000 at Cheesecake Factory ... in ONE sitting:

No clue if that actually happened or not, but Lordy, what a night that would be! Not sure how exactly you'd rack up a tab that big at a Cheesecake Factory, but with those menu sizes, I reckon it's conceivable.

What a weird, winding road we've taken to get this class off and running. This is what you get during one of these summer school sessions, though.

Speaking of summer ... let's get this class officially started with Danica Patrick sending up a heater from across the pond:

Danica! Welcome back to the states. You've missed a lot. Wait till you hear about the nonsense going on in the WNBA right now.

Patrick, by the way, takes these summer trips to Europe all the time. I believe this is the third year we've covered this here at OutKick. In fact, two summers ago, I believe we got a Part I and II.

Not 100% sure what's going on with the double-bikini look, but who am I to judge? In fact, according to sources (Google), this "layered" look is all the rage right now.

Singer Dua Lipa apparently made the trend popular last year, and it's now the "unexpected" look taking over the summer.

"Following fashion girls’ penchant for tying bikini tops upside down, it’s a new 'wrong way to wear' that feels oh-so right — and very fun," wrote the fashion website, PureWow.com.

LOS ANGELES, CA - JULY 12: Race car driver Danica Patrick attends The 2017 ESPYS at Microsoft Theater on July 12, 2017 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)

Good to see Danica's mystery boyfriend made the trip, too. Big step for those two lovebirds. Still have no idea who he is, but he was included in the annual Europe trip, which is a good sign.

Can't wait to see where these two go next.

Now, let's head back to the US of A and check in with Eagles DC Vic Fangio, who opened training camp today by pleading the fifth:

"I'm gonna be like Fauci and just take the Fifth Amendment on questions. Did you guys see that? Oh my god. What was the question?"

Amazing. Good stuff here from Vic Fangio. How embarrassing was that Fauci grilling yesterday? Never, ever let 2020 happen again, folks. Goodness, what a miserable time.

Not down here in Florida, of course. But everywhere else. Our Governor called out Fauci's BS about two months into that nonsense, and we never looked back.

Man, I'm going to miss him. DeSantis, not Fauci.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big Thursday night. First up? Might as well stick with the NFL theme today and check in on how NFL Live covered Day 1 of training camps yesterday.

Soap opera actress Donna Mills tells Fox News Digital her secret to staying fit at the age of 82.

Donna Mills is proving age is just a number.

The 85-year-old "Knots Landing" icon is taking fans by surprise with her latest career move — joining OnlyFans.

The actress, who became a television sensation playing the glamorous and ruthless Abby Cunningham on the hit show, said the platform will give her a chance to connect with fans in a more personal way.

'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS SAYS SHE WON'T 'BE QUIET' AFTER CRITIC TARGETED HER MAKEUP AT AGE 85

Donna Mills announced that she's joining OnlyFans this week. (Getty Images)

"I've always appreciated the incredible support and encouragement I've received from my fans over the years. Social media has been a wonderful way to stay connected, but I'm excited to join OnlyFans because it offers the opportunity for a more personal and direct connection," Mills told Variety.

Mills said fans can expect an authentic look at her life off-screen.

"I'll be sharing moments from my daily life, behind-the-scenes glimpses, and engaging with fans in a more meaningful way," she said. "It's simply another platform to spend quality time with the people who've supported me throughout my career while staying true to who I am."

JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'

Mills poses for a portrait session circa 1984. (Maureen Donaldson / Michael Ochs Archives)

OnlyFans executives noted the Hollywood veteran isn't switching up her image.

"This is not about changing who she is. It is about giving her longtime fans more access to the personality, style and behind-the-scenes moments they already love," Andy Bachman, CEO of OnlyFans owner Creators INC., said.

"Donna has always been fearless and ahead of her time. She told me, 'YOLO — let's do it,' and that perfectly captures her attitude. She is approaching OnlyFans on her own terms and creating a space that feels authentic, personal and completely true to her."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Mills recently spoke about how she keeps up her looks and health. (Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for Universal)

The announcement comes just weeks after Mills shared the habits she credits for looking and feeling her best at 85.

"I think the people out there have to realize it takes work. You can't just decide, 'Oh, I'm going to look good,' you know?" Mills said on Kara Mayer Robinson's "Really Famous" podcast. "I didn't wake up looking like this."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The actress said she works out almost every day and regularly plays tennis, adding that a lifetime of exercise has helped her avoid many of the physical ailments that often come with aging.

Mills said that working out consistently has saved her from needing hip or knee replacements. (Getty Images)

"I started out as a dancer, so I know how essential that is, and I know what it means for your body," she said. "And I know that I don't have, at my age, any of the things that happen to the body, you know? I mean I've not had any knees replaced or hips replaced or anything, you know, because I never stopped working out."

Mills also urged people not to give up on fitness as they get older.

"And so, for years they don't work out," she said. "You can't get that back. You really can't. You can start to work out again ... but you've lost something in that time."

Mills rose to fame on "Knots Landing," starring on the long-running series from 1980 to 1989. With her signature blonde hair, bold fashion and stellar performances, her character became one of television's most memorable soap opera villains.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Netflix sued for $105m over stolen Nicolas Cage war thriller
excerpt:
Makers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles office

Netflix is being sued for $105m over the theft of a hard drive including an unreleased Nicolas ...
body_text:
Makers of unreleased $45m film Fortitude sue after hard drive stolen from streamer’s Los Angeles office

Netflix is being sued for $105m over the theft of a hard drive including an unreleased Nicolas Cage war movie.

The streamer’s Los Angeles office was the target of a theft involving a number of hard drives, one of which contained a copy of second world war spy thriller Fortitude.

The makers of the $45m-budgeted film are now suing Netflix over the loss.

“Netflix disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards,” a spokesperson said in a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter. “While we do not own the rights to Fortitude, we take content security seriously and have taken extra measures to support the film-maker and his team. This includes conducting a thorough investigation and offering to monitor known piracy sites for any unauthorized distribution or sale.”

Netflix reportedly received a copy of the film in June after expressing interest in promotional materials at the end of last year. A digital copy was then sent so the film could be screened internally with the film’s producers instructing Netflix to delete the files afterward.

Sean Berney, head of Netflix film acquisitions, wrote in an email that it was a first for the company to be the subject of such a theft. “We’ve been working through this with our security teams to no luck,” he added. “Our piracy teams are on high alert with the breach and will monitor.”

Netflix is accused of failing to disclose details of whether a police report was initially filed as well as later declining a request by the film-makers to involve the LAPD after they filed their own report.

The lawsuit claims that any future sale of the film has now been put in jeopardy with any international release strategy and awards campaign paused.

“The resulting damage to plaintiffs is profound,” the lawsuit said, according to Page Six. “Through its mishandling of the film and subsequent dismissiveness, Netflix has jeopardized plaintiffs’ investment of over $45m and the significant value of the film itself. Netflix has also deprived the film, its cast and its creators of the opportunity to bring their work to market and receive recognition that a properly marketed worldwide release likely would have generated.”

Fortitude is a London-set espionage thriller focused on British intelligence operatives changing the course of the second world war. Cage stars alongside Matthew Goode, Michael Sheen and Ben Kingsley. The film is directed by Simon West, whose previous credits include Tomb Raider and The General’s Daughter.

Martin Scorsese was at one point attached to the project but was then the subject of a lawsuit claiming he took $500,000 from first-time screenwriter Simon Afram to help develop the film but failed to do so. Scorsese’s lawyers called it a “classic example of the novice film-maker who refuses to appreciate the stark difference between expectation and reality in the film-making business”. It was later settled.

“I spent seven years of my life bringing this incredible true story to the screen,” Afram said in a statement. “But this film was never mine alone. It belongs to the extraordinary cast and their performances of a lifetime that deserve to be seen and recognized. It represents the moment these artists have earned.”

title: House panel demands classified briefings on noncitizen voting, alleged Chinese election interference
excerpt:
A "Fox News Sunday" panel examines the controversy surrounding non-citizens found on New Jersey's voter rolls, with over 400 reported to have cast ballots.

The House committee charged with overseeing...
body_text:
A "Fox News Sunday" panel examines the controversy surrounding non-citizens found on New Jersey's voter rolls, with over 400 reported to have cast ballots.

The House committee charged with overseeing American elections is demanding more information on allegations of noncitizens voting in federal races.

The Committee on House Administration is requesting classified briefings on foreign interference in U.S. elections after President Donald Trump raised such concerns during a speech earlier this month.

"Reports of noncitizens casting illegal ballots continue to emerge, undermining election integrity and public confidence in American elections," wrote Committee Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis.

"To inform potential legislative reforms, the Committee therefore requests a Member-level, classified briefing from DHS on the number of non-citizens registered to vote across the country and cyber vulnerabilities present in current voting systems. Please contact the Committee by August 13, 2026, to set up a briefing to be held in the month of September. The Committee also requests that any relevant documents be provided alongside the briefing."

HOUSE REPUBLICANS CONFRONT NJ GOVERNOR OVER 6,600 NON-CITIZENS REGISTERED TO VOTE IN ALLEGED SOFTWARE FAILURE

Inside the Fairfax Government Center in Fairfax, Va., a voter is seen at a polling station during a referendum on redistricting. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

The classified briefing requests were sent to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI Director Kash Patel and acting Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Bill Pulte.

In the letters, Steil cited Trump's claim that DHS discovered roughly 278,000 noncitizens registered to vote as well as recent revelations that New Jersey mistakenly added 6,600 noncitizens to its voter rolls in 2023 and 2024.

TRUMP ACCUSED CHINA OF AN 'ELECTION SECURITY NIGHTMARE' BUT THEN UNDERCUT HIS OWN WARNING

Steil also pointed to Trump's comments in his speech on Chinese-led "cyberattacks on election infrastructure."

President Donald Trump during a primetime address to the nation in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 16, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The committee's release said there were "serious concerns about the security of American elections."

The briefing requests come less than 100 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide which party controls both houses of Congress for the latter half of Trump's final term in the Oval Office.

Republicans have long raised concerns about the security of American elections, which Democrats have argued are attempts to undermine people's faith in those elections.

House Administration Committee Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., holds a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2025. (Anna Rose Layden/Getty Images)

It is already a federal crime to vote in elections as a noncitizen, but the GOP is pushing for further guardrails such as proof of citizenship in the voter registration process and a federal voter ID standard at the polls.

To date, no evidence has been found that noncitizens have swayed the outcome of any federal election.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Fauci takes the Fifth 111 times – and the media still rush to defend him
excerpt:
Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley joins Fox News Digital to break down all the latest news on Dr. Fauci's hearing.

As I wrote this week, Dr. Anthony Fauci was not the only one taking the Fifth on ...
body_text:
Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley joins Fox News Digital to break down all the latest news on Dr. Fauci's hearing.

As I wrote this week, Dr. Anthony Fauci was not the only one taking the Fifth on Wednesday over his record during the pandemic. The media largely invoked the same privilege to avoid self-incrimination for its years of deifying the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

Across the cable networks, hosts and guests were having the vapors as Republican senators pummeled Fauci over his COVID-19 policies and the glaring contradictions found in his diary entries. Some, like Dr. Scott Ratzan, echoed Fauci's previous claim that any questioning of his judgment was an attack on science.

Once again, Fauci had every right to invoke his Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. That does not mean it was the right thing to do. Fauci already had a pardon that notably extended back to 2014, when his agency approved gain-of-function research at the Wuhan lab in China.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Any prosecution would be difficult in light of the pardon. It would not be impossible, since he could be charged with perjury for any false statements. Yet that was the same threat that existed during countless prior hearings involving Fauci.

So, what was the difference now? The answer is found in diary entries and other evidence that contradict Fauci's public statements on subjects ranging from the lab theory to school closures. It is not that Fauci would have been tripped up by false answers, but that he did not have any obvious answers to some of these criticisms.

Instead, Fauci invoked the privilege 111 times. That fell short of the record of Vito Genovese, who invoked the privilege 150 times.

Rather than address the long list of criticisms and contradictions involving Fauci, the media rallied around the scientist. Fauci was portrayed as something akin to the St. Sebastian of Science, taking barbs and arrows for his faith.

It did not matter that more than 1.2 million Americans died, the economy shut down and millions of children were prevented from going to school based on these alleged errors. Fauci would remain silent rather than risk being charged with false testimony.

'WOKE' SMITHSONIAN EXHIBIT LIONIZES EMBATTLED FAUCI AMID CONSERVATIVE SCRUTINY OF MUSEUM'S MESSAGING

On CNN, Dr. Scott Ratzan, editor-in-chief of the Journal of Health Communication, repeated Fauci's much-maligned claim from June 2021 that "attacks on me, quite frankly, are attacks on science."

On Wednesday, Ratzan declared, "This is an assault on science and scientists, and, unfortunately, Dr. Fauci is in that seat. Thirty-eight years of service to the country, one of the best-known scientists in infectious disease, unfortunately, has taken a lot of heat..."

Dr. Fauci owes the public explanations, including the millions who lost loved ones. Instead, he refused to take the risk of being accused of perjury.

It was a maddening statement, repeated by many, that treated Fauci as inviolate, if not infallible. Fauci was wrong about issues that imposed tragic costs on this country. When confronted with policies such as school closures, he insisted he had never recommended them while privately admitting he had.

Fauci owes the public explanations, including the millions who lost loved ones. Instead, he refused to take the risk of being accused of perjury.

ANTHONY FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY AND EMAILS SHOW HE KNEW LOCKDOWNS FAILED AND PUSHED MASKS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Fauci is no St. Sebastian. Notably, Sebastian remained silent in public to conceal his faith, but when discovered by Diocletian, he remained faithful. The price was to be shot through with arrows, but he somehow survived.

After being nursed back to health by Irene of Rome, he immediately confronted Diocletian in public and denounced his abuses. For that act, he was beaten to death with clubs and tossed into a sewer.

Fauci spoke endlessly in public and remained silent only when asked to address the contradictions in his diaries and the costs of his alleged errors.

What is also frustrating to many is the reappearance of figures who toed the line on prior narratives about masks, the virus's origin and other issues.

They are now claiming to be victims for being asked to account for evidence that they were wrong. As Dr. Scott Atlas, a neuroradiologist and health policy fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution, has laid out, many of those who abused dissenting scientists faced no repercussions after those scientists were largely vindicated by later research.

During this period, dissenting scientists were barred from social media, removed from positions and vilified for expressing views, despite later being vindicated on subjects ranging from the lab origin of the virus and the efficacy of masks to the six-foot rule, natural immunity and school closures.

Former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Dr. Anthony Fauci listens during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions, asserting his Fifth Amendment right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Many previously echoed Fauci's view that questioning these conclusions was an attack on science. One leading columnist wrote a piece titled "The COVID lab leak claim isn’t just an attack on science, but a threat to public health."

When courageous scientists put their careers at risk — and some lost their positions — to voice their opposition to Fauci's policies, neither he nor these acolytes said a thing in their defense. Fauci did not defend them as fighting for science and the need to challenge orthodoxy. When their views were later embraced, they received no apologies, let alone reinstatement.

For my part, I am not interested in hearing from scientists who remained silent as their counterparts were vilified, shadow-banned and fired. Their deep faith in science did not prompt them to defend those with opposing views, even though orthodoxy is the very antithesis of scientific thought.

Again, Fauci has every right to remain silent, but that does not make it right.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JONATHAN TURLEY

Jonathan Turley is a Fox News Media contributor and the Shapiro Professor of Public Interest Law at George Washington University.

He is the author of the new book "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution" (Simon & Schuster, Feb 3, 2026), on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.

He is a nationally recognized legal scholar who has written extensively in areas ranging from constitutional law to legal history to the Supreme Court. He has written over three dozen academic articles that have appeared in a variety of leading law journals.

Professor Turley also served as counsel in some of the most notable cases in the last two decades including the representation of whistleblowers, military personnel, former cabinet members, judges, members of Congress, and a wide range of other clients.

Professor Turley testified more than 50 times before the House and Senate on constitutional and statutory issues, including the Senate confirmation hearings of cabinet members and jurists such as Justice Neil Gorsuch. He also appeared as an expert witness in both the impeachment hearings of President Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.

Professor Turley received his B.A. at the University of Chicago and his J.D. at Northwestern. In 2008, he was given an honorary Doctorate of Law from John Marshall Law School for his contributions to civil liberties and the public interest.

A Georgia mother used a gas pump to fend off a man accused of trying to snatch her children at a gas station, with newly released surveillance video capturing the frightening encounter.

FAMILY STOPPED ALLEGED CHILD KIDNAPPER AS POLICE SAY STAFFING SHORTAGE DELAYED RESPONSE UP TO 40 MINUTES

Surveillance video shows a mother pumping gas moments before police say a shirtless man approached her family's vehicle and attempted to grab her children at a Shell station in Marietta, Georgia. (WAGA)
