title: George and Amal Clooney evacuate France home as wildfires spread across Europe
excerpt: Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergenc...
body_text:
Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergency. France has deployed the military, and the Tour de France has been shortened as firefighters battle the massive blazes.

A representative for George Clooney confirmed the evacuation to People and shared a letter the couple sent to Brignoles Mayor Didier Brémond

The couple and their 9-year-old twins left their home in Brignoles, in France's Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region, as fires threatened large swaths of the Mediterranean, the outlet reported. A representative for George Clooney confirmed to People that the couple sent a letter to Brignoles Mayor Didier Brémond before leaving.

"Dear Didier, At this point we have no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment," the letter began.

DEADLY FRENCH WILDFIRES THREATEN MISSILE PLANTS, NUCLEAR SITES AS FOURTH HEATWAVE LOOMS

George and Amal Clooney reportedly evacuated their home in southern France as fast-moving wildfires spread across parts of Europe. (Joe Maher; AP Photo/Emma Da Silva)

"As we evacuate Brignoles we want to emphasise 2 things, first we hope you and the people of our city are safe and second that Amal and i are committed to making sure that whatever happens to our village, we are part of this community and we’ll be part of making it whole," the letter continued. "We love Brignoles and our friends who live there."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Clooney's representatives for additional comment, including whether the family has safely evacuated and if there is any update on the condition of their home.

The evacuation comes as wildfires continue to scorch southern Europe.

EUROPE'S FIRES REVEAL DEADLY MIX OF RECORD HEAT, HUMAN ERROR, ARSON AND LAND MISMANAGEMENT

George and Amal Clooney reportedly left their home in Brignoles, France, as wildfires spread across the region, according to People. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for History)

As of Wednesday, an uncontained wildfire roughly four times the size of Paris was burning across southwestern France.  The blaze was separate from the fire threatening the Brignoles area, where about 3,000 people were evacuated. Fires also continued to threaten parts of southern Europe, and three firefighters died in Greece as crews battled extreme heat, drought and strong winds, according to The Associated Press.

More than 300,000 people have been forced to evacuate in France and Spain, including residents and tourists.

Temperatures climbed to nearly 104 degrees Wednesday in France's Gironde region, where the country's largest wildfire prompted the evacuation of roughly 220,000 residents and vacationers at its peak. While many have since returned, tens of thousands remain displaced.

HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE

Clooney and his family spend much of their time on a farm in France. (Christopher Anderson/Esquire)

In an October 2025 interview with Esquire , Clooney said he and Amal chose to raise their family on a farm in France to give their children a quieter upbringing away from Hollywood.

"A good portion of my life growing up was on a farm, and as a kid, I hated the whole idea of it," he said. "But now, for them, it’s like—they’re not on their iPads, you know? They have dinner with grown-ups and have to take their dishes in. They have a much better life."

Clooney also said he was "worried about raising our kids in L.A., in the culture of Hollywood."

"I felt like they were never going to get a fair shake at life," he said. "France — they kind of don’t give a s--- about fame. I don’t want them to be walking around worried about paparazzi. I don’t want them being compared to somebody else’s famous kids."

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Campaigners rail against ‘plundering’ of ancient Kent woodland to make way for quarry expansion
excerpt:
Forty hectares of Oaken Wood could be razed after it was identified as potential site of expansion by Reform-run council

It was at the confluence of seven forest paths that Allison Sweetman came to a...
body_text:
Forty hectares of Oaken Wood could be razed after it was identified as potential site of expansion by Reform-run council

It was at the confluence of seven forest paths that Allison Sweetman came to a stop. Trees rose on all sides, save for a recently coppiced section to the north-east. The noon heat had silenced most birds, but the quiet was peaceful.

“This is what they call Seven Wents,” she said. For centuries, the people of Kent had travelled this way, from East Malling to Barming, from Ditton to Teston, for church, commerce and friends. “It’s on maps going back 400 years.”

That may be about to end. Seven Wents is part of Oaken Wood, 40 hectares (100 acres) of which is all but condemned to be razed. Developers want the stone beneath. Kent county council, led by Reform, this month voted to include it in their mineral sites plan. That makes it a potential site of expansion for the quarry next door.

The council said its decision does not yet amount to planning permission – the plan needs government approval before that can happen. However, it does mean that they have identified the ground beneath the forest as an essential source of stone for building and restoration projects. Now, campaigners are on the march.

Continuously wooded since at least 1600, Oaken Wood is a plantation on ancient woodland site (paws), which means it is the site of an ancient forest that has been replanted. For centuries it has been worked as a sweet chestnut coppice, with whole sections felled in rotation, allowing the stumps to regrow.

The sun shone almost directly overhead, but the air was cool beneath the forest canopy. Sweetman, who knows the wood intimately and is a Green party councillor for the local area, led the way through green corridors flanked by almost impenetrable stands of plantation forest to another recently coppiced site.

With her were Rachel Rodwell, also a Green councillor; Julie Read, a campaigner; and Brontie Ansell, the managing director of Lawyers for Nature, who has been supporting their campaign to save the woods.

“It takes about seven years before they’re ready to be coppiced again,” Sweetman said. “And in the time they grow they’re actually absorbing more carbon from the atmosphere than a fully grown tree … Likewise their roots continue to grow, and that absorbs the surface water from rain.”

The wood is also a critical ecological site, supporting wildlife including dormice, nightjars and owls. Alongside the sweet chestnut coppices stand veteran trees, including old oaks. Bluebells and other wildflowers bloom here. The soil itself, bound by a mycorrhizal network that has built up over aeons, is a seed bank and a carbon sink, says Kent Wildlife Trust.

It is what is beneath the soil that developers want. Kentish ragstone has been quarried since at least the time of the Romans and was the building block of Roman London. Kent county council says it is crucial for the conservation of ancient buildings, including the Tower of London and Canterbury cathedral. Their opponents say it is wrong to place the conservation of the built environment over the conservation of nature. The council declined to comment.

There is little to distinguish Oaken Wood from any other ancient woodland site, said Ansell. “It’s protected in exactly the same way, legally, because it’s not just about the fact that there’s newish growth of trees,” she said. “You’ve got all the soils, you’ve got the fungi, you’ve got all of the wildlife.” But, she added: “It is still irreplaceable. You couldn’t just create this somewhere else.”

But that is precisely the plan, should development go ahead. Gallagher Group, which runs the Hermitage quarry, said the soil beneath the wood would be “translocated and retained” – dug up and moved elsewhere. The “non-native” chestnut trees, which have been in the UK since the time of the Roman empire, would be removed and they would “put back more than double the tree planting in restored, native woodland”.

Campaigners are sceptical. “Essentially they lift a lot of the topsoil … and then they chuck the topsoil down somewhere and go: ‘There you go, it’s been replaced,’” Ansell said. Rodwell added: “It’s just treated like garden topsoil. And they forget the interconnectivity. It’s not [just] the soil, it’s a living system.”

Last year, more than 25,000 voiced their concerns in a consultation on the plan. The Woodland Trust and Kent Wildlife Trust are opposed. Maidstone borough council, on which Sweetman and Rodwell sit, are to pass a rights of nature motion soon.

On from Seven Wents, the group walked north, towards the site of the existing quarry, which swallowed up 80 acres of the wood just over a decade ago. With every step, the sounds of machinery grew louder.

Soon the air was thick with the smell of exhaust fumes and the ra-ta-ta-ta-tat of pneumatic hammers against stone. White powder, apparently rock dust, lay in a film across the forest foliage. A dead shrew lay on the floor. “You can breathe it, you can smell it, you can feel it in your lungs,” Rodwell said.

In the course of just a few short minutes’ walk, the group had travelled from a sylvan idyll to what felt like a zone of war against nature.

“We’re treating nature as a commodity or a resource and we’re forgetting we’re part of the same system. And it’s this sense of entitlement that we can just strip it away and plunder it,” added Rodwell.

“It’s replicated across the country, across the globe.”

title: Polls open in Greater Manchester mayoral byelection overshadowed by new PM and Farage’s antics
excerpt:
Labour’s Bev Craig expected to win contest that lost column inches to Andy Burnham’s ascent and Reform UK leader’s self-imposed Clacton vote

Voting has begun in the biggest byelection in British poli...
body_text:
Labour’s Bev Craig expected to win contest that lost column inches to Andy Burnham’s ascent and Reform UK leader’s self-imposed Clacton vote

Voting has begun in the biggest byelection in British political history, with more than 2 million people eligible to choose Andy Burnham’s successor as Greater Manchester mayor.

In normal times, such a large and politically significant byelection would have dominated the headlines for weeks, particularly as senior Labour figures only weeks ago feared losing the prize mayoralty to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.

But now Labour’s Bev Craig is expected to win comfortably in a contest that has been largely overshadowed by Burnham’s rapid ascent to prime minister.

Labour has benefited from a Burnham bounce in the polls and Reform UK’s focus has shifted 200 miles south-east to Clacton, where Farage is fighting a self-imposed parliamentary byelection against Count Binface.

A poll by More in Common this week gave Craig, the leader of Manchester city council, a 20 percentage point lead over Reform UK’s Sian Astley. Most of the 1,000-voter survey was carried out before Burnham became prime minister. The Greens were in third on 14 points, just ahead of the Conservatives.

The contest was triggered by Burnham winning the Makerfield byelection on 18 June, meaning he had to step down as mayor of the most powerful combined authority outside London.

The mayor of Greater Manchester controls a £3bn annual budget and powers across housing, health, policing and transport, centred around a city that has grown faster economically than anywhere else in the UK over the past decade.

The byelection is taking place under the supplementary voting system, which means that if no single party achieves 50% then second-choice preferences will come into play.

Labour is widely seen as having an advantage under this system as it is more likely to be picked as the second choice for Green, Lib Dem and even some Conservative voters. Reform UK, by contrast, cannot count on such broad support.

The More in Common poll found that Labour’s lead would stretch to 30 points if Reform UK finished second, as Craig is the most popular second choice for most Greens and a sizeable chunk of Conservatives.

Anything short of a strong second-place finish would be a blow to Reform UK, which won more than 100 seats in Greater Manchester in the May elections, including all but one of the 25 up for grabs in Wigan – the council of Burnham’s new constituency – and 18 out of 19 in Tameside, both once solidly Labour areas.

One senior Labour figure said the party expected to do much better in these areas in the mayoral byelection, having won back voters who backed Reform UK only two months ago in what many saw as a protest vote against Keir Starmer.

Reform UK’s projected vote has fallen nationally in recent weeks – the hard-right party was overtaken at the top of the polls by Labour this week for the first time since March 2025 – as Farage faced intense scrutiny over his funding.

Green sources believe the Greater Manchester polls underestimate the party’s popularity and that its support extends far beyond Manchester city centre, where it won a swathe of previously Labour seats in May and which is near the parliamentary constituency of Gorton and Denton it won in a February byelection.

For the Greens, which won 7% of the vote against Burnham when the Greater Manchester mayoralty was last contested in 2024, a doubling or more of their vote share would demonstrate the party’s ability to expand outside its recently formed urban-liberal power base.

All parties will be scrutinising Friday’s result with a view to the next set of local elections in May 2027, when a third of all seats in the 10 Greater Manchester boroughs are up for grabs in what could present a real electoral headache for Burnham.

Reform UK will be eyeing up control of councils including Bolton, Wigan and Rochdale next year, while the Green party will hope to threaten Labour’s half-century grip on control of Manchester city council, where it is now the second biggest party.

Yet campaigners in both Labour and Green camps say awareness of Thursday’s vote is low, potentially complicating pollsters’ predictions. The result is expected on Friday afternoon.

Unlike in Makerfield and Gorton and Denton, there is little obvious sign on the streets that such a mammoth byelection is under way, largely due to the huge expense of campaigning across a region of 2 million voters.

Given some weary residents will have voted three times in the past five months, many expect turnout to be lower than the 32% in 2024. Yet if even a third of registered voters cast their ballot, the verdict of 600,000 people is worth taking seriously.

title: Viral finger-clicker suspended as cricket storm remains in global spotlight
excerpt:
An English ‌amateur cricketer at the centre of allegations ⁠of finger-clicking ⁠trickery has been suspended and will not play “for the foreseeable future”, his club has said.

The fielder, dubbed “Cli...
body_text:
An English ‌amateur cricketer at the centre of allegations ⁠of finger-clicking ⁠trickery has been suspended and will not play “for the foreseeable future”, his club has said.

The fielder, dubbed “Clicky Ponting” on social media in a punning nod to former Australia captain ⁠Ricky Ponting, allegedly tricked umpires by clicking his fingers to make the sound of a ball nicking the bat as deliveries were missed and caught by ‌the wicketkeeper.

The video footage went viral on social media and made international headlines.

Saltburn Cricket Club, run by volunteers, said on Wednesday in a statement it was treating the allegations “with the utmost seriousness”.

“The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended ⁠and will not play again ⁠for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation.”

It said initial discussions between club ⁠officials and the North Yorkshire and South Durham league had already taken ⁠place.

The league said on Tuesday ⁠it had received a formal complaint “regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25th July 2026”.

Saltburn said it had ‌been a distressing and stressful experience for all concerned and asked for “personal boundaries” to be respected.

The club ‌are ‌top of the Division Two table with 10 wins from 15 matches.

Historically, cricketers – even at the highest level of the game – have been accused of trying to trick umpires with noises, including chomping on a biscuit, to fool umpires into believing the ball hit the bat.

Cricket cheating allegations have even extended to dirt being applied to the ball, for which former England captain Michael Atherton was once fined, and the use of bottle tops to scuff the ball.

Both were attempts to create extra swing for the quick bowlers.

title: War and shortages push Gaza hospitals to breaking point
excerpt: Gaza City, Gaza Strip – On the dialysis floor of Gaza City’s al-Shifa Hospital, the same scene repeats itself every day. Machines run without stopping. Patients sit in closely arranged rows. Medical t...
body_text:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – On the dialysis floor of Gaza City’s al-Shifa Hospital, the same scene repeats itself every day. Machines run without stopping. Patients sit in closely arranged rows. Medical tubes connect bodies to life for limited hours.

In one of the chairs sits 14-year-old Ruwaa Muntasir Abdul Karim, from Jabalia in northern Gaza. Her small size makes her stand out in a crowded room full of patients.

Her left hand is connected to a dialysis machine. Her eyes follow the movement of the medical staff inside the room, but she remains silent throughout the session – the whole process has exhausted her.

Her father, Muntasir, sits next to her, his face full of concern.

“My daughter used to walk and play before the illness. Her life changed after surgeries and dialysis,” Muntasir said. “Every dialysis session keeps her alive. Any interruption causes her severe fatigue and shortness of breath.”

But the hospital department keeping Ruwaa alive is struggling itself, under the constant pressure to support the thousands of people in Gaza in need of treatment, without the necessary resources to do so.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has decimated the Palestinian enclave’s medical sector through repeated attacks on hospitals, including al-Shifa, as well as harsh limitations on what can enter Gaza.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, 50 percent of dialysis machines in Gaza have stopped working completely due to an ongoing shortage of sodium bicarbonate, which is required to operate the machines.

On top of that, the number of hospitals equipped to handle kidney failure patients has been reduced to four from seven, with some, such as the Noura al-Kaabi Dialysis Centre, destroyed by Israeli forces during the war.

The consequences mean that kidney failure patients are dying at an alarming rate in Gaza. Ministry of Health statistics show that there were 1,200 kidney failure patients before the war. That number has now dropped to about 700 patients after the death of more than 470, due to missed dialysis sessions and a lack of essential medications, according to the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights.

Osama Abu Rahma is head of the kidney department at Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza, one of the four hospitals that can still treat kidney failure patients in Gaza.

“We have 51 dialysis machines, but 25 of them are completely out of service,” he said, adding that this had placed severe pressure on the facility and negatively affected the 240 patients receiving treatment there.

The facility has been forced to reduce both the number of sessions provided each week and the duration of each session.

Medical complications among patients are rising: general weakness, shortness of breath, heart and lung problems, and dangerously high levels of potassium in the blood.

Abu Rahma is clear – the situation is putting the lives of hundreds of patients at direct risk.

Back at al-Shifa Hospital, Ruwaa stares at the ceiling. Some of the older patients are asleep; the scene inside the ward reflects a state of continuous exhaustion.

Ruwaa’s father, Muntasir, watches the medical monitor next to her constantly, fixing his gaze on the vital indicators.

He remembers when she was in better health, but her condition has since deteriorated. Her weight has dropped from 65kg to 35kg (143 pounds to 77 pounds), while the number of dialysis sessions she receives each week has fallen from three to two.

The only permanent solution – a kidney transplant – should be within reach. “Everything is ready for a kidney transplant,” Muntasir said. “Her mother is the donor. The tests match.”

But Israel is once again hindering Ruwaa’s treatment. Her trip abroad – Israel must approve all journeys out of Gaza – has been pending for six months. The reality of Gaza’s healthcare situation means that the transplant cannot take place in the enclave. And so Ruwaa must wait.

The lack of access to treatment evident at Gaza’s dialysis facilities is a common issue across the Strip’s healthcare system.

Israel’s war has left more than 43,000 people in Gaza with injuries described by the World Health Organization (WHO) as “life-changing” – including thousands of severe limb injuries that resulted in amputations and permanent disabilities.

Even after being treated for the initial injury, Palestinians in Gaza who have had amputations then face a new challenge: rehabilitation and access to basic mobility aids.

In Khan Younis, southern Gaza, physiotherapist Aya al-Shaltouni explained that the lack of prosthetics, wheelchairs, and crutches has become part of patients’ daily reality, with demand far exceeding supply.

“There is a clear and major shortage of mobility aids,” al-Shaltouni said. “Many patients wait for long periods, and some do not receive anything.”

She noted that this shortage does not only affect physical suffering but completely changes the patient’s life path. Ultimately, access to proper rehabilitation tools can determine whether a patient is able to recover to some form of independent life.

“We create treatment plans, but without proper assistive tools we cannot reach the desired results, and progress remains limited,” al-Shaltouni said.

The physiotherapist added that rehabilitation centres in Gaza are operating with limited resources and cannot compensate for the major shortage in essential equipment, leaving a clear gap in the treatment system.

Zaki Jumaa Salem Abu Harb has seen both sides of the coin. A 60-year-old farmer from northern Gaza, he lost a leg after being injured in an Israeli attack in March 2025.

“My whole day changed in a moment,” he said. “After the attack, I woke up injured and couldn’t move like before.”

Having spent his life active in his fields, his movement was suddenly severely limited, and he depended on others to move between home and hospital, with continuous medical visits and follow-ups.

But after months of waiting, he was recently able to receive a prosthetic limb. It’s been a major positive development, but Zaki is also aware of the others – WHO estimates that there are between 5,000 and 6,000 amputees as a result of the war as of October 2025 – most of whom are still waiting for prosthetics.

“There are many people who don’t have wheelchairs or crutches,” Zaki said. “They are forced to find any way to move, sometimes using a tree trunk or any piece of wood.”

“There are children who lost their limbs,” he added. “Some of them don’t have devices to help them walk properly. When I see them, I feel deeply affected. You feel they’ve been deprived of the simplest rights in life.”

With Gaza’s limited resources, the focus has often been on prioritising treatment for physical injuries. But the healthcare crisis in the Palestinian territory does not stop there, and extends into the psychological and social traumas that are the natural result of nearly three years of devastating war.

On the outskirts of al-Aqsa Hospital, inside a small tent surrounded by other displacement tents, 22-year-old Hadeel sits in front of a simple fire used for cooking. Instead of sitting in a university classroom preparing for exams, Hadeel divides her time between caring for her seven siblings, securing their needs inside the tent, and trying to continue a life that stopped at the beginning of the war.

At the beginning of the war, her family took shelter in a relative’s house, before a violent strike hit a nearby home, forcing them to flee in chaos and panic.

“That night of the bombing, we woke up to the sound of children and women screaming … we were running and trying to find each other,” Hadeel paused, and then continued. “My mother was under the rubble … only her fingers were visible. Neighbours helped us pull her out. The sound of my mother calling our names and her image never left me.”

While her mother was receiving treatment, Hadeel found herself fully responsible for her siblings as the eldest daughter. Life became a constant shift between grief and endurance, and responsibilities that never stop.

“Some days I feel depressed, and other days I have to continue and take care of them,” Hadeel said.

Over time, signs of psychological stress became more visible, including frequent crying episodes, difficulty sleeping due to constant thinking, and the weight of memories and responsibilities.

Hadeel added that she suffers from emotional exhaustion, where daily responsibilities mix with recurring memories of bombardment and loss of safety, making moments of calm rare and interrupted.

Hadeel’s is just one story among many in Gaza. According to Asil Abu Shaweesh, a 27-year-old psychologist in central Gaza, the mental health crisis in the enclave is widespread, due to the war, repeated displacement, loss of loved ones and destruction of homes.

“Everyone in these conditions needs psychological support, and this need will continue, making mental health a priority that needs to be responded to,” Abu Shaweesh, who works with an international organisation providing psychological support, said.

Abu Shaweesh has observed widespread disorders, including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, insomnia and panic attacks, as well as issues among children such as bedwetting, aggressive behaviour, difficulty concentrating, recurring nightmares and excessive attachment to caregivers.

And while providing support to people suffering from these disorders is essential, Abu Shaweesh noted that mental health workers face major challenges, including “constant psychological pressure, lack of safety, high demand, shortage of resources, and difficulty reaching patients”.

But Abu Shaweesh knows how important the services she provides can be – and is willing to be stretched thin to provide people with the help they need.

title: Judge orders Amy Winehouse’s father to pay nearly £1m to her friends
excerpt:
Mitch Winehouse ‘knowingly and deliberately’ made unfounded allegations against Naomi Parry and Catriona Gourlay, judge says

The father of British music sensation Amy Winehouse has been ordered to pa...
body_text:
Mitch Winehouse ‘knowingly and deliberately’ made unfounded allegations against Naomi Parry and Catriona Gourlay, judge says

The father of British music sensation Amy Winehouse has been ordered to pay £950,000 (US$1.26m, A$1.82m) to his late daughter’s friends, who he unsuccessfully sued for auctioning the singer’s clothes and other items.

Mitch Winehouse earlier this year lost a case in the high court in London against two of Winehouse’s friends who auctioned dozens of her clothes and other possessions years after her death.

The late singer-songwriter, who was famed for her distinctive husky voice and enjoyed global meteoric success at a young age, died in July 2011 from alcohol poisoning, aged just 27.

The late singer’s former stylist Naomi Parry and her friend Catriona Gourlay denied acting dishonestly in auctioning the items they said were given or lent to them.

Her father argued they had no right to sell the items.

The 155 items, which were auctioned between 2021 and 2023, included clothes, ballet slippers, handbags, earrings and makeup owned by the late singer, as well as a dress she wore on her final tour in 2011.

During the trial, the London court was told Winehouse’s friends “took advantage” of her father’s forgetfulness and pocketed more than $1.4m in sales.

The judge found the two women had not deliberately concealed any of the items from Winehouse’s father, who “knew all along” about the intended sale and only pursued them for money after it was completed.

“The claimant chose to bring an inherently weak claim, pursue it aggressively and relentlessly to the end, and make serious and unfounded allegations against the defendants which significantly damaged their reputations, career prospects, financial security and health,” judge Sarah Clarke said Wednesday.

“The fact that he knowingly and deliberately did this to two young women who had stood faithfully by Amy … makes his unreasonable conduct particularly serious.”

In the April ruling, the judge noted that Amy Winehouse was known for her “extraordinary generosity towards her friends and also those she barely knew”.

title: Storm co-owner suspended after incident with Sophie Cunningham fans as star breaks silence on controversy
excerpt:
Fans at a WNBA get into a heated altercation that allegedly stemmed from differing stances on Sophie Cunningham's support of the protection of women's sports.

Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton ha...
body_text:
Fans at a WNBA get into a heated altercation that allegedly stemmed from differing stances on Sophie Cunningham's support of the protection of women's sports.

Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton has been fined and suspended from attending the team's next five home games, the WNBA confirmed to Fox News Digital.

The suspension and fine come after Keaton allegedly called a pair of teenage Sophie Cunningham fans "f—ing insane"  during a game on Tuesday, independent Seattle-based journalist Brandi Kruse told Fox News Digital. Kruse was in the arena and accompanied the girls, who were there to watch Cunningham and the Indianaa Fever take on the Storm.

Cunningham addressed the incident involving Keaton in an X repost of Fox News Digital's report late Wednesday night.

WHITE HOUSE DEFENDS WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AFTER SHE SPEAKS OUT IN SUPPORT OF PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

"I truly believe there is a safe space and love for EVERYBODY. Biological girls, biological boys, trans women, and trans men. Everyone is welcome at my table! You can disagree and still be kind. Bravo to those girls for standing up for what they believe. You’ll be hearing from me soon yay for gifts. Truly embarrassing of the co-owner. Unfortunately shows the type of leader she is," Cunningham wrote.

Storm majority owner Ginny Gilder issued a statement Wednesday apologizing for the co-owner’s comments during the game.

"We are aware one of our co-owners made comments to two fans in attendance at last night's game. We apologize that this happened. Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome, and we remain committed to creating an inclusive environment where every fan is treated with respect," the statement read.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM RALLY ROCKS WNBA GAME AS 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS FACE COUNTERPROTEST

Two girls went to the game wearing XX-XY Athletics gear to celebrate Cunningham coming out in support of saving women's sports, and even got to sit court-side. But the night took a dark turn, and now they are viral martyrs. The Storm put out an apology after a team co-owner allegedly shouted insults at the girls during the game. Additional footage, distributed by Fox News Digital, of them in a confrontation with another fan at the game has ignited further outrage.

The incident drew so much attention that famed "Harry Potter" author J.K. Rowling even cast judgment on the night that is bound to live in WNBA infamy.

Rowling and other prominent social media users amplified the girls’ account of the incident.

The night began with a rally outside Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle to celebrate Cunningham's recent public stance.

A small group of counterprotesters supporting transgender inclusion also gathered outside the arena.

Kruse, who helped organize the event and went into the game to accompany the girls during portions of the night, said she saw Storm players make mocking gestures toward them. Separately, the girls alleged that Keaton approached them and used profane language.

"They were giving them thumbs down — like, to their faces," Kruse said.

Kruse said the girls then told her that an older woman associated with the Storm had approached them, yelled at them and called them "f---ing insane."

The girls later pointed out the woman sitting directly across from them beside Storm legend and team co-owner Sue Bird, according to Kruse. When Kruse alerted an arena security guard, she said the guard identified the woman as "one of the owners of the team."

Kruse later identified the woman as Keaton, who has previously been publicly identified as a member of the Storm’s ownership group.

Kruse said she pressed security to confront the woman, arguing that the alleged conduct violated the arena’s code of conduct. Climate Pledge Arena prohibits abusive or obscene language and says violators may be ejected.

"Had this been any other fan under any other circumstances who swore at and called some teenage girls ‘f---ing insane’ until they cried, they would’ve been ejected," Kruse said.

Kruse said one of the girls broke down in tears during the game after the alleged exchange.

"I look over at halftime, and she’s sobbing," Kruse said. "They were so excited for those seats, like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see some of their favorite players. They stayed up the night before making signs."

Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever handles the ball against Flau'jae Johnson of the Seattle Storm during the first half at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle, Wash., on July 28, 2026. (Getty Images)

Kruse also claimed that the girls were not forced to put down their signs in support of Cunningham, despite online rumors, but that they chose to put them down after the alleged harassment.

"The report that they told the girls to put those signs away is not true," Kruse said. "The girls put their signs away because of what happened with Celeste, and they just felt so scared and uncomfortable, they decided not to hold them anymore."

Before the game, the Storm said it was aware of the planned demonstration and was "tracking it closely." The team said it remained committed to providing a safe and inclusive environment for all guests.

Storm head coach Sonia Raman addressed the rally after the game but did not discuss the allegations involving the girls.

"We always want to be an area where people feel welcome coming into this building," Raman said, adding that the organization coordinated with arena security. "From what I understand, that was successful."

A fan holds an Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham sign during the first half between the Seattle Storm and the Indiana Fever at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle, Wash., on July 28, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The comments came before Kruse publicly detailed the allegations involving the teenagers.

The Fever, meanwhile, distanced the organization and Cunningham from the rally. A team public relations representative interrupted when head coach Stephanie White was asked about the gathering during her postgame press conference.

"Neither our organization nor Sophie had any knowledge of this demonstration and no contact with its organizers," the representative said.

The representative added that the Fever remained united around winning games and building its fan base before directing reporters back to basketball questions.

Neither Cunningham nor Clark was made available to reporters after the game. Mitchell and Monique Billings appeared beside White instead. When White was asked about the rally, she also said the team and its players were not aware of it and had not been in touch with the organizers.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: NSW to send paramedics not police to some mental health emergencies after multiple deaths
excerpt:
Mental health experts to triage triple zero calls, but not all of the changes will be implemented 24/7 or statewide

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email...
body_text:
Mental health experts to triage triple zero calls, but not all of the changes will be implemented 24/7 or statewide

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

New South Wales will send specialist nurses rather than police to some mental health emergencies after the state announced long-fought-for reform in the wake of multiple deaths at the hands of police.

Rose Jackson and Yasmin Catley, the mental health and police ministers, announced on Thursday a statewide change to how triple zero calls are triaged, with a new team of mental health experts assessing mental health calls 24/7 in a bid to provide better support.

The change, funded by $270m over ten years, will also establish a hub providing real-time clinical advice to NSW Ambulance first responders and assisting them in making safer decisions.

This will be bolstered by eight new mental health teams that will provide a health-led response to call-outs and include a paramedic and specialist mental health nurse. But this initiative will only operate 12 hours a day and won’t be statewide.

Outside those 12 hours, police or existing responses such as the co-response model known as Police Ambulance and Clinical Early Response (Pacer) – which has been criticised by advocates for not operating 24/7 and statewide – will respond.

The mental health minister, Rose Jackson, said reform, which was shaped by the UK’s “right person, right care” model, was “only the beginning” and could be scaled statewide.

“We’re committing $270m as a first step. But I recognise that mental health crises don’t happen within neat 12-hour windows. They’re things that can occur any time of day, any day of the week,” she said.

Police and government had been under pressure to enact reforms after fatalities while people were in mental health distress. This included 42-year-old Jesse Deacon, who lived with schizophrenia and was fatally shot by police at his home in a public housing estate after he was reported to be self-harming in July 2023.

Deacon’s mother, 82-year-old Judy Deacon, has since become one of the state’s loudest voices for change in pushing for change, and has called for mental health experts to triage triple zero calls.

Deacon welcomed the change as an important first step that might have saved her son’s life.

“I think the outcome might have been different,” she said. “Me and other victims’ families will be closely watching and making sure it will end up making a difference.”

Police will continue to be the lead responder in instances where there’s a risk to safety, such as if someone is armed with a knife.

Grace Cameron-Lee, a senior solicitor in the police accountability practice at Redfern Legal Centre, welcomed the change but said NSW police training and operational changes that prioritise de-escalation techniques “remains critical”.

Asked on Thursday if the reform would include more training for police, Catley said: “Police are trained in mental health. That’s a component of their training in Goulburn now, but … they are not mental health clinicians, and that has to be recognised.

“This model is exactly what we need to ensure that those people who are experiencing a mental health incident get the right care.”

Dr Pramudie Gunaratne, the chief executive of the Australian Society of Psychiatrists, also welcomed the reform, describing it as “a stronger front door into the mental health system”.

But, she said, “a front door is only useful if there’s a house behind it” and urged more funding for community mental health support.

“Without enough community mental health services, people will still find themselves stuck in the cycle of crisis, emergency response and discharge, instead of receiving the sustained care they need to recover,” she said.

Jackson has been under pressure to release analysis into the mental health system which is expected to have outlined the resource gaps in the system.

She said on Thursday she planned to release the report publicly but didn’t give a timeline.

“There are gaps in the system, particularly in community mental health care. And yes, this is about a different response for crisis and emergency … It’s obviously preferable if we can invest earlier so that we don’t get to that crisis point.”

title: ‘Warring kingdoms’: cofounder of religious Reformers compares NSW Liberal party factionalism to Braveheart
excerpt:
Robert Assaf tells Icac that Angus Taylor wasn’t ‘that involved’ but the federal opposition leader ‘definitely wasn’t opposed’ to work of conservative group

A member of a group of young conservative ...
body_text:
Robert Assaf tells Icac that Angus Taylor wasn’t ‘that involved’ but the federal opposition leader ‘definitely wasn’t opposed’ to work of conservative group

A member of a group of young conservative Liberal power brokers being investigated for allegedly soliciting illegal donations has compared their factional work to Mel Gibson’s Braveheart – and said they “didn’t think the law applied to us” when it came to political funding.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday heard from Robert Assaf, the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.

Icac is investigating whether Liberal figures, including Assaf, “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch-stacking”. The Reformers allegedly wanted more conservative policies on issues including same-sex marriage, transgender rights, abortion and euthanasia.

Assaf, 30, who admitted to being one of two founding members of the Reformers in 2017, said the group was started in the context of a factional split in the Liberal party between the religious conservative hard right and the centre-right.

“My observations at the time were, the right faction was like – I’m not sure if you’ve seen Braveheart – but like these warring kingdoms, and they would slaughter each other, and then every now and then they’d come together for a big fight,” Assaf said.

While branch-stacking is not of itself illegal, Icac is investigating whether the alleged conduct of the Reformers involved possible offences under NSW’s Electoral Funding Act. Asked about his knowledge of the laws governing donations, Assaf told Icac that the group “didn’t think the law applied to us”.

“Because it was an electoral law, we’re not campaigning in elections in that sense,” he told counsel assisting peggy Dwyer SC.

“We’re internal Liberal party machinations. My understanding the whole way through was, until very recently … was it’s internal. It doesn’t count as anything to do with electoral laws or any other law.”

He defended the Reformers, which includes members being investigated over a second allegation: that they took $2m in payments from the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for outcomes sought by Nassif.

“The Reformers sound really spooky in the media right now, but it was just a bunch of 20-year-old people trying to figure things out,” Assaf said.

Assaf appeared after two days of evidence from former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, who was associated with the group but has not been named in allegations against the Reformers.

After being mentioned during Whitelaw’s examination on Tuesday and Wednesday, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, dodged further questions on Thursday after denying he had ever donated to the Reformers.

“I’ve answered these questions yesterday. I’m not going to give a running commentary on it,” Taylor said. The federal Liberal leader is not accused of wrongdoing.

On Thursday, Assaf claimed Taylor was one of several state and federal Liberal politicians who were aware of and supported the Reformers’ work.

“Angus was around it, but I don’t think he was really that involved,” Assaf said. “He definitely wasn’t opposed.”

He said the former NSW Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, whose brothers Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet are named in the Icac allegations, was “pretty absent in the whole thing, but supportive from what I understood”. Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.

The commission heard Assaf went to the same independent Catholic schoolas Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet, as well as another member of the Reformers, Jeremy Greenwood.

After spending a year in a Catholic seminary, Assaf later worked in federal parliament for various ministers, senators and MPs, including Tony Abbott, who the commission heard gave talks at recruitment events hosted by the Reformers.

He described having an “icky feeling” about getting involved in politics, but said he was convinced to join the Liberal party after attending a 2015 talk at the Sydney University Liberal club by NSW upper house member Damien Tudehope, against the Safe Schools program, whose stated aim was to keep gay and transgender students safe.

Assaf, who described Tudehope as “a warrior for the values that he cared about”, said the politician subsequently gave numerous talks at events hosted by the Reformers.

Tudehope, who is not accused of wrongdoing, stepped aside from his role as shadow attorney general and Liberal upper house leader after being called as a witness by Icac.

The inquiry heard that Assaf and fellow Reformer, Christian Ellis, started the group in 2017, after forming a strong friendship while working together on the No campaign for the same-sex marriage plebiscite.

The inquiry heard that adopting the model that had seen Assaf recruited, the group began to organise talks on conservative issues, aiming to sign up new members afterwards.

Dwyer on Thursday showed Assaf a draft document sent to him by Ellis which detailed a plan to recruit 5,000 Christian conservative members to the party to take control of the NSW division of the Liberal party, which had 4,000 members at the time.

Assaf said the main aim of the Reformers was “policy change” but increasing the number of members in the Liberal party was “certainly part of the process”.

Asked about a stated aim “to take over left-wing branches through stealth”, Assaf said “ideally, we would not want to take branches through stealth”.

“I prefer to be a front stabber than a back stabber,” he added, stating the group’s intention was to create a “broad church” within the party. Assaf said they wanted to “change the terrible situation of factionalism”.

“Christians obviously don’t like lying,” he said. “But there was a strategy to it, and some people needed to be more comfortable with that than others.”

title: UK government reviews why police ceding criminal cases to US military
excerpt:
Exclusive: ministers and police chiefs examining how cases involving US military personnel on UK soil are handled after Guardian revelations

The UK government and police chiefs are reviewing the proc...
body_text:
Exclusive: ministers and police chiefs examining how cases involving US military personnel on UK soil are handled after Guardian revelations

The UK government and police chiefs are reviewing the process through which US military personnel accused of committing serious crimes on UK soil are avoiding the British justice system.

The effort, involving multiple government departments, is examining why UK police forces, which have primary responsibility for investigating such cases, have been ceding jurisdiction to US military investigators.

Such decisions pave the way for alleged perpetrators to be tried in a US military court martial process, an alternative justice system in which victims are often not given the same protections as they would get in a British court.

The government and police reviews were launched after the Guardian uncovered a series of cases in which British police forces allowed the American military to take over investigations into allegations of serious sexual offences.

When the first case was revealed in June, Downing Street said it was “very concerning” that UK authorities were not involved in the prosecution of an American fighter pilot accused of raping and strangling a British woman, Sarah Steele, in his apartment after they met on a dating app.

After Cambridgeshire police allowed US military police to take control of the case, the pilot, Capt Jacob Wulfson, was prosecuted in a court martial on a US airbase in Suffolk. The jury, an all-male panel of air force officers, convicted Wulfson of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted him of sexual assault.

Victims of sexual attacks by US military personnel that would meet a common definition of rape in the UK are finding that their attackers are instead being prosecuted for lesser offences.

Under the set of laws that govern US forces, known as the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), the crime of rape carries a narrower definition than that adopted by the British courts, meaning many cases are charged instead as sexual assault.

Wulfson was given a six-month sentence which he is serving at the US base RAF Lakenheath.

In recent weeks, Home Office and justice ministers met Steele to discuss her case and whether changes should be made to how UK police and prosecutors handle cases involving US military personnel.

A government spokesperson said Steele had “shown incredible bravery in coming forward” and ministers had “committed to identifying and learning any lessons from this case to ensure that victims are supported and treated with the seriousness, dignity and compassion they deserve”.

The spokesperson said officials were working closely with the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) “to look at the guidance in place to ensure that cases are correctly referred to the Crown Prosecution Service for advice”.

Ministers have promised to press the US government for a full account of what happened in the Wulfson case. In a statement, the Foreign Office said it had “been engaging with the US on this matter”.

The Guardian has unearthed several other cases involving US air force personnel who avoided UK courts despite their alleged crimes occurring while off duty. In each, local police handed over the investigation to military prosecutors, sometimes within days of receiving a report of a crime on UK soil.

Hannes Marschalek allegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girl and four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He admitted a charge of indecent conduct after negotiating a plea bargain at a court martial. The conviction was later quashed on technical grounds.

Tyrion Davis allegedly raped two British woman in Suffolk. He was convicted of one count of sexual assault when he was court martialled but acquitted of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.

James Loubeau, who was accused of a “spree” of rapes and sexual assaults in East Anglia, drugging some women and breaking into the homes of others, also avoided the British courts.

He was acquitted at a court martial where he was tried over allegations from just one of the six women who accused him of attacking them. He was later convicted in a court in Miami over another woman’s allegations, after an FBI investigation into his alleged attacks on women in England.

Suffolk police had handed over the Loubeau case to military prosecutors just 11 days after two British women contacted the force to say he and another US airman had drugged and raped them after a meeting in a nightclub.

In response to the Guardian’s reporting on such cases, Gavin Stephens, the chair of the NPCC, has written to all chief constables in England and Wales to ensure forces understand their legal obligations in cases involving visiting US forces.

A source familiar with discussions in government said ministers were alarmed to learn that UK police forces may not be seeking advice from the CPS before handing over investigations to the US military.

Under legislation dating back to the 1950s, visiting US armed forces in the UK can prosecute their own personnel if the offences were committed while they were on duty or against another member of the military, its property, or a dependant such as a spouse or child.

In all other cases, the British police have the first option on whether to launch an investigation into visiting US military personnel. However, the cases uncovered by the Guardian suggest the US has pushed to take control of investigations over which it does not have primary jurisdiction. British police appear to be acquiescing to these requests.

Two police forces – Suffolk and Cambridgeshire – are conducting their own reviews of how they handle investigations involving US military personnel.

In a statement, Cambridgeshire police said: “We are conducting a policy review being led by our investigation standards department.” The force added that the review was looking at cases going back to 2018, and it did not yet know how many there had been.

Suffolk police said: “We are in the process of reviewing the decision-making surrounding the transfer of primacy to the US air force and around case transfer practices more generally.”

More than 12,000 US military personnel are stationed in the UK, operating from at least 15 bases and facilities. The largest concentration of personnel is at two US military installations in Suffolk, RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall. Large numbers of US forces live in the surrounding areas, including in Norfolk and Cambridgeshire.

Concern about US service personnel avoiding the British justice system has been raised by MPs from across the political parties. Nick Timothy, the Conservative justice spokesperson, said Wulfson “should have been fully investigated by the English police and prosecuted in our courts”.

Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrats’ justice spokesperson, said: “The British public expect crimes committed in England to be prosecuted in the English courts under English law. That expectation should not change simply because the accused is a member of the foreign military.”

Responding to a question in parliament about the Steele case earlier this month, the justice minister, Sarah Sackman, said: “Our thoughts are with the victim, and with the other victims whose experiences have subsequently come to light.”

title: A quarter of young Africans believe USAID cuts could be positive, survey finds
excerpt:
Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influence

A quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US coul...
body_text:
Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influence

A quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US could have a positive impact, saying that losing foreign money will force leaders to confront and solve their own challenges, according to a new survey.

In Ghana and Nigeria, almost half (41% and 40% respectively) of young people aged 18 to 24 were optimistic, with Liberia not far behind (37%). A further one in 10 (11%) young people were uncertain about the impact, according to the African Youth Survey, which interviewed almost 5,000 people across 16 of the continent’s 54 recognised countries.

The Trump administration announced in early 2025 that it was eliminating more than 90% of USAID’s foreign contracts and $60bn in overall US assistance around the world. US foreign aid had been designed to play a critical role in tackling poverty, hunger and inequality worldwide.

Other countries, including Britain, France and Germany, have also been slashing aid budgets. The UK announced in February 2025 that the aid budget would be cut from 0.5% of gross national income to 0.3% in 2027, its lowest level as a percentage of national income since records began. The UN target is 0.7%.

Ivor Ichikowitz, whose South African family foundation commissioned the report, said: “The big picture [from the survey] is that the youth is concerned about governments that are overly influenced by foreign powers. What they’re saying is that African governments need to take agency and responsibility for their own reality.”

Africa has the youngest population in the world, with 70% of sub-Saharan Africa under the age of 30, according to the UN. The median age of the continent is 19 years and six months. By 2030, Africa will be home to more than 40% of the world’s youth.

The sudden USAID cuts were met with public outrage and pushback from development and humanitarian organisations. They caused the closure of vital services, including maternity clinics, and medicine shortages at a time when UN agencies are struggling to find money for their humanitarian work and food insecurity has been worsened by the climate crisis.

According to the survey, nearly half of African youth (46%) did believe the closure of USAID would have a damaging impact on their countries, with healthcare services and disease prevention seen as the areas most affected. This anxiety is highest in Mozambique (76%), followed by Kenya (63%) and Rwanda (63%), where youth feel the cuts will disproportionately affect the most vulnerable members of society.

Degan Ali, executive director of Adeso, an African non-profit incubating ideas and enterprises to lower aid dependency, said that while the cuts were carried out in a “hugely irresponsible and inhumane” manner, she was not surprised that a significant proportion of young people saw positivity there. “I think it’s a reflection of the general feeling. A lot of people find aid very demeaning,” she said. “They didn’t feel that the aid was being used for the right things and there is a sense of ‘We can do this for ourselves’. The younger generation feel like our leaders are the duty bearers and are supposed to be handling the needs of our communities.”

She said people believed that the aid that comes into a country is not going to the right causes or the right people. “There’s all this money going into the development sector, but they’re not really seeing major changes on the ground,” she said. “The younger generation is very politically active and more savvy. They are pushing back and trying to hold their leaders accountable.”

She also said that the youth was looking towards African role models on the continent, a move exemplified by the popularity of Burkina Faso’s military leader, Ibrahim Traoré, who portrays himself as a pan-Africanist figure leading his nation out of the clutches of western imperialism and neocolonialism.

“He is one of the more popular leaders across the entire continent of Africa,” said Ali. “There are matatus (minibus taxis) that have his name on in Nairobi, Kenya. The youth see that he is turning around a very poor country and that he really cares about his people. That further motivates young people to protest and say, ‘We don’t need aid, we have enough resources in our country and we need our leaders to behave differently.’”

Hibak Kalfan, executive director of Near, a network of civil society organisations from the global south, said the shuttering of USAID had led to the closure of initiatives and organisations across the whole continent, but had also created the opportunity to reconsider resources and sustainability. “It has put a real light on the fact that [organisations] have been highly dependent on bilateral external funding for years, and the future of aid will depend on a diversity of resources,” she said.

title: ‘Lenin was an enemy of humanity’: Why Kyiv wants to put Cossack chief statue in place of Soviet leader
excerpt:
Removal of Soviet-era statues sped up when Russia seized Crimea in 2014, and since Putin’s 2022 invasion has moved at pace as Ukrainians question their identity

Since 2013 the plinth at the bottom of...
body_text:
Removal of Soviet-era statues sped up when Russia seized Crimea in 2014, and since Putin’s 2022 invasion has moved at pace as Ukrainians question their identity

Since 2013 the plinth at the bottom of Taras Shevchenko Boulevard in Kyiv has been eerily empty. The scruffy monument is daubed in white paint and graffiti. Someone has stuck a Ukrainian trident where Lenin once stood, gazing down during the years of Soviet communism. A crowd toppled the sculpture during Ukraine’s Maidan revolution, which ousted the pro-Russian government, and smashed it with sledgehammers.

In June, Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed putting a new figure on the plinth: Ivan Mazepa, a Cossack military and political leader, who broke with Moscow and fought for Ukraine’s independence. “I am certain that where Lenin fell, Mazepa will stand firm,” Zelenskyy said. He spoke next to a bust of Mazepa in the Pechersk Lavra, an ancient Kyiv monastery hit by Russian missiles.

The proposed swap of Lenin for Mazepa has triggered a lively debate about monuments and what they say about changing national identity. After winning independence in 1991, Ukraine removed large numbers of Soviet-era statues and renamed streets as part of “decommunisation”. The process sped up in 2014 when Russia seized Crimea and fighting began in the Donbas, and moved even faster after Vladimir Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion that aimed to scrub Ukraine from Europe’s map.

Nataliia Kryvda, a professor of the history of culture at Taras Shevchenko National University in Kyiv, said Ukraine was going through an unfinished period of decolonisation. “The USSR absorbed national cultures. It tried to make a single nation of Soviet citizens. Russia today looks at Ukraine and says we are one people. It isn’t true. We have our own mindset, historical destiny, beliefs and dreams. Our identity is a dynamic process,” she said.

Standing next to the ex-Lenin plinth, Kryvda said she was in favour of a Mazepa monument. “Why not? He’s our leader. Each culture needs to mark its space with memorials. They objectify memory,” she said. She described Mazepa as a “contradictory personality” and not an “ideal hero”.

“He really was a friend and political partner of Russia, right up until the moment he dramatically changed his life and history,” she added.

As hetman, or head, of Cossack Ukraine, Mazepa sought to balance the demands of neighbouring Moscow and Warsaw. In 1708, the Russian emperor Peter the Great refused to protect Ukrainian territory from invading Swedes. Mazepa abandoned the tsar and formed an alliance with the Swedish King Charles XII, an act that ended in defeat and led the Bolsheviks to call modern Ukrainian patriots “Mazepists”.

“Mazepa was the architect of European Ukraine,” Kryvda said.

In his speech at the Pechersk Lavra, Zelenskyy said Russia had smeared Mazepa for centuries, depicting him as a traitor. Their goal, he said, was to make Ukrainians “view their own history through the eyes of others”.

Alim Aliev, a writer and Crimean Tatar campaigner, said Ukraine was belatedly recovering its identity. “We are reclaiming our own voices and names,” he said. He cited the example of the 20th-century Ukrainian poet and dissident Vasyl Stus, whose image will appear in September on a new 2,000 Hryvnia note. Stus studied in Donetsk, the eastern Donbas city occupied by Russia, and led Ukraine’s national revival. He died in 1985 in a Soviet prison camp.

In Aliev’s view, Ukraine was now speaking about its past “without mediators” and said it was appropriate that statues of the 19th-century Russian poet Pushkin had been taken down across the country. “He had a totally imperial view of Crimea,” Aliev said, citing Pushkin’s narrative poem, The Fountain of Bakhchisarai. “He exoticises Crimean Tatars and describes us from a colonial perspective.” Of the Mazepa statue, he added: “I don’t think it’s a controversial idea.”

Last month workmen took away a monument to another Russian literary giant Mikhail Bulgakov. It had stood since 2007 outside the house where Bulgakov lived, in one of Kyiv’s most attractive streets, St Andrew’s Descent. Kyiv’s city council voted to remove it. Other plaques to Bulgakov, born in Kyiv to a Russian family when it was part of the Russian empire, have already been taken down, including one outside the university where he studied medicine. Bulgakov’s museum – housed in the writer’s home – remains open.

The museum’s director, Liudmyla Habianuri, said she was not opposed to the sculpture’s removal and dismissed a petition to keep it as “bland”. She acknowledged that Bulgakov had written negatively about Ukrainian nationalist forces in his Kyiv novel The White Guard, set in the winter of 1918-19, amid revolution and war. She stressed, however: “Bulgakov was a witness to his times. And a satirist. He didn’t like anybody. That included communists and priests.”

Habianuri said Russia’s war had prompted Ukrainians to ask: “‘Who am I?’ It’s a very painful question,” she said. “If I speak Russian and watch Russian films and the Russians are killing me then I must give all that up. Then I’m Ukrainian. And if I’m Ukrainian, I must become Ukrainian as quickly as possible.”

This has led people to join the struggle for identity, she said, either via social media or by attacking monuments.

Bulgakov, she said, was a frequent subject of such struggles. “Right now there is a table with only two columns: plus or minus. As a Russian, who didn’t write from the perspective of Ukraine’s defenders, Bulgakov can’t get a plus sign.”

Habianuri said a process of “simplification” was under way but was delighted when demonstrators pulled down the Lenin statue, saying: “The man was an enemy of humanity itself.” Mazepa, she said, was a “unique person” who had inspired a notable poem by Lord Byron. But she questioned whether the plinth was a fitting spot for a memorial.

“I understand it’s a quick jab at Russia. But it’s not the right place for a hero,” she said. “The Germans hanged people there during the second world war.”

Unlike Lenin, the Bulgakov statue was carefully packed up and returned to the family of its late sculptor, Mykola Rapay. His daughter, Kateryna, declined a request from the Guardian for the work to be photographed at its new location. She said she had given official guarantees that the monument would remain “out of public space”.

“These are not my whims,” she said. “The sculpture is not my property. I am the guarantor of its preservation.”

Over at the Pechersk Lavra tourists walked past the new Mazepa bust, which has been erected in front of a fountain and a pleasant shady garden. It sits next to the complex’s 11th-century Dormition Cathedral, used in medieval times for the burial of prominent figures. Last week a boy photographed his father next to the new monument.

Mazepa, a patron of the arts, donated money to pay for the cathedral’s baroque renovation. In June, a Russian drone crashed into its roof, causing a fire, and blackening external pictures of saints. Other icons and religious artefacts were rescued.

One Ukrainian visitor, Olena Polishchuk, said she had come to the Lavra from the UK, where she has lived since Putin’s big invasion. What did she think of Mazepa? “He’s a famous man. I’m glad he’s being commemorated. He’s an important part of our history,” she said.
